gre.s: The two economists' forecasts are sharply ____, one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession.
gre.clue: one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession

en: Ecstatically happy
hook: ELATED: ELEVATED with joy.
story: Elated. At midnight, Nadia's phone buzzed with an email from Germany. She opened it, read the first line, read it again, and screamed. Full scholarship. She ran into her parents' room, jumped on the bed, hugged her mother, called her grandmother, and danced in the kitchen until two in the morning. She was elated: ecstatically happy and excited. Think: elevated with joy, floating above the ground. It is the opposite of crestfallen.
example: She was elated to receive the news of her promotion.

gre.s: The team was ____ after the unexpected victory, celebrating late into the night in the streets of their small town.
gre.clue: celebrating late into the night

en: To fill with delight; to charm
hook: EN-CHANT: like a magical CHANT that casts a spell.
story: Enchant. Every winter, an old storyteller visits Joya's village. He sits under the banyan tree and tells tales of clever tigers, foolish kings, and flying horses, changing his voice for every character. The children sit silent for hours, eyes wide, forgetting to blink. Even the adults stop to listen. He enchants them: fills them with delight, charms them as if by magic. An enchanting smile captures every heart. Think of a magical chant.
example: The children were enchanted by the magician's tricks.

gre.s: The village's winding lanes and flower-covered cottages never fail to ____ visitors, many of whom return year after year.
gre.clue: many of whom return year after year

en: Firmly established and difficult to change
hook: EN-TRENCHED: dug deep into a TRENCH, impossible to move.
story: Entrenched. The government banned dowry decades ago. Yet in some villages, families still quietly exchange cash, furniture, and motorbikes at weddings. Change is slow because the custom is entrenched: firmly established and very difficult to change. Picture soldiers dug deep into a trench, impossible to move. Entrenched beliefs, entrenched interests, entrenched corruption. Reformers must dig them out patiently, one family at a time.
example: Corruption was deeply entrenched within the government.

gre.s: Reformers found it difficult to challenge the ____ bureaucracy, whose habits and privileges had been established over generations.
gre.clue: established over generations

en: Originating from a distant foreign country; strikingly unusual
hook: EXOTIC: EXternal, from the outside world.
story: Exotic. At the international food festival, Sara tried Ethiopian injera, Peruvian ceviche, Korean kimchi, and Moroccan tagine, each more surprising than the last. Meanwhile, foreign visitors crowded around the Bangladeshi stall, photographing panta bhat and shutki as if they were rare treasures. Exotic means originating in a distant foreign country, or strikingly unusual. What feels exotic depends on where you stand. Think: external, from outside.
example: The market sold exotic spices from all over the world.

gre.s: The botanist travelled to remote islands in search of ____ plants that had never been described in any European catalogue.
gre.clue: had never been described in any European catalogue

en: Taking unfair advantage of people or resources for selfish benefit
hook: EXPLOITATIVE: EXPLOITS people.
story: Exploitative. A journalist went undercover in a factory. Workers there earned two dollars for fourteen hours, had no breaks, no fans in forty-degree heat, and were fined for using the toilet too long. Some were only fourteen years old. Her report called the factory exploitative: taking unfair advantage of people for selfish profit. To exploit is to use unfairly. Child labour is the clearest example of an exploitative practice.
example: The company was accused of exploitative labor practices.

gre.s: Labor activists condemned the company's ____ practices, which included paying workers far below the minimum wage.
gre.clue: paying workers far below the minimum wage

en: Able to be predicted or expected
hook: FORE-SEE-able: can be SEEN BEFORE it happens.
story: Foreseeable. Developers built a row of houses right on the riverbank, with no embankment and no drainage. Engineers warned them. Villagers warned them. The very first monsoon, the river swallowed three houses. Everyone said the disaster had been foreseeable: able to be predicted or expected. For the foreseeable future means as far ahead as we can reasonably predict. Fore means before, see means see.
example: The economic crisis had foreseeable consequences.

gre.s: The collapse was entirely ____, since engineers had warned for years that the dam could not withstand a major flood.
gre.clue: engineers had warned for years

en: To abandon or give up entirely
hook: FOR-SAKE: abandon FOR your own SAKE.
story: Forsake. When Kamal's business collapsed and he lost everything, his so-called friends vanished. Nobody returned his calls; nobody visited. Only one old school friend came every Friday with tea and good advice. His other friends had forsaken him: abandoned him entirely when he needed help. Forsake can also mean to give up something: that difficult year, Kamal forsook gambling forever. Think: abandoning someone for your own sake.
example: He felt forsaken by his friends when he needed them most.

gre.s: Many of the reformer's early allies were quick to ____ her once her proposals became unpopular, leaving her to fight alone.
gre.clue: leaving her to fight alone

en: To give pleasure or satisfaction to
hook: GRATIFY: makes you GRATEFUL and happy.
story: Gratify. Forty years ago, Master Rahim taught a poor, barefoot boy to read under a mango tree. Last month, that boy, now a famous heart surgeon, returned to the village, touched the old teacher's feet, and dedicated a new clinic to him. The old man wept. It gratified him deeply: gave him great pleasure and satisfaction. Instant gratification is the pleasure of getting what you want immediately, like scrolling instead of studying.
example: Her success in the competition gratified her parents.

gre.s: It must ____ the elderly inventor to see his once-ridiculed idea now used by millions of people every day.
gre.clue: his once-ridiculed idea now used by millions

en: To pay careful attention to (advice or warning)
hook: HEED: use your HEAD and listen.
story: Heed. When the cyclone warning sounded over Kuakata, Rahim's father ordered the family to the concrete shelter immediately. Their neighbour laughed. "It will miss us, like last time." That night, the storm surge flattened the neighbour's house. Rahim's family was safe. They had heeded the warning: paid careful attention to it and acted. Heedless means careless. Think: use your head, and listen.
example: Please heed my advice and proceed with caution.

gre.s: The near-collision could easily have been avoided if the pilots had bothered to ____ the repeated warnings from air traffic control.
gre.clue: could easily have been avoided

en: Having or showing good judgment
hook: JUDICIOUS: like a wise JUDGE.
story: Judicious. Mitu had three months, a full-time job, and a tight budget for her GRE preparation. She made judicious choices: she spent her time on her weakest areas first, took timed practice tests every Saturday, bought one excellent book instead of five average ones, and slept eight hours every night. She scored 324. Judicious means having or showing good judgment. Think of a wise judge. Synonyms: prudent, sagacious.
example: A judicious investor makes careful decisions.

gre.s: With only limited funds available, the museum made a ____ decision to repair its roof before purchasing any new artworks.
gre.clue: repair its roof before purchasing any new artworks

en: Expressed clearly; easy to understand; mentally clear
hook: LUCID: full of LIGHT (lux), crystal clear.
story: Lucid. Rafi had failed math twice. Then a new teacher arrived and explained compound interest using a single bank account, three years, and a cup of tea. Every step made sense. For the first time, Rafi understood. Her explanation was lucid: expressed clearly and easy to understand. Lux means light, as in lucid, light shining through. Lucid also describes a mind that is thinking clearly: a patient having a lucid moment.
example: He presented a lucid explanation of the complex concept.

gre.s: Despite the complexity of the subject, her ____ explanation allowed even beginners to grasp the theory.
gre.clue: allowed even beginners to grasp the theory

en: Directly relevant to the matter at hand
hook: PERTINENT: PERTAINS to the topic.
story: Pertinent. In his job interview, Arif was asked about his teamwork skills. He resisted the urge to talk about his childhood or his love of cricket. Instead he gave three short examples, each directly related to the job's demands. The panel nodded approvingly. His answers were pertinent: directly relevant to the matter at hand. Pertinent pertains to the topic. Interestingly, impertinent once meant irrelevant, and now means rude.
example: Please keep your questions pertinent to the topic being discussed.

gre.s: The judge excluded the testimony as not ____ to the case, since it concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime.
gre.clue: concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime

en: Conformity to accepted standards of behavior or morals
hook: PROPRIETY: PROPER behavior.
story: Propriety. Sixty years ago in Joya's grandmother's village, rules of propriety meant that a young woman could not speak with a young man unless an elder was present. Today the rules are different, but propriety still exists. You do not answer a phone call during a funeral prayer, and you do not wear shorts to a mosque. Propriety means conformity to accepted standards of behaviour. Think: proper behaviour. It is a synonym of decorum.
example: A sense of propriety prevented her from making a rude remark.

gre.s: The minister resigned not because he had broken the law but because his conduct raised serious questions of ____.
gre.clue: not because he had broken the law

en: Sparkling; brilliantly lively and clever
hook: SCINTILLATING: sparkles like a tiny spark (scintilla).
story: Scintillating. At the national debate final, Ishita stepped up to the microphone. For seven minutes, she was brilliant: sharp jokes, clever examples, perfectly timed pauses, a devastating closing line. The audience laughed, gasped, and finally rose to its feet. Even the opposing team applauded. Her speech was scintillating: sparkling, brilliantly lively and clever. A scintilla is a tiny spark. Scintillating conversation sparkles with wit.
example: The conversation was scintillating and full of wit.

gre.s: Guests looked forward to the novelist's dinner parties, where her ____ wit kept the conversation sparkling until dawn.
gre.clue: kept the conversation sparkling until dawn

en: Causing great excitement; presented in a shocking way to attract attention
hook: SENSATIONAL: designed to excite the SENSES.
story: Sensational. "CELEBRITY'S SHOCKING SECRET LIFE REVEALED!" screamed the online headline in giant red letters. Lamia clicked. The article said the actor had once eaten pizza with a spoon. That was all. Sensational journalism exaggerates or shocks to attract attention, often at the expense of truth. Sensational means causing great excitement, often through exaggeration. Informally, it can also mean wonderful: a sensational goal.
example: The sensational news story spread quickly through the town.

gre.s: Serious journalists criticized the tabloid's ____ coverage of the trial, which emphasized lurid details while ignoring the legal issues.
gre.clue: emphasized lurid details while ignoring the legal issues

en: Highly developed and complex; having refined, worldly taste
hook: SOPHISTICATED: from SOPHIA, wisdom; refined and advanced.
story: Sophisticated. Imran's new phone can unlock using his face in total darkness, translate speech in real time, and identify plants from a photo. The software inside is extraordinarily sophisticated. Its designer is a sophisticated woman too: she has lived in four countries, collects modern art, and speaks five languages. Sophisticated means highly developed and complex, or worldly and refined. Sophia means wisdom.
example: The device had a sophisticated design.

gre.s: The fraud was so ____, involving dozens of shell companies across several countries, that investigators needed years to untangle it.
gre.clue: involving dozens of shell companies across several countries

en: Angry or bitter disagreement; conflict
hook: STRIFE: STRIKES and FIGHTS.
story: Strife. For three years, the country was torn by political strife: strikes, burning buses, protests, and violent clashes in the streets. Schools closed; businesses failed. In Tanvir's family, a similar strife broke out over inheritance: brothers who once shared a bed stopped speaking. Strife means angry or bitter disagreement, conflict. Civil strife is conflict within a nation. Think of strikes and fights.
example: The region was plagued by years of political strife.

gre.s: Years of ethnic ____ had left the region impoverished, its villages divided and its farms abandoned.
gre.clue: its villages divided and its farms abandoned

en: Presented in a subtle, restrained, and effective way
hook: UNDER-STATED: stated less loudly than it could be.
story: Understated. At the wedding, guests glittered in heavy gold, sequins, and bright silk. Nadia wore a simple white sari with a thin silver border, small pearl earrings, and no other jewellery. Yet she received more compliments than anyone in the hall. Her elegance was understated: presented in a subtle, restrained, effective way. Understated is the opposite of ostentatious. Sometimes less really is more.
example: Her understated elegance was more charming than any flashy display.

gre.s: Unlike the flashy designs of her rivals, the architect's ____ buildings blend quietly into their surroundings.
gre.clue: blend quietly into their surroundings

en: Having no moral principles; dishonest
hook: UN-SCRUPULOUS: has no SCRUPLES (conscience).
story: Unscrupulous. A travel agent in Narayanganj promised fifty families jobs in Malaysia: good salaries, free housing, flights included. Each family paid two lakh taka, some selling their land to do so. One morning the agent's office was empty and his phone was switched off. He had vanished with everything. He was unscrupulous: having no moral principles, willing to cheat anyone. Scruples are your conscience. The unscrupulous have none.
example: The unscrupulous politician abused their power for personal gain.

gre.s: The ____ landlord evicted elderly tenants on false pretexts so that he could rent their apartments at triple the price.
gre.clue: evicted elderly tenants on false pretexts

en: Truthfulness; accuracy
hook: VERACITY: VERy accurate. 'Vera' means true.
story: Veracity. In a speech, the minister claimed that unemployment had fallen by half in a single year. Journalists checked every source: government data, surveys, international reports. Nothing supported the claim. Newspapers questioned the veracity of his statement: its truthfulness and accuracy. Vera means true. Do not confuse veracity with voracity, which means a huge appetite. A witness whose veracity is doubted will not be believed.
example: The witness's veracity was questioned by the defense.

gre.s: Historians question the ____ of the memoir, noting that several events it describes could not possibly have happened.
gre.clue: could not possibly have happened

en: Extremely harmful or poisonous; bitterly hostile
hook: VIRULENT: like a VIRUS, spreading poison.
story: Virulent. In one cold season, a new strain of influenza spread through Dhaka's hostels. It was virulent: it spread rapidly and caused severe illness, sending dozens of students to hospital. Online, arguments about the outbreak became virulent too, full of insults and hatred. Virulent means extremely harmful or poisonous, or bitterly hostile. Think of a virus spreading poison. Virulent criticism is vicious and venomous.
example: The virus was a particularly virulent strain.

gre.s: The pamphlet's ____ attacks on the minority community, full of hateful slurs, led to its immediate ban.
gre.clue: full of hateful slurs

en: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse
hook: VOLATILE: like a VOLCANO, could explode any moment.
story: Volatile. On Monday, the stock market rose five percent. On Tuesday, it crashed seven. On Wednesday, it soared again. Investors could not sleep. Rafi's uncle has a volatile temper too: calm and joking one moment, shouting and slamming doors the next. Volatile means liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse. In chemistry, volatile liquids evaporate quickly. Picture a volcano that could erupt at any moment.
example: The volatile stock market made investors nervous.

gre.s: Investors fled the ____ market, where prices could swing by double digits in a single afternoon.
gre.clue: where prices could swing by double digits in a single afternoon

en: To come before in time; to precede
hook: ANTE = before. Dated BEFORE.
story: Antedate. On a school trip to Mahasthangarh in Bogura, Imran's class walked among ancient brick walls and the ruins of a city more than two thousand years old. Their guide pointed out that this city antedates the Mughal Empire by well over a thousand years, and even antedates most of the famous kingdoms they had studied. To antedate is to come before in time. Ante means before, as in antecedent. Its synonyms are predate and precede.
example: The ancient city antedates recorded history.

gre.s: Recent excavations suggest that farming in the valley may ____ the arrival of the first nomadic herders by several thousand years.
gre.clue: the arrival of the first nomadic herders by several thousand years

en: To send someone away officially as punishment; to get rid of
hook: BANISH: make them VANISH.
story: Banish. In the old epic, a jealous queen tricked the king into banishing his own son, the prince, to the forest for fourteen years. The prince left the palace with nothing but his wife and brother. Centuries later, Mitu banished her phone from her bedroom every night to sleep better, and it worked. To banish is to send someone away officially as punishment, or to get rid of something. You can banish fears and doubts too. Think: make them vanish.
example: The dictator banished all his political opponents.

gre.s: Determined to ____ every trace of the old regime, the new government renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks.
gre.clue: renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks

en: To restrain or control; also, to show resentment or anger
bn: সংযত করা; লাগাম টানা, ক্ষোভ প্রকাশ করা
hook: BRIDLE: the straps on a horse's head that hold it back.
story: Bridle. At the market, a shopkeeper insulted Arif's mother over a few taka. Arif felt his face burn and his fists tighten. But he took a long breath, bridled his anger, paid, and walked away calmly. A bridle is the leather harness used to control a horse. To bridle is to restrain or control. Tricky: bridle can also mean to bristle with anger: "She bridled at the insult." Read the context carefully.
example: She bridled her anger and spoke calmly.

gre.s: The coach urged his young striker to ____ his temper, since another red card would mean missing the final.
gre.clue: since another red card would mean missing the final

en: To act according to a rule, request, or command
hook: COMPLY: COMPLETE what's asked.
story: Comply. The new law said that every bus must have a speed limiter and that drivers must rest after six hours. Most transport companies complied within a month, installing the devices and changing shifts. Three companies ignored the law and were fined heavily. To comply is to act according to a rule, request, or command. Compliance with safety rules keeps everyone alive. Think: complete what was asked.
example: The company was forced to comply with the new regulations.

gre.s: Companies that refuse to ____ with the new environmental regulations will face heavy fines and possible closure.
gre.clue: will face heavy fines and possible closure

en: Sad and disappointed
hook: CREST-FALLEN: a rooster whose proud crest has drooped.
story: Crestfallen. Tanvir had studied for eight months for the scholarship exam. When the results were posted, he searched the list three times. His name was not there. He had missed the cut-off by two marks. He walked out with his head down, shoulders slumped, unable to speak. He was crestfallen: sad and deeply disappointed. Picture a proud rooster whose bright crest has suddenly drooped. It is the opposite of elated.
example: The team was crestfallen after losing the championship.

gre.s: The usually confident candidate looked ____ as the results came in, his campaign having fallen far short of expectations.
gre.clue: having fallen far short of expectations

en: To reduce or cut short
hook: CUR-TAIL: cut the TAIL short.
story: Curtail. The school's annual sports day began brightly. Then the radio announced an approaching cyclone. The principal stopped the races after only two events and sent everyone home. The day had been curtailed: cut short. That year, the government also curtailed its spending, reducing budgets for new buildings. To curtail is to reduce or cut short. Curfews curtail freedom of movement. Think: cutting the tail short.
example: Bad weather forced us to curtail our trip.

gre.s: Fearing a budget shortfall, the university was forced to ____ its research programs, eliminating nearly a third of them.
gre.clue: eliminating nearly a third of them

en: To make clear; to explain
hook: E-LUCID-ATE: make it LUCID (clear).
story: Elucidate. Half the biology class looked confused about photosynthesis. Their teacher put down the textbook, drew a simple picture of a leaf, and added three arrows: sunlight in, water from the roots, and sugar and oxygen out. "That is all it is." Suddenly every face relaxed. She had elucidated it: made it clear and explained it. E means out, lucid means clear: bringing clarity out. Good writers elucidate rather than confuse.
example: The professor elucidated the complex scientific concept.

gre.s: In an appendix, the author attempts to ____ the more technical concepts for readers without a background in physics.
gre.clue: for readers without a background in physics

en: To escape or avoid, especially by cleverness or trickery
hook: EVADE: like an EVASIVE dodge.
story: Evade. For ten years, a wealthy businessman evaded paying taxes by hiding money in foreign bank accounts and fake companies. When journalists finally asked him about it at a press conference, he evaded the question too, talking at length about his charity work instead. To evade is to escape or avoid something, especially by cleverness or trickery. Tax evasion is illegal; tax avoidance can be legal. An evasive answer dodges the question.
example: The criminal evaded capture for months.

gre.s: The fugitive managed to ____ capture for nearly a decade by moving constantly and using a series of false identities.
gre.clue: by moving constantly and using a series of false identities

en: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective
hook: FECK-LESS: 'feck' is old Scottish for effect. No effect at all.
story: Feckless. The new office manager never made decisions, never answered emails, and disappeared whenever a problem arose. When projects failed, he blamed his team. When clients complained, he forwarded the emails without comment. After six months, staff simply stopped asking him anything. He was feckless: irresponsible, lacking initiative, and ineffective. Feck is an old Scottish word for effect. Feckless means without any effect at all.
example: The feckless leader was unable to control the situation.

gre.s: Voters grew frustrated with the ____ government, which announced ambitious plans every year but never carried any of them out.
gre.clue: never carried any of them out

en: To become worse, especially through neglect; to rot
hook: FESTER: like an untreated wound that grows worse.
story: Fester. Rafi cut his foot on a rusty nail and ignored it. A week later the small cut had festered: red, swollen, infected, and painful. He spent three days on antibiotics. His anger toward his brother was the same: never discussed, just buried, slowly growing worse for years until one small comment caused an explosion. To fester is to become worse, especially through neglect. Unresolved problems fester. Wounds fester when untreated.
example: The infected wound festered without treatment.

gre.s: Left unaddressed, the resentment among the workers continued to ____, eventually erupting in a bitter strike.
gre.clue: eventually erupting in a bitter strike

en: Attacking cherished beliefs or established traditions
hook: ICON-O-CLAST: one who smashes ICONS.
story: Iconoclastic. The young director's first film questioned everything society held sacred: arranged marriages, exam rankings, hero worship of politicians, even the sanctity of family dinners. Some viewers walked out; others called it brilliant. Critics called it iconoclastic: attacking cherished beliefs and established traditions. Originally, iconoclasts literally smashed religious images, or icons. Today, an iconoclastic thinker shatters accepted ideas.
example: The artist's iconoclastic paintings shocked the public.

gre.s: The economist's ____ theories, which challenged nearly every assumption of her field, were initially ridiculed but are now widely accepted.
gre.clue: challenged nearly every assumption of her field

en: To confine or imprison within walls
hook: IM-MURE: 'mur' is wall (mural). Walled in.
story: Immure. In old legends, a cruel king punished his enemies by immuring them inside the palace walls, sealing them in with bricks. Centuries later, Nadia immured herself in her bedroom for the whole month before her exam, coming out only for meals and the bathroom. Her family slid tea under the door. To immure is to confine or imprison within walls. Mur means wall, as in mural. Think: walled in.
example: The villain was immured in a dungeon.

gre.s: Rather than mingling with other scholars, the reclusive historian chose to ____ himself in the archive for months at a time.
gre.clue: Rather than mingling with other scholars

en: To create or perform without preparation
hook: IMPROVISE: IM-PRO-VISE, not foreseen (pro-vise), done on the spot.
story: Improvise. Halfway through Sara's big presentation, the projector died. Two hundred people stared at a blank screen. Sara paused, smiled, picked up a marker, and drew her charts on the whiteboard from memory, telling the story of her research as she went. The audience loved it even more. She had improvised: created or performed something without preparation. Jazz musicians improvise solos. Improvise means unforeseen, done on the spot.
example: We had to improvise a meal with the limited ingredients available.

gre.s: When the main speaker failed to arrive, the host was forced to ____, delivering a twenty-minute talk with no notes at all.
gre.clue: with no notes at all

en: To restrain, hinder, or prevent
hook: INHIBIT: keeps you IN, holding you back.
story: Inhibit. Tanvir knew every answer in English class, but fear of making mistakes inhibited him from speaking. Every time he opened his mouth, his throat closed. His teacher started a small conversation club, and slowly he found his voice. To inhibit is to restrain, hinder, or prevent. Certain medicines inhibit the growth of bacteria. Inhibitions are feelings that hold you back socially. Think: keeps you in.
example: Fear can inhibit people from trying new things.

gre.s: Researchers hope the new compound will ____ the growth of tumors without damaging healthy tissue.
gre.clue: without damaging healthy tissue

en: Impossible to understand or interpret
hook: IN-SCRUTABLE: can't be SCRUTINIZED.
story: Inscrutable. At the national poker tournament, the final player sat absolutely still. No smile. No frown. No twitch. Not even a blink. Opponents studied his face for clues and found nothing. Was he holding a perfect hand or bluffing with nothing at all? He won the tournament without anyone ever reading him. His face was inscrutable: impossible to understand or interpret. In means not, scrutable means able to be scrutinized. Synonym: enigmatic.
example: The painting's meaning was inscrutable.

gre.s: The cat's ____ expression gave no hint of whether it was about to purr contentedly or lash out with its claws.
gre.clue: gave no hint

en: To treat someone as a celebrity
bn: বীরের মতো সম্মান করা; তারকা বানিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: LIONIZE: treated like the LION, king of the jungle.
story: Lionize. A shy girl from a fishing village in Bhola won the international mathematics olympiad. Within a week she was everywhere: TV interviews, newspaper covers, reception ceremonies, a meeting with the prime minister. People asked for her autograph in the street. She was lionized: treated as a celebrity and hero. Picture being treated like the lion, king of the jungle. Societies often lionize their heroes, though sometimes the wrong ones.
example: The media lionized the young athlete.

gre.s: Although the press rushed to ____ the scientist after her discovery, she found the constant attention exhausting and retreated from public life.
gre.clue: she found the constant attention exhausting

en: Dull and tedious because of lack of variety
hook: MONO-TONE: one tone, over and over.
story: Monotonous. At the factory, Kamal's job was to put the same bolt into the same hole on the same machine part. Eight thousand times a day. Six days a week. Same sound, same motion, same view. After a month, he felt his mind switching off by ten in the morning. His work was monotonous: dull and tedious because nothing ever changed. Mono means one, tone means sound: one single note, forever.
example: The factory work was monotonous.

gre.s: The ____ landscape, mile after mile of identical wheat fields, made the long drive feel endless.
gre.clue: mile after mile of identical wheat fields

en: Strange or unusual; belonging exclusively to one person or place
hook: PECULIAR: PECULIAR things are PECULIARLY yours.
story: Peculiar. When Mitu walked into the kitchen, there was a peculiar smell: burnt sugar, wet socks, and something like cinnamon. Her brother was attempting his first cake. Mitu's family also has a peculiar habit: everyone says "Bismillah" before switching on the generator. Peculiar means strange and unusual, or belonging distinctively to one person or place. A custom peculiar to Sylhet is found only there.
example: She had a peculiar way of dressing.

gre.s: The custom of exchanging salt as a gift is ____ to the region and is unknown even in neighboring provinces.
gre.clue: unknown even in neighboring provinces

en: To plan something, often a crime, in advance
hook: PRE-MEDITATE: MEDITATE on it BEFORE doing it.
story: Premeditate. The jewellery shop robbery looked spontaneous. But police discovered that the thieves had watched the shop for six weeks, recorded the guard's shift times, bought masks in advance, and even timed the traffic lights outside. The crime had been premeditated: planned beforehand. Pre means before, meditate means think deeply. Premeditated crimes are punished more severely than crimes of passion, committed in a moment of anger.
example: The murder was premeditated.

gre.s: The prosecution argued that the defendant had taken weeks to ____ the crime, pointing to receipts for tools bought a month earlier.
gre.clue: pointing to receipts for tools bought a month earlier

en: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful; shamelessly immoral
hook: PROFLIGATE: PRO at wasting.
story: Profligate. When the old zamindar died, his son inherited a fortune. Within three years it was gone: luxury cars, endless parties, gambling in Singapore, gifts for friends he barely knew. When the money ran out, so did the friends. He was profligate: recklessly extravagant and wasteful. Profligate can also mean shamelessly immoral. Synonyms: prodigal, spendthrift. Think: a pro at wasting everything.
example: The profligate heir squandered his inheritance.

gre.s: Critics attacked the government's ____ spending, noting that it had borrowed billions to build a stadium that would rarely be used.
gre.clue: borrowed billions to build a stadium that would rarely be used

en: To restore friendly relations; to make two things consistent
hook: RE-CONCILE: bring back to COUNCIL, back together.
story: Reconcile. Two brothers in Jessore had not spoken for ten years after a dispute over land. When their mother fell gravely ill, both came to the hospital. They stood on opposite sides of her bed. She took one hand of each and joined them together. That night, the brothers hugged and cried. They reconciled: restored friendly relations. Reconcile also means to make two things consistent: accountants reconcile bank statements so the numbers match.
example: The estranged couple finally reconciled.

gre.s: The theory struggles to ____ two sets of findings that appear to contradict each other.
gre.clue: that appear to contradict each other

en: To improve by making small changes; to remove impurities
hook: RE-FINE: make it FINE again and again.
story: Refine. Rafi wrote his statement of purpose in one evening. Then he refined it: twelve drafts over three weeks, cutting weak sentences, sharpening examples, and replacing vague words with precise ones. The final version was half the length and twice as powerful. To refine is to improve something through small changes, or to remove impurities. Factories refine sugar until it is pure white. Refined manners are polished and elegant.
example: The engineers refined the design for the new car.

gre.s: Over decades, the craftsmen continued to ____ their techniques, gradually eliminating flaws until their porcelain was the finest in the world.
gre.clue: gradually eliminating flaws

en: To voluntarily give up or let go
hook: RELINQUISH: RELease and finISH.
story: Relinquish. For fifty years, Mr. Haque ran the textile company he had founded with a single sewing machine. At seventy-five, he finally relinquished control to his daughter, signing the papers with a trembling hand. It was the hardest thing he had ever done. To relinquish is to voluntarily give up or let go of something: power, a claim, a position, or your grip on a rope. Think: release and finish.
example: She reluctantly relinquished control of the company.

gre.s: The aging dictator refused to ____ power, even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin.
gre.clue: even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin

en: To think deeply about something
hook: RUMINATE: like a cow chewing cud, chewing a thought over and over.
story: Ruminate. Sitting on the steps of the river ghat at dusk, Tanvir ruminated on his future. Stay in Bangladesh near his family, or go abroad for a better career? He turned the question over and over for hours, chewing on every possibility. To ruminate is to think deeply about something, for a long time. Cows ruminate too: they chew their cud again and again. Too much rumination on past mistakes leads to anxiety.
example: He ruminated on the meaning of life.

gre.s: Instead of acting decisively, the general would ____ for days over every decision, by which time the opportunity had usually passed.
gre.clue: Instead of acting decisively

en: Nervous and easily frightened; unpredictable
hook: SKITTISH: like a SKITTERING kitten, jumps at every sound.
story: Skittish. Joya tried for weeks to befriend a stray kitten outside her building. It was skittish: whenever someone moved, even slightly, it bolted under a car. A door slamming three floors away would send it running. Investors can be skittish too, selling all their shares at the first sign of bad news. Skittish means nervous, easily frightened, and unpredictable. Picture a kitten skittering away at every sound.
example: The skittish horse shied away from every sound.

gre.s: The horse was so ____ that the slightest rustle in the bushes would send it bolting across the field.
gre.clue: the slightest rustle in the bushes would send it bolting

en: More than needed; unnecessary
hook: SUPER-FLUOUS: flows (flu) OVER (super) the top.
story: Superfluous. Arif's first draft described the building as "very extremely big huge enormous." His editor deleted four words and left one: "enormous." The rest were superfluous: more than needed, unnecessary. Super means over, fluous means flowing: flowing over the top of the cup. A superfluous remark adds nothing to a conversation. Good GRE essays contain no superfluous words.
example: The instructions included several superfluous steps.

gre.s: The editor cut several paragraphs that she considered ____, since they merely repeated points made earlier in the chapter.
gre.clue: merely repeated points made earlier

en: Giving a brief general summary or overview
hook: SYN-OPTIC: seeing (optic) everything together (syn). A SYNOPSIS.
story: Synoptic. On the first day of the semester, Professor Rahman did not start with details. Instead, she spent ten minutes drawing one large diagram on the board, showing the five main topics of the course and how they connected. For the first time, students saw the big picture before diving in. Her overview was synoptic: giving a brief, general summary. Syn means together, optic means seeing. A synopsis summarizes a film's plot.
example: The professor gave a synoptic review of the topic.

gre.s: The chapter offers a ____ view of the war, condensing four years of campaigns into a few concise pages.
gre.clue: condensing four years of campaigns into a few concise pages

en: Complete with regard to every detail
hook: THOROUGH: goes THROUGH everything.
story: Thorough. Before submitting her university application, Mitu printed everything and checked it line by line: every document, every date, every spelling, every signature. It took a whole day. She found two small mistakes, a wrong year and a misspelled professor's name, that could have cost her admission. Her check was thorough: complete with regard to every detail. Its opposite is cursory. Think: it goes through everything.
example: The detective conducted a thorough investigation.

gre.s: Unlike the hasty earlier investigation, the new inquiry was ____, interviewing every witness and examining every document.
gre.clue: interviewing every witness and examining every document

en: Thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom
hook: VISIONARY: has a VISION of the future.
story: Visionary. Fifty years ago, a village schoolteacher in Gopalganj stood in an empty field and announced, "One day, a university will stand here." People laughed. He raised money for decades, one taka at a time. Today, that university has ten thousand students. He was a visionary: someone who thinks about the future with imagination and wisdom. Depending on context, visionary can also mean idealistic but impractical.
example: The visionary leader inspired her followers.

gre.s: Dismissed in her own time as a dreamer, the urban planner is now hailed as a ____ whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities.
gre.clue: whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities

en: Expressing opinions loudly and forcefully
hook: VOCI-FEROUS: a VOICE that's FEROCIOUS.
story: Vociferous. When the cricket board dropped the country's favourite batsman, the fans were not quiet about it. They shouted outside the board's office, chanted in the streets, flooded social media with angry posts, and called radio shows all day. Their criticism was vociferous: expressing opinions loudly and forcefully. Vox means voice, ferous means carrying: a voice carried far. A vociferous critic makes sure everyone hears.
example: The protesters made vociferous demands.

gre.s: The proposal met with ____ opposition from residents, who packed the town hall and shouted down every speaker in favor.
gre.clue: shouted down every speaker in favor

en: To praise enthusiastically and publicly; public praise
hook: AC-CLAIM: everyone CLAIMS it's great — loudly.
story: Acclaim. A young Bangladeshi director made her first feature film on a tiny budget, shooting in her grandmother's village with local actors. She sent it to an international festival without much hope. At the premiere, the audience stood and applauded for ten minutes. Critics from Paris to Tokyo praised it. The film received worldwide acclaim: enthusiastic public praise. As a verb, to acclaim is to praise publicly. Critical acclaim means strong praise from experts.
example: The critics unanimously acclaimed the artist's latest exhibition.

gre.s: Although her early novels were ignored, her final book won universal ____, earning every major literary prize that year.
gre.clue: earning every major literary prize that year

en: To find something out for certain
hook: AS-CERTAIN: make CERTAIN.
story: Ascertain. A rumour spread through the hostel that the bus to Sylhet would leave at five instead of seven. Some students rushed to the station at dawn. Nadia did not trust rumours. She called the bus company twice, then checked their website, to ascertain the real departure time. It was seven. To ascertain is to find something out for certain. Investigators work to ascertain the cause of an accident. Think: make certain.
example: Investigators worked tirelessly to ascertain the cause of the plane crash.

gre.s: Before publishing the story, the editor insisted that reporters ____ the facts from at least two independent sources.
gre.clue: from at least two independent sources

en: Confident and forceful in stating one's views or rights
hook: ASSERTIVE: firmly ASSERTS what she wants.
story: Assertive. At the end of a successful project, Sara's manager prepared to present it to the board, with his own name on every slide. Sara walked into his office. "I led this project for six months. I would like my name on the report, and I would like to present the results myself." She stayed calm and polite, but she did not back down. She was assertive: confident and forceful in stating her views or rights, without being aggressive.
example: The team leader needed to be more assertive to steer the project in the right direction.

gre.s: Once timid in meetings, the young analyst became increasingly ____, confidently defending her proposals against senior colleagues.
gre.clue: confidently defending her proposals against senior colleagues

en: Not genuine; fake
hook: BOGUS sounds like a fake BOGEYMAN — not real.
story: Bogus. An advertisement on social media promised: "Official GRE score certificate, guaranteed 330, only five hundred dollars! No test needed!" Imran's cousin almost paid. Imran explained that scores come only from ETS, sent directly to universities, and cannot be bought. The offer was bogus: fake, not genuine, fraudulent. Bogus degrees, bogus charities, bogus claims. If something sounds too good to be true, it is probably bogus.
example: Police arrested the street vendor for selling bogus designer watches.

gre.s: Investigators discovered that the clinic's impressive medical certificates were ____, printed by a shop that specialized in forgeries.
gre.clue: printed by a shop that specialized in forgeries

en: Causing sudden, violent, and widespread destruction or change
hook: CATACLYSMIC: a CATastrophe, a total CRASH.
story: Cataclysmic. On the night of 12 November 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck the coast of what is now Bangladesh. A wall of seawater several metres high swept across the islands in the darkness. By morning, hundreds of thousands of people had died, and entire villages had vanished. It remains one of the deadliest natural disasters in history. It was cataclysmic: causing sudden, violent, widespread destruction. A cataclysm changes everything that follows.
example: The cataclysmic earthquake left the city in ruins.

gre.s: Geologists believe that a ____ asteroid impact, which triggered firestorms and years of darkness, wiped out the dinosaurs.
gre.clue: which triggered firestorms and years of darkness

en: To restrict within limits; to draw a line around
hook: CIRCUM-SCRIBE: draw (scribe) a CIRCLE around it.
story: Circumscribe. Lamia's grandmother was a brilliant student in the 1960s, top of her school in mathematics. But her choices were circumscribed by tradition: which subjects she could study, whether she could attend university, and whom she would marry were all decided for her. Her world was drawn inside a small circle. To circumscribe is to restrict within limits. Circum means around, scribe means draw. In geometry, you circumscribe a circle around a shape.
example: The school's strict dress code circumscribed students' freedom of expression.

gre.s: The new law sought to ____ the president's powers, limiting his ability to declare emergencies without parliamentary approval.
gre.clue: limiting his ability to declare emergencies

en: Combining so as to complete or enhance each other
hook: COMPLEMENTARY with an E COMPLETES. Complimentary with an I means free or praising.
story: Complementary. Mitu is full of creative ideas but terrible with deadlines and money. Her business partner, Sara, is organised, careful, and great with numbers, but rarely has new ideas. Together, they built the most successful bakery in Dhanmondi. Their skills are complementary: combining to complete and enhance each other. Remember the spelling: complementary with an E completes. Complimentary with an I means praising or free of charge.
example: The chef's choice of herbs provided a complementary flavor profile to the dish.

gre.s: The two researchers' skills proved ____: her expertise in statistics filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge of biology.
gre.clue: filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge

en: Causing or likely to cause argument; quarrelsome
hook: CONTENTIOUS: creates CONTENTION (conflict).
story: Contentious. At Eid dinner, someone mentioned the upcoming election. Within thirty seconds, uncles were shouting, aunties were taking sides, and a cousin had stormed off to the balcony. Grandmother banged her spoon on the table: "No politics at dinner!" Politics in that family is a contentious topic: likely to cause argument. A contentious person loves to argue. Contention means dispute. GRE passages often discuss contentious scientific debates.
example: The proposed tax reform became a contentious issue in the election campaign.

gre.s: The proposal to build the dam proved highly ____, provoking furious debates in parliament and protests across the region.
gre.clue: provoking furious debates in parliament and protests

en: Not sincere; pretending to know less than one does
hook: DIS-INGENUOUS: NOT ingenuous (innocent). Fake innocence.
story: Disingenuous. The exam questions had been leaked, and one student had shared them in three WhatsApp groups. When the principal asked him about it, he widened his eyes. "Leaked? Me? I had no idea the questions were leaked, sir!" Everyone knew he had shared them. His surprise was disingenuous: insincere, pretending to know less than he did. Dis means not, ingenuous means innocent. Disingenuous means fake innocence. Its opposite is candid.
example: The politician's apology seemed disingenuous and calculated.

gre.s: It is ____ of the company to claim it was unaware of the defect, since internal emails show executives discussed it for months.
gre.clue: internal emails show executives discussed it for months

en: To reveal private or secret information
hook: DIVULGE: DIVE into the secrets and BULGE them out.
story: Divulge. Arif's best friend told him a secret: she was applying to Oxford, but she did not want anyone to know in case she was rejected. Arif promised not to tell. Two days later, at a family dinner, he accidentally mentioned it. Her mother called within the hour. He had divulged her secret: revealed private or sensitive information. Doctors cannot divulge patient information. Synonyms: disclose, reveal.
example: The spy was forced to divulge the names of his collaborators.

gre.s: The journalist went to prison rather than ____ the identity of her source.
gre.clue: went to prison rather than

en: Asserting opinions as undeniably true, refusing to consider other views
hook: DOGMATIC: as stubborn as a DOG with a bone; sticks to DOGMA.
story: Dogmatic. Uncle Jamal has opinions about everything, and he is always certain. "Doctors are always wrong." "Young people know nothing." "Rice can never make you fat." When his nephew showed him a medical study, he waved it away without reading it. No evidence has ever changed his mind about anything. He is dogmatic: asserting his opinions as undeniable truths, refusing to consider other views. A dogma is a fixed belief. Good scientists avoid being dogmatic.
example: The professor's dogmatic teaching style discouraged open debate in the classroom.

gre.s: Unlike his ____ colleagues, who refused to consider any evidence against their theory, the young professor welcomed criticism.
gre.clue: who refused to consider any evidence against their theory

en: Based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning
hook: FALLACIOUS: built on a FALLACY, so it FALLS apart.
story: Fallacious. "My grandfather smoked forty cigarettes a day and lived to ninety-five," Tanvir's uncle announced. "So smoking is perfectly safe." Tanvir shook his head. One lucky person does not cancel out millions of studies. His uncle's argument was fallacious: based on faulty reasoning or a mistaken belief. A fallacy is an error in logic. GRE argument questions often ask you to spot fallacious reasoning.
example: The lawyer demonstrated the fallacious nature of the witness's testimony.

gre.s: The report's conclusion was ____, since it assumed that because two events occurred together, one must have caused the other.
gre.clue: assumed that because two events occurred together, one must have caused the other

en: Recklessly bold or rash
hook: FOOL-HARDY: a FOOL who's too HARDY for his own good.
story: Foolhardy. During the monsoon floods, a group of young men dared each other to swim across the swollen Padma for a bet of five hundred taka. The current was strong enough to drown expert swimmers. One of them nearly did, rescued only by a passing fisherman. The stunt was foolhardy: recklessly bold, brave in a stupid way. Being intrepid is admirable; being foolhardy is dangerous. Think: a fool who is too hardy.
example: It was foolhardy to attempt to climb the mountain without proper equipment.

gre.s: Experienced mountaineers considered the attempt ____, since the climbers planned to ascend in midwinter without oxygen or guides.
gre.clue: in midwinter without oxygen or guides

en: To create difficulties that slow or delay something
hook: HINDER: holds you BEHIND.
story: Hinder. Every ten minutes, Sara's phone buzzed: a message, a notification, a reminder, an offer. Each buzz pulled her eyes away from her GRE book. By the end of the evening she had read just four pages. The notifications hindered her studying: they created delays and obstacles. To hinder is to slow progress or make it difficult. Lack of funding hinders research. Think: it holds you behind. Synonyms: impede, hamper.
example: The road construction hindered traffic flow for several days.

gre.s: Bureaucratic delays continue to ____ the delivery of aid, leaving thousands of flood victims without food.
gre.clue: leaving thousands of flood victims without food

en: To weaken or damage something
hook: IMPAIR: makes it IMPERFECT.
story: Impair. For years, Rafi listened to music through headphones at full volume, on buses, while studying, while sleeping. At twenty-five, he noticed he could not follow conversations in noisy rooms. The doctor confirmed it: his hearing was permanently impaired. To impair is to weaken or damage something. Lack of sleep impairs memory and judgment; alcohol impairs driving. Hearing-impaired means having reduced hearing.
example: Smoking can significantly impair lung function over time.

gre.s: Doctors warn that even moderate sleep deprivation can ____ judgment as severely as alcohol.
gre.clue: as severely as alcohol

en: To challenge or call into question someone's honesty or integrity
hook: IMPUGN: IM-PUNCH someone's reputation.
story: Impugn. In court, the defence lawyer could not disprove the witness's testimony. So she tried another strategy: she brought up a lie the witness had told twenty years earlier. "If he lied then," she asked the jury, "why should you believe him now?" She was impugning his honesty: calling his integrity into question. To impugn is to attack someone's truthfulness or reputation. A rumour can impugn an innocent person's character.
example: The defense attorney tried to impugn the witness's credibility.

gre.s: Rather than addressing the substance of the study, critics tried to ____ the researchers' motives, suggesting they had been paid by industry.
gre.clue: suggesting they had been paid by industry

en: Continuing without pause; unending
hook: IN-CESSANT: does NOT CEASE.
story: Incessant. In July, the rain in Sylhet began on a Monday and did not stop. Not for an hour. Not for a minute. Nine days of steady, drumming rain. Roads flooded, walls grew green moss, and Joya's clothes never dried. Children forgot what the sun looked like. The rain was incessant: continuing without any pause. In means not, cessant means ceasing. Incessant barking, incessant complaining, incessant traffic noise.
example: The incessant rain caused widespread flooding.

gre.s: The ____ noise from the construction site, which continued day and night for months, drove many residents to move away.
gre.clue: which continued day and night for months

en: Having a tendency or willingness to do something
hook: INCLINED: LEANING toward something, like an inclined plane.
story: Inclined. After a long day at the office, Arif's body leaned toward the sofa and the TV remote. He was inclined to skip the gym. Then his friend called: "I am outside. Let's go." He went anyway, and felt great afterward. Inclined means having a natural tendency or willingness to do something. "I am inclined to agree" means you lean toward agreement. Picture an inclined plane: everything tends to slide one way.
example: Sarah was inclined to agree with her friend's persuasive argument.

gre.s: Having been burned by investments before, she was not ____ to trust the salesman's promises of guaranteed returns.
gre.clue: Having been burned by investments before

en: Having a long-standing habit that is unlikely to change
hook: INVETERATE: a VETERAN habit, too old to break.
story: Inveterate. Grandfather drinks twelve cups of tea a day, and has done so for sixty years. Strong, milky, with two spoons of sugar. Doctors have begged him to cut down. He nods politely and pours another cup. The habit is too deep to change now. He is an inveterate tea drinker: someone with a long-established habit that is unlikely to change. Think of a veteran habit. An inveterate liar has lied so long he cannot stop.
example: The inveterate smoker found it difficult to break the habit.

gre.s: An ____ gambler, he had lost three fortunes and still could not pass a card table without placing a bet.
gre.clue: still could not pass a card table without placing a bet

en: Unwilling to spend money; stingy
hook: MISERLY: a MISER is MISERABLE about spending.
story: Miserly. The landlord of Ishita's building refused to fix the leaking roof, buy a new water pump, or even replace the broken bulb in the stairwell, though he collected rent from thirty families. Tenants climbed the stairs in darkness with phone torches. He hoarded every taka. He was miserly: extremely unwilling to spend money, stingy. A miser is miserable about spending. Synonyms: parsimonious, penny-pinching. The opposite is generous.
example: The miserly old man refused to donate to charity.

gre.s: Despite his enormous wealth, the banker was famously ____, reusing old envelopes and refusing to heat his mansion in winter.
gre.clue: reusing old envelopes and refusing to heat his mansion

en: Obvious and clearly visible
hook: GRE trick: PATENT (adj.) means obvious — a patent lie is obvious to everyone.
story: Patent. Little Babu was asked if he had eaten the chocolate cake meant for the guests. "No, Ammu!" he said firmly, with chocolate smeared across his mouth, his cheeks, and the front of his shirt. His mother burst out laughing. It was a patent lie: obvious to everyone. On the GRE, patent as an adjective usually means obvious and clearly visible, not the legal right to an invention. Patently false means clearly false.
example: The patent flaws in the experimental design were quickly noticed by the scientists.

gre.s: The witness's claim was ____ false, contradicted by video footage that showed him miles away at the time.
gre.clue: contradicted by video footage

en: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered
hook: PETULANT: a PET who sulks when not given treats.
story: Petulant. When the coach benched him for the semifinal, the team's star batsman sulked on the sideline. He refused to cheer for his teammates, kicked his water bottle across the grass, and complained loudly to anyone who would listen. Fans who saw the video called him a spoiled child. He was petulant: childishly sulky and bad-tempered. A petulant child throws tantrums over small things. Picture a pet that sulks when it does not get treats.
example: The toddler threw a petulant tantrum when he didn't get his way.

gre.s: The critic dismissed the actor's ____ outburst at the press conference, where he stormed off after a mildly critical question, as childish.
gre.clue: stormed off after a mildly critical question

en: Brief but full of meaning; concise and forceful
hook: PITHY: like the PITH, the dense core of a fruit — all substance.
story: Pithy. A young journalist asked the old businessman, who had started with nothing and built a huge company, for the secret of his success. Everyone expected a long speech. He thought for a moment and said: "Work hard. Spend less. Stay honest." Six words, a whole philosophy. His answer was pithy: brief but full of meaning. The pith is the dense core of a fruit. Proverbs are often pithy.
example: The author was known for his pithy and insightful observations.

gre.s: Unlike her long-winded opponent, the candidate was praised for her ____ answers, which captured complex ideas in a single memorable sentence.
gre.clue: captured complex ideas in a single memorable sentence

en: Easily bent; easily influenced
hook: PLIANT: PLIABLE, bends easily.
story: Pliant. Young bamboo in Bandarban bends almost to the ground in a cyclone, then springs back upright, unbroken, when the wind stops. It is pliant: easily bent without breaking. The new committee members were pliant too, agreeing to whatever the chairman proposed, never pushing back. Pliant means flexible physically, or easily influenced. Synonyms: pliable, malleable, tractable. The opposite is rigid or obstinate.
example: The sculptor preferred working with pliant clay for its versatility.

gre.s: The dictator surrounded himself with ____ advisers who never challenged his decisions, however reckless.
gre.clue: who never challenged his decisions

en: Making a show of being morally superior to others
hook: SANCTIMONIOUS: acts like a SAINT, but it's all for MONEY and show.
story: Sanctimonious. At every press conference, the politician lectured citizens about honesty, family values, and serving the nation with clean hands. He quoted holy books and wagged his finger at the camera. Then journalists discovered that he had taken bribes for twenty years and owned four secret flats abroad. His speeches had been sanctimonious: making a show of being morally superior to others. Holier-than-thou is a close synonym.
example: The politician's sanctimonious speech was at odds with his questionable past.

gre.s: Voters grew tired of the senator's ____ speeches about honesty, particularly after he was caught concealing his own debts.
gre.clue: after he was caught concealing his own debts

en: Based on valid reasoning; in good condition; reliable
hook: GRE trick: SOUND means solid and valid — a sound argument.
story: Sound. Mitu's plan to study abroad impressed her parents: she had savings for the first year, a partial scholarship, a part-time job lined up, and a clear career goal. Her reasoning was sound. Meanwhile, the old bridge outside her village had cracked pillars and was declared structurally unsound. On the GRE, sound means logically valid, solid, or reliable, not just a noise. Sound advice, a sound argument, a sound investment.
example: The lawyer presented a sound argument that convinced the jury.

gre.s: Although the argument's conclusion was surprising, its reasoning was ____, resting on well-established data and careful logic.
gre.clue: resting on well-established data and careful logic

en: To dull the shine of; to damage someone's reputation
hook: TARNISH: like silver that turns dark over time.
story: Tarnish. Grandmother's silver plates are beautiful at Eid, but if they are not polished every month, they turn dull and dark. They tarnish. A famous sprinter learned that reputations tarnish too: after twenty years of medals and respect, one failed drug test darkened his name forever. To tarnish is to dull the shine of something, or to damage someone's reputation. Synonyms: sully, besmirch, stain.
example: His reputation was tarnished by the corruption allegations.

gre.s: A single scandal can ____ a reputation that took decades to build.
gre.clue: that took decades to build

en: Lukewarm; showing little enthusiasm
hook: TEPID: like TEPID water, neither hot nor cold.
story: Tepid. The tea at Farhan's office was always tepid, neither hot nor cold, just sadly lukewarm. When the company announced a new logo at the annual meeting, the staff's response was equally tepid: a few polite claps, no cheering, people checking their phones. Tepid means lukewarm, literally in temperature or figuratively in enthusiasm. A tepid review is half-hearted praise. Its opposite is fervent.
example: The movie received a tepid response from critics.

gre.s: The director's latest film received only ____ reviews, with critics conceding that it was competent but hardly memorable.
gre.clue: competent but hardly memorable

en: To scold or criticize severely
hook: UP-BRAID: grab someone's BRAID and pull them UP for a scolding.
story: Upbraid. The players arrived for training late, out of shape, and laughing. The coach blew his whistle and gathered them in a circle. For twenty minutes he upbraided them: "You call yourselves athletes? You disrespect this shirt!" Nobody looked up. To upbraid is to scold or criticize someone severely. Picture someone grabbing a braid and pulling you up for a scolding. Synonyms: castigate, reprimand, rebuke, berate.
example: The coach upbraided his players for their lack of effort in the game.

gre.s: The editor would ____ any reporter who missed a deadline, sometimes in front of the entire newsroom.
gre.clue: sometimes in front of the entire newsroom

en: The state of being annoyed, frustrated, or worried
hook: VEXATION: VEXED, constantly bothered.
story: Vexation. Tanvir spent four hours completing his university application, carefully uploading every document. Three hours before the deadline, he clicked Submit. The page froze. The internet had died. The router lights blinked red. He nearly threw his laptop out of the window. To his great vexation, he had to run to a cyber café across the city. Vexation means the state of being annoyed, frustrated, or worried. A vexing problem is irritatingly hard to solve.
example: Sarah felt a growing sense of vexation at the long delay.

gre.s: Much to the ____ of the organizers, heavy rain forced them to cancel the outdoor concert just an hour before it was due to begin.
gre.clue: forced them to cancel the outdoor concert

en: To encourage or assist someone in doing something wrong
hook: ABET: placing A BET on the criminal and helping him win.
story: Abet. During the term final, one student slipped a folded answer sheet to his friend, while the boy at the next desk kept watch for the invigilator. All three were caught. The lookout protested that he had not cheated himself. "You abetted it," said the exam committee chairman. To abet is to encourage or help someone do something wrong. Lawyers speak of aiding and abetting a crime. Abet always carries guilt: you abet a thief, never a charity.
example: The rogue scientist abetted the villain's plans for world domination.

gre.s: Although the guard never touched the jewels himself, prosecutors argued that he chose to ____ the theft by deliberately leaving the vault unlocked.
gre.clue: by deliberately leaving the vault unlocked

en: Easy to reach, use, obtain, or understand
hook: ACCESSIBLE: easy ACCESS.
story: Accessible. Professor Kamal's first physics lectures were full of equations nobody could follow. After a dismal midterm, he changed his style. He explained gravity with a falling mango and electricity with the classroom ceiling fan. Suddenly even the history students taking his course as an elective understood him. His lectures had become accessible: easy to reach, use, or understand. A building with ramps is accessible to wheelchair users. Think: access is a way in, and accessible means there is a way in.
example: The library aims to make its resources accessible to everyone in the community.

gre.s: Unlike his dense earlier treatises, which only specialists could follow, the philosopher's final book is remarkably ____, written in plain prose for a general audience.
gre.clue: written in plain prose for a general audience

en: Excessively eager to acquire money or possessions
hook: ACQUISITIVE: always ACQUIRING more.
story: Acquisitive. Mr. Haque already owned three flats in Gulshan, two cars, and a shop in a busy market. Yet every weekend he went hunting for another plot of land, another apartment, another bargain. His children joked that he could not see anything without wanting to own it. He was deeply acquisitive: excessively eager to acquire money or possessions. The word comes from acquire, to get. An acquisitive society judges people by what they own. Synonyms: grasping, avaricious, covetous.
example: The acquisitive corporation ruthlessly bought out smaller businesses.

gre.s: Far from being content with his considerable wealth, the tycoon remained relentlessly ____, buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings.
gre.clue: buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings

en: To combine or unite into one
hook: AMALGAMATE: A MALL that GATHERs many shops into one.
story: Amalgamate. Two small banks in Chattogram were both struggling. Each had loyal customers but too little capital. Their boards met and agreed to join together as one larger bank, with a new name, one head office, and one set of accounts. They amalgamated. To amalgamate is to combine or unite into one. In chemistry, an amalgam is mercury mixed with another metal, like the silver tooth fillings dentists once used. Synonyms: merge, fuse, consolidate. Opposite: separate.
example: The two rival companies decided to amalgamate to increase their market share.

gre.s: Rather than keep the three struggling departments separate, the dean decided to ____ them into a single school with one budget and one administration.
gre.clue: into a single school with one budget and one administration

en: To reduce the force, effect, or value of; to make thin
hook: ATTENUATE: makes it THIN, TENUOUS.
story: Attenuate. Rumana's hostel room faced a road where buses honked all night. She hung a thick quilt over the window and stuffed towels under the door. The noise did not vanish, but it softened to a dull hum, and at last she slept. The quilt had attenuated the sound: reduced its force. To attenuate is to weaken, reduce, or make thin. Scientists attenuate a virus to make a safe vaccine. Think of tenuous, which also means thin and weak.
example: The medicine helped attenuate the patient's pain.

gre.s: Although the new drug does not cure the disease, it can ____ its most severe symptoms, making the illness far more bearable for patients.
gre.clue: making the illness far more bearable for patients

en: To make greater by adding to
hook: AUGMENT: like AUGMENTED reality adding layers to the world.
story: Augment. Tanvir's tuition fees swallowed most of his monthly allowance, leaving almost nothing for books. So he began teaching mathematics to two schoolchildren in the evenings. The extra eight thousand taka a month augmented his income enough to buy his GRE prep books. To augment is to make greater by adding to. You can augment a salary, a collection, or a team. Augment shares a Latin root with the name Augustus: augere, to increase. Synonyms: increase, supplement, boost.
example: The company sought to augment its profits by expanding into new markets.

gre.s: Because her scholarship barely covered tuition, she took a part-time job to ____ her income, adding enough each month to pay the rent.
gre.clue: adding enough each month to pay the rent

en: A strong dislike or disinclination
hook: AVERSION: you AVERT (turn away) your eyes from it.
story: Aversion. Ishita loves almost every Bangladeshi dish except bitter gourd. Since childhood, the sight of karela on her plate makes her push it away. Her mother tried frying it crisp, mixing it with potatoes, even hiding it in dal. Ishita still found it and refused. She has a strong aversion to it: a deep dislike. Aversion is usually followed by to: an aversion to crowds, an aversion to risk. Think of averse, turning away. Synonyms: distaste, antipathy, repugnance.
example: I have a strong aversion to spiders.

gre.s: The novelist's lifelong ____ to publicity explains why, despite her enormous commercial success, she has given almost no interviews.
gre.clue: she has given almost no interviews

en: Cheerfully carefree; casually indifferent to something serious
hook: BLITHE: BLISSfully unaware.
story: Blithe. Two days before his thesis was due, Shuvo was still singing in the hostel corridor, playing carrom, and planning a trip to Cox's Bazar. His roommate panicked on his behalf. Shuvo just smiled and said everything would work out. His attitude was blithe: cheerfully carefree, but dangerously indifferent to something serious. A blithe dismissal of a warning cheerfully ignores real danger. Blithe sounds light, like a bird singing, and that lightness is the point. Synonyms: carefree, nonchalant, heedless.
example: She strolled along with a blithe spirit, enjoying the sunshine.

gre.s: The CEO's ____ dismissal of the auditors' warnings, delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand, alarmed investors who knew how serious the losses were.
gre.clue: delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand

en: The feeling that someone or something is worthless or beneath consideration
hook: CONTEMPT: CON + TEMPT; you're not even tempted to respect it.
story: Contempt. At a wedding in Dhaka, a wealthy guest snapped his fingers at the young waiter, never once looking at his face, and complained loudly that people like him should be grateful for any work. Everyone at the table felt the sting. His tone showed contempt: the feeling that someone is worthless or beneath consideration. Contempt of court means disrespecting a judge's authority. The proverb says familiarity breeds contempt. Synonyms: scorn, disdain, derision. Opposite: respect.
example: The critic's review of the play was filled with contempt.

gre.s: Far from offering measured criticism, the reviewer made no attempt to hide her ____ for the film, dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph.
gre.clue: dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph

en: To waste time; to be slow
hook: DAWDLE: like a DOODLE, wasting time drawing nothing.
story: Dawdle. Babu was sent to the bazaar to buy fish for lunch. On the way he stopped to watch a cricket match, chatted with the tea seller, and spent twenty minutes admiring a new motorbike. He came home at two o'clock, and his mother had already cooked dal and rice without him. "Stop dawdling," she said. To dawdle is to waste time or move slowly. Students dawdle before starting homework. Synonyms: dally, linger, loiter. Opposite: hasten.
example: Stop dawdling and get your homework done!

gre.s: With the deadline only hours away, the team could not afford to ____; every minute spent idling would make the final report weaker.
gre.clue: every minute spent idling

en: To cause something to change direction; to avoid
bn: বিচ্যুত করা; ভিন্ন দিকে ফিরিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: DEFLECT: like a shield DEFLECTING an arrow.
story: Deflect. At a press conference, a reporter asked the minister about missing flood relief funds. The minister smiled and began talking about the new metro rail. The reporter asked again; the minister praised the national cricket team. He had deflected the question: turned it aside without answering. To deflect is to make something change direction, or to avoid it. A goalkeeper deflects a shot over the bar. Think: de means away, and flect means bend, so deflect means bend away.
example: The goalkeeper skillfully deflected the penalty shot.

gre.s: Rather than address the allegations directly, the spokesperson tried to ____ them, steering every question back toward the company's charitable work.
gre.clue: steering every question back toward the company's charitable work

en: To regard as unimportant or untrustworthy; to disregard
hook: GRE trick: DISCOUNT means to ignore, not just lower the price.
story: Discount. Mitu's grandmother has diabetes. When a neighbour insisted that bitter lemon water could replace her insulin, the doctor did not argue. He simply discounted the advice and kept her on her medicine. Some claims deserve to be discounted: regarded as unimportant or untrustworthy, and set aside. In a shop, a discount reduces the price; in an argument, discounting a claim reduces its weight to almost nothing. Never discount a theory just because it is new. Synonyms: disregard, dismiss.
example: Don't discount her ideas just because she's new to the team.

gre.s: Scientists were quick to ____ the anonymous report, since its author offered no data and had a long history of fabricating results.
gre.clue: had a long history of fabricating results

en: A person who opposes official policy, especially of an authoritarian state
hook: DIS-SIDE-ent: on the other SIDE.
story: Dissident. Under a military regime, a young journalist kept publishing articles that criticised the generals, even after her newspaper was shut down. She printed leaflets at night, was arrested twice, and finally had to flee the country. Yet her essays kept circulating. She was a dissident: a person who openly opposes official policy, especially in an authoritarian state. Dissident comes from dissent, to disagree. As an adjective, we speak of dissident voices or dissident writers. Opposite: loyalist.
example: The dissident group protested against the government's actions.

gre.s: The regime claimed to tolerate free speech, yet any ____ who criticized its policies in print could expect to be imprisoned or forced into exile.
gre.clue: who criticized its policies in print

en: Successful in producing the desired result; effective
hook: EFFICACIOUS: EFFECTIVE.
story: Efficacious. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, cholera and diarrhoea killed huge numbers of children in Bangladesh. Researchers in Dhaka helped show that a cheap drink of clean water, salt, and sugar could keep these children alive. Oral saline proved astonishingly efficacious: successful in producing the desired result. Efficacious is a formal word for effective, used mostly of treatments, methods, and policies. The noun is efficacy. Synonyms: effective, potent, successful. Opposite: ineffectual.
example: The new medicine proved to be efficacious in treating the illness.

gre.s: The manufacturer touted the supplement as highly ____, yet independent trials showed that it relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill.
gre.clue: relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill

en: Fair and impartial
hook: EQUITABLE: EQUAL for all.
story: Equitable. When their father died, three brothers in a Rajshahi village had to divide his mango orchard. The eldest wanted the biggest share. Their uncle walked the land, counted the trees, and drew the lines so that each brother received the same number of fruiting trees and equal access to the pond. Everyone agreed the division was equitable: fair and impartial. Equitable shares a root with equal and equity. Synonyms: fair, just, even-handed. Opposite: biased.
example: The goal is to create an equitable distribution of resources.

gre.s: Critics argued that the new tax was hardly ____, since it fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched.
gre.clue: fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched

en: Not regular or predictable; inconsistent
hook: ERRATIC: full of ERRORS, all over the place.
story: Erratic. Electricity in Joya's village came and went without any pattern. Some days it stayed on all evening; other days it vanished at noon, returned for ten minutes, and vanished again. Nobody could plan anything. The supply was erratic: irregular and unpredictable. Behaviour can be erratic too, like a driver swerving between lanes for no reason. Erratic shares a root with error and errant, meaning to wander. Synonyms: inconsistent, unpredictable, capricious. Opposite: steady.
example: The weather has been quite erratic this season.

gre.s: The athlete's performances have been so ____ this season, brilliant one week and dismal the next, that even her coaches cannot predict how she will do.
gre.clue: brilliant one week and dismal the next

en: Hardworking and diligent
hook: INDUSTRIOUS: works like a whole INDUSTRY.
story: Industrious. Farhan's mother runs a small tailoring shop in Mirpur. She opens at seven, sews until midnight during the Eid rush, keeps careful accounts, and still checks her son's homework. Neighbours say they have never once seen her idle. She is industrious: hardworking and diligent. Do not confuse it with industrial, which relates to factories. An industrious person works hard; an industrial zone has factories. Synonyms: diligent, assiduous, sedulous. Opposite: indolent.
example: The industrious student spent hours each day in the library.

gre.s: Though he had a reputation for laziness as a student, as an apprentice he proved remarkably ____, often staying at the workshop long after everyone else had gone home.
gre.clue: often staying at the workshop long after everyone else had gone home

en: To give information to; also, to give an essential quality to or influence
bn: জানানো; প্রভাবিত করা, বৈশিষ্ট্য দান করা
hook: GRE trick: experience INFORMS art means it SHAPES it from within.
story: Inform. Priya grew up in a fishing village near the Sundarbans, watching her father mend nets and survive cyclones. Years later, as an architect, she designed storm shelters for coastal towns. Every drawing carried what she had learned as a child about wind, water, and fear. Her childhood informed her work: it gave the work its essential quality and shaped it. Usually inform means to tell. On the GRE, it often means to shape or permeate, as in faith informs her poetry.
example: Please inform me of any changes in the schedule.
