hook: CHASTISE: CHASE them with words until they're CHASTE (corrected).
story: Chastise. Tanvir came home at two in the morning after a friend's wedding, without calling anyone. His father was waiting in the drawing room. For twenty minutes he chastised Tanvir: how careless, how selfish, how worried his mother had been. Tanvir stared at the floor and said nothing. To chastise is to scold or criticize severely. It shares a root with chaste and chasten, from a Latin word meaning to make pure, as if the scolding cleans out the fault. Synonyms: rebuke, reprimand, castigate.
example: The teacher chastised the student for repeatedly disrupting the class.

gre.s: Far from praising the minister's handling of the flood, the committee's report went out of its way to ____ him for delays that had cost lives.
gre.clue: Far from praising

en: Difficult to handle because of size, weight, or complexity
hook: CUMBERSOME: ENCUMBERS you, weighing you down.
story: Cumbersome. Nadia's family was moving from Chittagong to Dhaka, and the hardest item was her grandmother's old wooden almirah. It was enormous, heavy, and impossible to turn on the narrow stairs. Four men struggled with it for an hour. Cumbersome means difficult to handle because of size, weight, or complexity. The word also fits rules and systems: a cumbersome visa process with twelve forms and four offices is just as hard to carry. Synonyms: unwieldy, clunky, awkward.
example: Moving the cumbersome old piano proved to be a real challenge.

gre.s: The old registration process was so ____, requiring eleven separate forms and three office visits, that many applicants simply abandoned it halfway through.
gre.clue: requiring eleven separate forms and three office visits

en: Careful management of resources; thrift and efficiency in use
hook: GRE trick: ECONOMY of words means using no more words than needed.
story: Economy. Every month Sara's mother received a small salary, yet the family never went short. She bought vegetables in season, used cooking oil carefully, and turned leftover rice into breakfast. Her neighbours admired her economy: careful management of resources, wasting nothing. On the GRE, economy often describes style, too. A writer with economy of language never uses ten words when three will do. So economy means thrift and efficiency, not only a nation's finances. Synonyms: thrift, frugality, efficiency.
example: The company practiced strict economy in order to survive the economic downturn.

gre.s: Her prose is admired for its remarkable ____: she never uses three words where one will do, and every sentence seems to earn its place.
gre.clue: she never uses three words where one will do

en: Basic; relating to the simplest beginning stages
hook: ELEMENTARY: the basic ELEMENTS.
story: Elementary. On the first day of the GRE quant course, Arif felt almost insulted. The teacher began with fractions, percentages, and the area of a triangle, things he had learned in class six. But the teacher explained that elementary ideas are the foundation for everything harder. Elementary means basic, relating to the simplest beginning stages. An elementary school teaches the first steps of learning, and an elementary mistake is one even a beginner should avoid. Synonyms: basic, rudimentary, fundamental.
example: The teacher explained the elementary principles of arithmetic.

gre.s: Although the textbook advertises itself as an advanced treatment of the subject, its exercises are so ____ that a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon.
gre.clue: a first-year student could finish them in an afternoon

en: To decorate; to add details, often untrue, to make a story more interesting
hook: EMBELLISH: add BELLS to it, decorate.
story: Embellish. Every time Kamal told the story of the snake in his village pond, it grew. First it was a small water snake. A year later it was six feet long. By the time he told it at the hostel, it was a cobra that had chased him up a coconut tree. Kamal embellished the story: he added exciting details that were not true. To embellish also means to decorate, like embellishing a sari with embroidery. Synonyms: embroider, exaggerate, adorn.
example: The designer embellished the dress with intricate embroidery.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed when editors discovered her habit of choosing to ____ her reports with vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken.
gre.clue: vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken

en: Feeling intense happiness and excitement
hook: EUPHORIC: feeling EU-phoria, extreme 'yay!'
story: Euphoric. Late at night, Bangladesh won a cricket match in the very last over against one of the strongest teams in the world. Within minutes, the streets around Dhaka University filled with students shouting, singing, waving flags, and hugging strangers. Nobody could sleep. The whole city felt euphoric: intensely happy and excited. The noun is euphoria. Euphoria is more than contentment; it is a rush of joy, often brief. Its opposite is despair. Synonyms: elated, ecstatic, jubilant.
example: Winning the championship filled the team with a euphoric sense of victory.

gre.s: The mood among investors was ____ on the day the merger was announced, but within a week the celebration had given way to anxiety as share prices collapsed.
gre.clue: the celebration had given way to anxiety

en: To officially clear someone from blame
hook: EX-ONERATE: remove the ONUS (burden) of guilt.
story: Exonerate. A cashier at a Gulshan bank was accused of stealing two lakh taka. For weeks, colleagues whispered about her. Then the security camera footage was finally reviewed. It showed a different employee taking the money. The bank's inquiry exonerated her: it officially cleared her of all blame. Ex means off, and onus means burden: to exonerate is to take the burden of guilt off someone. Its opposite is incriminate. Synonyms: clear, absolve, vindicate.
example: The new evidence exonerated the wrongly convicted man.

gre.s: The new DNA evidence did more than cast doubt on his conviction; it served to ____ him entirely, and the court ordered his release that same afternoon.
gre.clue: the court ordered his release that same afternoon

en: To estimate unknown values by extending known trends
hook: EXTRA-POLATE: extend the line EXTRA far beyond the data.
story: Extrapolate. Zayan had been tracking his GRE practice scores: three hundred in March, three hundred and five in April, three hundred and ten in May. He drew a straight line on graph paper and extended it. 'By August I will score three twenty-five,' he announced. He was extrapolating: estimating unknown values by extending a known trend. His teacher warned that progress rarely stays a straight line. Extra means outside: you extrapolate beyond the data you actually have. Synonyms: project, infer.
example: Scientists extrapolated population growth patterns based on birth and death rates.

gre.s: Since reliable gauge records existed only up to 1990, the analysts had to ____ from earlier trends to estimate how high the river might be rising today.
gre.clue: Since reliable gauge records existed only up to 1990

en: To lose strength or momentum; to hesitate
hook: FALTER: like a FAULT in your step.
story: Falter. Joya had practised her debate speech twenty times. She began confidently, but halfway through, she glanced at the judges, saw one of them frowning, and lost her place. Her voice faltered. She paused, stammered, and searched her notes. To falter is to lose strength or momentum, or to hesitate. Economies falter, engines falter, and courage falters. Think of a fault in a machine making it falter and stall. Synonyms: waver, stumble, flag.
example: The speaker faltered for a moment, then regained his composure.

gre.s: The runner led for most of the marathon, but in the final kilometre her legs began to ____, and two rivals swept past her before the finish line.
gre.clue: two rivals swept past her

en: Having or showing intense passion
hook: FERVENT: burning with FERVOR.
story: Fervent. Every evening during the election season, Babu's uncle stood at the village tea stall, arguing passionately for his candidate. He printed posters with his own money, walked miles to rallies, and could recite every campaign promise from memory. He was a fervent supporter: full of intense passion. Fervent comes from a Latin word meaning to boil, the same root as fervour. A fervent prayer is one said with burning sincerity. Synonyms: ardent, zealous, passionate.
example: The crowd erupted in fervent applause for the inspiring speech.

gre.s: Though once a ____ supporter of the policy, attending every rally and writing letters to every newspaper, he became its harshest critic after seeing its effects.
gre.clue: attending every rally and writing letters to every newspaper

en: To stir up trouble or rebellion
hook: FOMENT: FERMENT trouble, let it bubble.
story: Foment. During a dispute at a garment factory, a few outsiders began spreading false rumours that the owners were about to cut everyone's wages. They held secret meetings and handed out angry leaflets. Within days, workers were blocking the gates. The outsiders had fomented unrest: they deliberately stirred it up. To foment is to stir up trouble or rebellion. Picture someone stirring a pot until it boils over. Synonyms: incite, instigate, provoke. Its opposite is quell.
example: Political activists were accused of fomenting unrest among the workers.

gre.s: Officials accused the pamphleteers of trying to ____ unrest among the factory workers, though the workers insisted their anger needed no outside encouragement.
gre.clue: their anger needed no outside encouragement

en: An embarrassing social mistake
hook: GAFFE: a GAFFE makes everyone LAUGH at you.
story: Gaffe. At his first office party, Shuvo met a tall woman by the snack table and complained loudly about the new managing director, who, he said, was strict and boring. The woman smiled politely and said, 'I am the new managing director.' Shuvo wanted to disappear. It was a terrible gaffe: an embarrassing social mistake. Politicians are famous for gaffes, like forgetting the name of the town they are visiting. Synonyms: blunder, faux pas, slip.
example: The politician's gaffe during the interview became a media sensation.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ was mocked for weeks: at a state dinner, he raised his glass to the host country using the name of its bitter rival.
gre.clue: he raised his glass to the host country using the name of its bitter rival

en: Not conforming to accepted or orthodox beliefs
hook: HETERO-DOX: DIFFERENT belief (orthodox = correct belief).
story: Heterodox. In a university economics seminar, every student repeated the standard textbook view. Then Ishita stood up and argued that the whole model ignored how real villages share risk through family networks. Some professors frowned; a few were intrigued. Her views were heterodox: not conforming to accepted beliefs. Hetero means other, and dox means opinion, as in orthodox, meaning right opinion. So heterodox means holding a different opinion. Synonyms: unorthodox, dissenting, nonconformist.
example: The artist's heterodox techniques shocked the conservative art world.

gre.s: Her ____ views on monetary policy, which rejected nearly every assumption of mainstream economics, made her unpopular with central bankers but fascinating to her students.
gre.clue: rejected nearly every assumption of mainstream economics

en: Overly theatrical or dramatic in behavior
hook: HISTRIONIC: like a HISTORIC actor overacting.
story: Histrionic. When an opponent barely brushed his shoulder, the football player threw himself to the ground, clutched his leg, rolled over three times, and raised his arms to the sky as if he had been shot. Moments later he was sprinting happily. His reaction was histrionic: overly theatrical and dramatic. Histrio was the Latin word for an actor, so histrionic behaviour is acting in real life. Synonyms: melodramatic, theatrical, overwrought.
example: Her histrionic outburst seemed out of proportion to the situation.

gre.s: The defence lawyer's ____ outbursts, complete with tearful pleas and pounding fists, struck the jury as calculated theatre rather than genuine emotion.
gre.clue: calculated theatre rather than genuine emotion

en: Implied though not directly expressed; absolute and unquestioning
hook: IMPLICIT: IMPLIED. Opposite: EXPLICIT.
story: Implicit. Lamia's mother never said, 'Do not come home late.' But every time Lamia returned after dark, her mother sat silently at the dining table, looking at the clock. The message was implicit: implied, though never directly expressed. Implicit is the opposite of explicit, which means clearly stated. A second sense means absolute and unquestioning, as in implicit trust: deep down, Lamia trusted her mother implicitly. Synonyms: implied, unspoken, tacit.
example: There was an implicit agreement that they would help each other.

gre.s: Although the contract never states it outright, both parties share the ____ understanding that the tenant will maintain the garden in exchange for lower rent.
gre.clue: never states it outright

en: Free from injury or violation; untouched
hook: IN-VIOLATE: NOT VIOLATED.
story: Inviolate. In one village near Sylhet, there is a small forest beside an old shrine. For generations, nobody has cut a single tree there, hunted a bird, or even carried away fallen branches. The villagers believe the grove is sacred. It has remained inviolate: free from injury or violation, completely untouched. In means not, so inviolate means not violated. A promise or a principle can also be inviolate. Synonyms: untouched, intact, sacrosanct.
example: The treaty aimed to protect the inviolate rights of all citizens.

gre.s: For centuries the sacred grove remained ____: villagers believed that anyone who cut even a single branch would bring disaster on the whole community.
gre.clue: anyone who cut even a single branch would bring disaster

en: Something that puts one at a disadvantage; legal responsibility
hook: LIABILITY: something you're LIABLE for, a burden.
story: Liability. Farhan was the fastest bowler on his university team, but he also argued with umpires in almost every match. Twice the team was penalised, and once they nearly lost a final because he was suspended. The captain finally told him, 'Your temper is a liability.' A liability is something that puts you at a disadvantage. In law and accounting, liability also means legal responsibility, or a debt. Its opposite is an asset. Synonyms: burden, handicap, drawback.
example: The company's outdated technology became a major liability.

gre.s: His reckless remarks to the press, once dismissed as charming, had become a serious ____ for the campaign, costing it the support of several key donors.
gre.clue: costing it the support of several key donors

en: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion
hook: OBSTINATE: an OBSTACLE that won't move.
story: Obstinate. Rahim's grandfather refused to take his blood pressure medicine. The doctor explained the risks, his children begged, and his grandchildren hid the sweets. Still he insisted that he had never been sick in seventy years and needed no pills. He was obstinate: stubbornly refusing to change his opinion. Obstinate often suggests unreasonable stubbornness. Hear the word obstacle in it: an obstinate person stands in your way like a rock. Synonyms: stubborn, intransigent, mulish.
example: The obstinate child refused to eat her vegetables.

gre.s: Despite overwhelming evidence that the bridge design was flawed, the chief engineer remained ____, refusing even to open the inspectors' report.
gre.clue: refusing even to open the inspectors' report

en: Done with or employing great care and thoroughness
hook: PAINS-TAKING: TAKING great PAINS.
story: Painstaking. Tania, a conservator at a Dhaka museum, was restoring a two-hundred-year-old manuscript. Using a tiny brush and a magnifying lens, she cleaned each page, mended each tear with special tissue, and checked each letter against old photographs. One page took her a whole week. Her work was painstaking: done with great care and thoroughness. The word literally means taking pains. Synonyms: meticulous, thorough, scrupulous. Its opposites are careless and slapdash.
example: The restoration of the antique vase required painstaking work.

gre.s: The restoration was ____: over eleven years, a small team of conservators cleaned the enormous mural one square centimetre at a time.
gre.clue: one square centimetre at a time

en: Calm and unemotional; not easily excited
hook: PHLEGMATIC: slow and calm, like thick PHLEGM.
story: Phlegmatic. The cyclone signal rose to number ten, and the coastal shelter was in panic. Children cried and men shouted over each other. Old Abdul the boatman simply sat in a corner, sharing out puffed rice and calmly telling families where to put their things. He was phlegmatic: calm and unemotional, not easily excited. Ancient doctors believed that too much phlegm in the body made a person sluggish and calm. Synonyms: imperturbable, stolid, unflappable.
example: The phlegmatic negotiator remained unfazed by the heated debate.

gre.s: While the other passengers screamed as the plane lurched through the storm, the ____ pilot calmly announced that they would still land on schedule.
gre.clue: calmly announced

en: Remarkably impressive in size, extent, or degree
hook: PRODIGIOUS: like a PRODIGY, extraordinary.
story: Prodigious. At the book fair, Mahin's little cousin amazed everyone. She had read over four hundred books by the age of eleven and could recite long poems by Rabindranath Tagore from memory. Her appetite for reading was prodigious: remarkably impressive in size and degree. The word is related to prodigy, a child with exceptional talent. A prodigious amount of rain, or prodigious energy, means an enormous amount. Synonyms: enormous, colossal, phenomenal.
example: The whale's prodigious size awed the onlookers.

gre.s: Mozart's output was ____: although he died at only thirty-five, he had already composed more than six hundred works.
gre.clue: more than six hundred works

en: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way
hook: PROPENSITY: a PRONE tendency.
story: Propensity. Sabbir had one strange habit. Whenever he was nervous, he bought snacks. Before every exam, every job interview, and every family wedding, his pockets filled with chanachur and biscuits. His friends teased him about his propensity to stress-eat: his natural tendency to behave that way. Pro means forward and pend means hang, as in pendulum: a propensity is the way you naturally lean. We speak of a propensity for violence or for risk. Synonyms: tendency, inclination, penchant.
example: He had a propensity for getting into trouble.

gre.s: Given his well-known ____ to exaggerate, his colleagues learned to divide every figure he quoted by at least two.
gre.clue: his colleagues learned to divide every figure he quoted by at least two

en: A feeling of doubt or unease, especially about one's conduct
hook: QUALM: a small QUALITY check of your conscience.
story: Qualm. Anika found a wallet near the Mirpur bus stand containing ten thousand taka. Her rent was overdue, and for a moment she thought of keeping the money. But the student card inside showed a young girl's face, and Anika felt a qualm: a sudden uneasy feeling that keeping it would be wrong. She returned it. A qualm is a feeling of doubt or unease, especially about one's conduct. Ruthless people have no qualms. Synonyms: misgiving, scruple, pang.
example: He had no qualms about accepting the ethically questionable job offer.

gre.s: She felt not the slightest ____ about reporting her own manager to the auditors, since she had watched him falsify the accounts with her own eyes.
gre.clue: since she had watched him falsify the accounts with her own eyes

en: To go back on a promise or agreement
hook: RENEGE: RE-NEG(ATE) your promise.
story: Renege. Before the election, a candidate promised Imran's village a new bridge. He shook hands with the elders and even laid a foundation stone. After winning, he announced that the money would go to a highway instead. He had reneged on his promise: gone back on it. Renege is almost always followed by on. Hear the word negative inside it: reneging is saying no to what you once said yes to. Synonyms: backtrack, default, go back.
example: The team accused their star player of reneging on his contract.

gre.s: Having promised in writing to fund the new library, the company later tried to ____ on the deal, claiming the agreement had never been binding.
gre.clue: claiming the agreement had never been binding

en: Ungenerous; restricting in amount
hook: STINTING: giving only a tiny STINT.
story: Stinting. Rumana's landlord was famously stinting. He allowed the water pump to run only one hour a day, fixed nothing until it broke completely, and gave the night guard a bonus of one hundred taka at Eid. Stinting means ungenerous, restricting the amount given. The word appears most often in its opposite form: unstinting praise means generous, wholehearted praise. To stint on something is to give too little of it. Synonyms: stingy, miserly, tight-fisted.
example: The stinting portions of food left the guests unsatisfied.

gre.s: Critics accused the government of being ____ with flood relief: families that had lost everything received barely a week's rations.
gre.clue: received barely a week's rations

en: To moderate or soften the intensity of something
hook: GRE trick: to TEMPER is to TONE DOWN, like tempering spicy food with yogurt.
story: Temper. Priya wrote a furious online review of a restaurant that had served her cold biryani. Before posting it, she read it again and decided it was too harsh. She removed the insults, mentioned the friendly waiter, and tempered her criticism: she moderated and softened it. As a verb, to temper is to moderate. Blacksmiths temper steel, heating and cooling it so it is less brittle. Losing your temper is the opposite of tempering anything. Synonyms: moderate, soften, mitigate.
example: The negotiator tried to temper the increasingly hostile atmosphere.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the committee's harsh conclusions, the chair added a paragraph acknowledging the team's genuine achievements under difficult conditions.
gre.clue: acknowledging the team's genuine achievements

en: Not certain or fixed; hesitant
hook: TENTATIVE: like a TENT, temporary, not permanent.
story: Tentative. Nadia's friends were planning a weekend trip to Cox's Bazar. 'Let us say Friday morning,' said Rafi, 'but nothing is final until we know the bus tickets are available.' They wrote the plan in pencil. It was tentative: not certain or fixed. Tentative can also describe a manner, as in a tentative smile or tentative first steps, meaning hesitant. It comes from a Latin word meaning to try: a tentative plan is only a trial. Synonyms: provisional, hesitant.
example: The scientists presented tentative findings, awaiting further data.

gre.s: The two governments reached only a ____ agreement, one that both sides stressed could be revised or even abandoned after further talks.
gre.clue: could be revised or even abandoned after further talks

en: Never done or known before
hook: UN-PRECEDENT-ED: no PRECEDENT, never happened before.
story: Unprecedented. In 2022, floodwater in parts of Sylhet rose higher than anyone could remember. Elders who had lived through decades of monsoons said they had never seen anything like it. Newspapers called the flood unprecedented: never done or known before. A precedent is an earlier example that guides later decisions, so unprecedented means having no earlier example at all. Lawyers search for precedents; an unprecedented case has none. Synonyms: unparalleled, unheard of, novel.
example: The magnitude of the humanitarian crisis was unprecedented.

gre.s: The flood was truly ____: in two hundred years of written records, the river had never risen even half as high.
gre.clue: had never risen even half as high

en: Lively and full of energy, especially in personality
hook: VIVACIOUS: full of VIVA (life).
story: Vivacious. When Mitu joined the office, the quiet accounts department changed overnight. She greeted everyone by name, told funny stories at lunch, organised a birthday party for the tea boy, and laughed so warmly that even the grumpy manager smiled. Colleagues called her vivacious: lively and full of energy. Viv means life, as in vivid and revive. A vivacious person seems more alive than everyone else in the room. Synonyms: lively, bubbly, spirited.
example: The vivacious puppy brought joy to the household.

gre.s: Unlike her reserved older sister, Shathi was ____, filling every room with laughter and chatter from the moment she arrived.
gre.clue: Unlike her reserved older sister

en: Containing indirect references or hints to something
hook: ALLUSIVE: full of ALLUSIONS (hints), not to be confused with elusive (hard to catch).
story: Allusive. In Ishita's literature class, the teacher read a poem about 'a river that remembers nineteen seventy-one' and 'a rebel who wrote in fire.' No names were given, yet every Bangladeshi student understood the hints. The poem was allusive: full of indirect references to things outside it. Do not confuse allusive with elusive, which means hard to catch, or illusive, which means deceptive. An allusion is a hint, and allusive writing is full of them. Synonyms: suggestive, referential.
example: The poem's allusive style left readers wondering about its deeper meaning.

gre.s: Her poems are deeply ____, packed with veiled references to Persian mystics and Bengali folk songs that most readers miss on a first reading.
gre.clue: packed with veiled references

en: Clever at understanding situations and turning them to one's advantage
hook: ASTUTE: A STUDENT who sees through everything.
story: Astute. When Mahin's uncle heard that a new private university would open beside his village market, he did not simply celebrate like everyone else. He quietly rented the empty shop opposite the main gate and turned it into a photocopy and stationery store. Within a year it was the busiest shop in the area. He was astute: clever at understanding situations and turning them to his advantage. Astute observers notice what others miss. Synonyms: shrewd, perceptive, canny.
example: The astute detective immediately noticed the inconsistencies in the suspect's story.

gre.s: The investor proved remarkably ____: while others panicked and sold, she quietly bought shares she knew were undervalued and tripled her money within a year.
gre.clue: while others panicked and sold

en: To begin
hook: COMMENCE: COMMENCEMENT is when graduates BEGIN their new life.
story: Commence. The invigilator walked to the front of the exam hall, checked the clock, and announced in a formal voice, 'You may now commence.' Two hundred students turned their papers over at once. Commence means to begin, but it sounds more formal, and it is used for ceremonies, trials, and official events. Interestingly, a graduation in America is called a commencement: not an ending but the beginning of a new life. Synonyms: begin, start, initiate. Its opposite is conclude.
example: The graduation ceremony commenced with a processional of faculty members.

gre.s: Although the ceremony was scheduled to ____ at nine, the chief guest's late arrival meant that nothing actually happened until nearly noon.
gre.clue: nothing actually happened until nearly noon

en: Recovering from illness
hook: CONVALESCENT: gaining back VALOR (strength) after illness.
story: Convalescent. After dengue fever kept Farhan in hospital for a week, he went home to his village to recover. For a month he sat on the veranda, drinking green coconut water, eating his mother's soups, and taking slow walks to the pond. He was a convalescent: someone recovering from illness. The recovery period is called convalescence. The root val means strong, as in valiant and valid: convalescing is growing strong again. Synonyms: recovering, recuperating.
example: The convalescent patient enjoyed short walks in the hospital garden.

gre.s: Though no longer in any danger, the ____ patient was still too weak to climb stairs, and her doctors advised another month of rest at home.
gre.clue: Though no longer in any danger

en: To restrain or keep in check
hook: CURB: the street CURB keeps cars from going too far.
story: Curb. Joya's monthly allowance kept disappearing on food delivery apps. By the twentieth of every month, she was borrowing money from her roommate. So she made a rule: no deliveries on weekdays, and only one treat on Friday. She was curbing her spending: restraining it and keeping it in check. A curb is also the raised edge of a road that keeps cars off the footpath, and a curb on a horse's bridle holds it back. Synonyms: restrain, check, rein in.
example: The city passed regulations to curb noise pollution.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the spread of the disease, health officials closed schools and banned large gatherings for a month, despite protests from businesses.
gre.clue: closed schools and banned large gatherings

en: To publicly denounce or strongly criticize
hook: DE-CRY: CRY out AGAINST it.
story: Decry. When a famous old banyan tree in a Dhaka park was cut down to build a car park, newspapers printed angry editorials, students held protests, and writers posted furious essays. Everyone decried the decision: they publicly denounced it. Think of it as crying out against something: de, cry. Do not confuse it with descry, which means to catch sight of something far away. Synonyms: denounce, condemn, deplore. Its opposite is to praise or extol.
example: Environmentalists decry the destruction of rainforests.

gre.s: Although the minister hailed the new law as a triumph for free speech, journalists were quick to ____ it as a thinly disguised tool of censorship.
gre.clue: a thinly disguised tool of censorship

en: Threats or force used to make someone do something
hook: DURESS: DURE (hard) STRESS.
story: Duress. A small shop owner in Old Dhaka signed a paper giving away his land. Months later, in court, he explained that local thugs had stood behind him and threatened his family while he signed. The judge cancelled the contract, because it had been signed under duress: under threats or force. Duress comes from a Latin word for hard, like durable and endure: duress is hard pressure. The usual phrase is under duress. Synonyms: coercion, compulsion, intimidation.
example: The suspect signed the confession under duress.

gre.s: The judge ruled the confession inadmissible because it had been obtained under ____: the suspect had been threatened and denied sleep for three days.
gre.clue: had been threatened and denied sleep for three days

en: To bring a feeling, memory, or image to mind
hook: E-VOKE: call (voke, voice) OUT a memory.
story: Evoke. Nadia had lived in Toronto for six years. One evening, in a small Bengali grocery, she smelled freshly fried shingara and heard an old Runa Laila song on the radio. Instantly she was nine years old again, sitting with her grandmother on a rainy afternoon in Comilla. The smell and the song evoked her childhood: they called those memories to mind. E means out, and voc means voice: to evoke is to call out a feeling. Synonyms: summon, conjure, awaken.
example: The old photograph evoked memories of her childhood.

gre.s: For many people, the smell of rain on dry earth seems to ____ childhood memories more powerfully than any photograph ever could.
gre.clue: more powerfully than any photograph ever could

en: To flatter or please someone excessively to gain favor
hook: FAWN: like a puppy wagging its tail, licking boots.
story: Fawn. Whenever the company chairman visited the branch office, Imran's manager became a different person. He held doors open, laughed loudly at every joke, praised the chairman's tie, and kept saying, 'Excellent idea, sir.' The moment the chairman left, he went back to shouting at everyone. He fawned over the chairman: he flattered him excessively to win favour. Picture an eager puppy wagging its tail. A fawn is also a baby deer, but the verb is about flattery. Synonyms: grovel, toady, kowtow.
example: The courtiers fawned over the king, hoping to gain his favor.

gre.s: Whenever the visiting director appeared, the junior staff would ____, laughing politely at his weakest jokes and praising his every remark, while the senior engineers remained coolly professional.
gre.clue: praising his every remark

en: To worry anxiously
hook: FRET: FRETTING like fingers on guitar FRETS, never still.
story: Fret. The night before her visa interview, Sara could not sleep. What if they asked about her funding? What if she forgot her bank statement? What if her English sounded nervous? Fret also means to wear away, like water fretting stone, which is exactly what worry does. Synonyms: worry, agonize, stew.
example: She fretted about her son's safety during the storm.

gre.s: Although her doctors assured her that every test result was normal, she continued to ____ about her health, waking at night convinced that something was wrong.

en: Fluent and smooth but insincere or shallow
hook: GLIB: GLIdes off the tongue too easily.
story: Glib. When a customer complained that his new phone had stopped working after two days, the salesman smiled and replied instantly: 'Sir, no problem, these things happen, our quality is the best, come back next week.' He said it all smoothly, without even looking at the phone. His answer was glib: fluent and smooth, but shallow and insincere. A glib speaker has a ready answer for everything but means very little. Synonyms: slick, facile, smooth-tongued.
example: The politician's glib answers failed to impress the voters.

gre.s: The spokesman's ____ answers, delivered smoothly and without a moment's hesitation, did little to reassure families who wanted a genuine explanation of the factory fire.

en: Stubbornly determined to have one's own way
hook: HEAD-STRONG: a head too strong to be turned.
story: Headstrong. At sixteen, Tania announced that she would become a professional photographer, not a doctor. Her parents argued, her aunts lectured, and her teachers warned her. Picture someone charging ahead head first, ignoring everyone. Compare obstinate, which stresses refusing to change one's mind. Synonyms: wilful, self-willed, wayward.
example: The headstrong child refused to listen to her parents.

gre.s: The ____ young officer ignored every warning from his superiors, insisting on leading the patrol along a route that he alone believed was safe.
gre.clue: ignored every warning from his superiors

en: Occurring at irregular intervals; not continuous
hook: INTER-MITTENT: stopping and starting, with gaps IN BETWEEN.

His online GRE mock test kept freezing. The connection was intermittent: occurring at irregular intervals, not continuous. Inter means between, and mit means send: something sent in bursts with gaps between. Intermittent rain falls on and off all day. Synonyms: sporadic, fitful, irregular. Its opposite is continuous or constant.
example: The intermittent rain showers made outdoor activities difficult.

gre.s: Electricity in the village was ____ at best, flickering on for an hour or so and then vanishing for the rest of the evening.
gre.clue: flickering on for an hour or so and then vanishing

en: Anger
hook: IRE: IRATE = angry.
story: Ire. The bus conductor in Mirpur charged Kamal double fare and then refused to give back his change. Its opposite is calm or approval.
example: The unfair decision aroused the ire of the crowd.

gre.s: The new tax on mobile data drew the ____ of students across the country, who staged noisy protests outside the ministry for an entire week.
gre.clue: staged noisy protests outside the ministry

en: Lacking energy; relaxed and slow
hook: LANGUID: LANGUISHING, lazy.
story: Languid. On a hot Friday afternoon in May, after a heavy lunch of rice and beef curry, the whole family lay on the floor under the ceiling fan. Nobody wanted to talk, read, or move. Even the cat stretched slowly and closed its eyes. The mood was languid: lacking energy, relaxed and slow. Languid can be pleasant, like a languid stroll by the river, or a sign of weakness. Related words are languish and languor. Synonyms: listless, sluggish, lethargic.
example: The humid weather made everyone feel languid.

gre.s: The afternoon heat made everyone ____: even the usually restless children lay on the cool floor, too sluggish to play or even talk.

en: A temporary period of calm; to calm or send to sleep
hook: LULL: a LULLABY puts you to sleep.
story: Lull. All afternoon the storm pounded the tin roof of Babu's house. Then, around sunset, the wind suddenly dropped and the rain stopped. Everyone rushed outside to check the cows and gather firewood before the next wave arrived. It was only a lull: a temporary period of calm. As a verb, to lull is to calm someone or send them to sleep, as a mother lulls a baby with a soft song. A lullaby lulls. Synonyms: pause, respite, break.
example: There was a lull in the conversation before the argument resumed.

gre.s: After weeks of relentless fighting, a brief ____ allowed aid workers to deliver food to the city, though the shelling resumed within two days.
gre.clue: allowed aid workers to deliver food

en: Full of spirit and courage
hook: METTLESOME: full of METAL, tough spirit. To test your METTLE.

Rumana's little brother, the smallest player on the field, tackled fearlessly, chased every ball, and scored the winning goal with a bleeding knee. Synonyms: spirited, plucky, gutsy.
example: The mettlesome young athlete was not afraid of challenges.

gre.s: Although she was the smallest player on the team, she was also the most ____, diving for every ball and never backing down from a challenge.
gre.clue: never backing down from a challenge

en: To calm someone's anger or anxiety
hook: MOLLIFY: make MOLLY soft and calm again.
story: Mollify. Priya forgot her best friend's birthday. Joya was hurt and stopped answering her messages. So Priya cooked Joya's favourite payesh, wrote a long handwritten apology, and turned up at her door with a small gift. Slowly Joya smiled. Priya had mollified her: she had calmed her anger. Moll comes from a Latin word meaning soft: to mollify is to soften someone's feelings. Synonyms: placate, appease, pacify. Its opposite is to provoke or enrage.
example: She tried to mollify her angry friend with kind words.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious passengers, the airline manager promised full refunds and apologized personally to each traveller.
gre.clue: promised full refunds and apologized personally

en: To make ineffective or harmless by an opposite force
hook: NEUTRALIZE: make NEUTRAL, neither acid nor base.
story: Neutralize. During a chemistry practical, Shuvo spilled a few drops of acid on the bench. The lab assistant calmly sprinkled baking soda over it. The fizzing stopped, and the acid became harmless. The baking soda had neutralized it: made it ineffective with an opposite force. example: The antidote neutralized the effects of the poison.

gre.s: Her rivals hoped the scandal would sink the senator's campaign, but her swift and candid apology served to ____ its effects almost entirely.
gre.clue: swift and candid apology

en: So surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react

Careful: many people wrongly use it to mean calm and unbothered. The true meaning is bewildered. Non plus is Latin for no more: nothing more to say. Synonyms: baffled, perplexed.
example: The strange question left him nonplussed.

gre.s: The professor, who seemed to have an answer for everything, was utterly ____ by the child's simple question and stood in silence for a full minute.
gre.clue: stood in silence for a full minute

en: Dangerously steep; sudden and dramatic
hook: PRECIPITOUS: like a PRECIPICE, a sheer cliff.

Think of a precipice, the edge of a cliff. Related is precipitate, meaning hasty or rash. Synonyms: steep, sheer, abrupt. Its opposite is gradual.
example: The stock market took a precipitous drop.

gre.s: The company's decline was ____: in a single quarter, its share price fell by ninety percent, wiping out a decade of steady growth.
gre.clue: in a single quarter

en: Trying to appear more important or cultured than one is
hook: PRETENTIOUS: PRETENDING to be grand.

He sprinkled his conversation with French words, said Dhaka had no real culture, and kept mentioning his famous friends. Everyone at the table rolled their eyes. example: Their pretentious house was filled with expensive but tasteless decorations.

gre.s: Critics found the novel ____, stuffed with Latin quotations and obscure philosophical references that seemed designed to impress rather than to illuminate.
gre.clue: designed to impress rather than to illuminate

en: Very great or intense; having deep insight

Those few words had a profound effect on her: very great and intense. A profound remark is one with deep insight. Pro means forward and fund means bottom: profound reaches toward the bottom, deep. Its opposite is superficial or shallow. Synonyms: deep, intense, insightful.
example: The philosopher's work had a profound impact on modern thought.

gre.s: Although the lecture was delivered in simple language, its insights were ____, forcing listeners to reconsider assumptions they had held all their lives.
gre.clue: forcing listeners to reconsider assumptions they had held all their lives

en: To spread widely; to breed or reproduce
hook: PROPAGATE: like PROPAGANDA spreading everywhere.

example: The rumor propagated quickly through the town.

gre.s: Rather than suppress the rumour, the agency's clumsy denial served only to ____ it, as thousands of users shared the statement with mocking comments.

en: A source of help in a difficult situation

The phrase have recourse to means to turn to something for help, as in recourse to the courts. Do not confuse it with resource, though a recourse is a resource you fall back on. Synonyms: option, remedy, refuge.
example: When negotiations failed, their only recourse was legal action.

gre.clue: Because their insurance policy explicitly excluded flood damage

hook: REFUTE: REFUSE to accept, and PROVE it false.

example: The scientist's experiments refuted the earlier theory.

gre.s: The scientist did not merely question the theory; she set out to ____ it decisively, publishing data showing that its central prediction was simply false.

Within weeks he was using single words again. He had regressed: returned to an earlier, less developed state. Re means back and gress means step, as in progress, which steps forward. Regress steps backward. Synonyms: relapse, revert, backslide. Its opposite is to progress or advance.
example: The patient's health regressed after the treatment stopped.

Synonyms: consequence, aftermath, fallout.

example: Before the long hike, they replenished their water bottles.

hook: VIGILANT: keeping a VIGIL all night, watching.

en: To attack violently, physically or with criticism
hook: ASSAIL: ASSAULT someone.

example: The buoyant hot air balloon drifted across the clear sky.

en: To support or strengthen

Engineers built thick brick supports against it from the outside, and the wall stopped moving. Those supports are called buttresses. Gothic cathedrals in Europe are famous for their flying buttresses. Synonyms: bolster, reinforce, shore up.

example: The school has a strict policy against condoning any form of bullying.

gre.s: The monsoon rains that year were heavy enough to ____ the low-lying villages, forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground with whatever they could carry.

en: Impossible to break or contradict

story: Steadfast. When Babu's small grocery shop was failing, most of his friends stopped visiting. One old friend, Habib, came every evening anyway. Three years later the shop was thriving, and Babu still calls Habib his most steadfast friend: resolutely firm and loyal. Stead means place, as in instead: a steadfast person stays fast in their place. Synonyms: loyal, unwavering, constant.
example: Her steadfast support throughout the ordeal was a great comfort.

gre.s: Through years of exile and imprisonment, she remained ____ in her commitment to democracy, refusing every offer of freedom that required her to renounce it.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of freedom

en: Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality
hook: GRE trick: SUSPECT as an adjective means questionable.
story: Suspect. A website promised Ishita a full scholarship abroad if she paid a ten-thousand-taka registration fee within twenty-four hours. The site had spelling mistakes, no physical address, and a phone number nobody ever answered. Her professor said the offer was suspect: not to be trusted, of doubtful quality. As an adjective, suspect is stressed on the first syllable and means questionable. Suspect data and suspect motives cannot be relied on. Synonyms: dubious, questionable, fishy.
example: The police investigated a suspect package found in the building.

gre.s: The study's conclusions are ____, since it was funded by the very company whose product it praises and its raw data have never been released.
gre.clue: funded by the very company whose product it praises

en: Too long, slow, or dull; tiresome
hook: TEDIOUS: like TED talking forever.
story: Tedious. Every Monday morning, Rumana's office held a three-hour meeting. The manager read every line of the weekly report aloud, slowly, including numbers everyone had already seen. People yawned, checked their phones, and stared at the clock. The meeting was tedious: too long, slow, and dull. Tedious comes from tedium, meaning boredom. Copying a thousand addresses by hand is a tedious task. Synonyms: boring, monotonous, wearisome. Its opposite is exciting or engaging.
example: The tedious paperwork took hours to complete.

gre.s: Although the documentary covered a fascinating subject, its endless statistics and droning narration made it ____ for most viewers.
gre.clue: endless statistics and droning narration

en: The state of being strong and energetic
hook: VITALITY: VITAL life energy.
story: Vitality. Every morning at six, Shuvo's eighty-year-old grandmother walks two kilometres around the lake in Dhanmondi, tends her rooftop garden, and argues cheerfully with the vegetable sellers. Her grandchildren, still half asleep, cannot keep up with her. She is full of vitality: the state of being strong and energetic. Vit means life, as in vital and vitamin. A city or an economy can also have vitality, meaning liveliness and growth. Synonyms: vigour, energy, vibrancy.
example: The dancer's performance was full of vitality.

gre.s: Even at eighty, the sculptor retained a remarkable ____, working twelve hours a day and climbing scaffolding that exhausted assistants half her age.
gre.clue: working twelve hours a day

en: Playfully quaint or fanciful; acting on sudden impulses
hook: WHIMSICAL: full of WHIMS.
story: Whimsical. Lamia's art teacher painted the classroom ceiling with flying fish, umbrellas growing like flowers, and a cat riding a rickshaw through the clouds. The students loved it. Her style was whimsical: playfully quaint and fanciful. The word also describes acting on sudden impulses: one day she whimsically cancelled a test and took everyone to see the river. A whim is a sudden, unexplained desire. Synonyms: playful, fanciful, capricious.
example: The whimsical design of the building looked like something from a fairy tale.

gre.s: The architect's otherwise sober design included one ____ touch: a staircase painted to look like a row of giant piano keys.
gre.clue: otherwise sober design

en: To produce or provide; to give way under pressure
hook: YIELD has two meanings: PRODUCE (a crop yields rice) and GIVE WAY (a yield sign).
story: Yield. In a northern village, farmers tried a new variety of rice developed by agricultural scientists. At harvest time, each field yielded nearly twice as much grain as before: it produced more. The amount produced is also called the yield. But yield has a second meaning: to give way under pressure. Drivers yield to an ambulance, letting it pass, and an old bridge may yield under a heavy truck. Synonyms: produce, give way, surrender.
example: The apple tree yielded a bountiful harvest this year.

gre.s: Researchers hoped the new irrigation method would ____ larger harvests, but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever.
gre.clue: but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever

en: Anxiety or fear that something bad will happen; also, understanding or arrest
hook: APPREHENSION: feeling like you're about to be APPREHENDED (arrested).
story: Apprehension. The night before her first viva, Mitu could not sleep. She kept imagining the examiners frowning, a question she could not answer, her voice cracking. By morning her hands were cold and her stomach was tight. That uneasy dread about what might go wrong is apprehension: anxiety or fear that something bad will happen. The word has two other senses: understanding, and the arrest of a criminal. Think of the mind grasping a danger before it arrives. Synonyms: dread, unease.
example: Sarah's apprehension about her job interview was palpable.

gre.s: Although the villagers greeted the new dam with ____, fearing floods and lost farmland, their worries proved unfounded when the first monsoon passed without incident.
gre.clue: fearing floods and lost farmland

en: Very enthusiastic or passionate
hook: ARDENT: burning with ARDOR.
story: Ardent. Every Friday at dawn, Rafi's grandfather walks two kilometres to the field where the village boys play cricket. He has not missed a match in thirty years. He knows every player's batting average and shouts advice from the boundary until he is hoarse. He is an ardent fan: passionate and intensely devoted. Ardent comes from the Latin word for burning, the same root as arson. An ardent supporter burns with enthusiasm. Synonyms: fervent, zealous, passionate.
example: The team's ardent fans cheered them on throughout the game.

gre.s: Even her most ____ admirers, who had defended every one of her earlier films against hostile reviewers, conceded that her latest effort was a disappointment.
gre.clue: who had defended every one of her earlier films

en: Self-evident; accepted as true without proof
hook: AXIOM: a basic truth in math, needing no proof.
story: Axiomatic. In his first geometry class at university, Tanvir watched the professor write on the board: a straight line can be drawn between any two points. Tanvir raised his hand and asked for the proof. The professor smiled. 'There is none. We simply accept it, because it is obvious.' Such a statement is an axiom, and anything treated this way is axiomatic: self-evident, accepted as true without proof. In economics, it is almost axiomatic that people respond to incentives.
example: The laws of physics are often considered axiomatic.

gre.s: It was once considered ____ that the sun revolved around the earth, a truth so plain that no one thought to question it, yet the assumption proved entirely false.
gre.clue: so plain that no one thought to question it

en: To come to an end; to stop
hook: CEASE: CEASE-FIRE, stop shooting.
story: Cease. For three days, construction drills roared outside the hostel from dawn to midnight, and students could not study for their exams. Finally the city authorities issued an order: all work must cease after eight in the evening. That night, at exactly eight, the noise stopped, and the whole hostel cheered. To cease is to come to an end, or to bring something to an end. A ceasefire is when guns stop firing. Something that never stops is unceasing. Synonyms: stop, halt.
example: The rain will cease later this evening.

gre.s: The two factions agreed to ____ hostilities during the festival, but the fragile truce collapsed only days after the celebrations ended.
gre.clue: the fragile truce

en: Making a certain outcome likely; helpful
hook: CONDUCIVE: CONDUCTS you toward a result.
story: Conducive. Sara could never study in her family's crowded flat in Mirpur, with the television blaring and cousins dropping by. So she found a corner of the university library: soft light, a big window, total silence. In that corner she finished two chapters in one afternoon. The library was conducive to study: it made good work likely. Conducive means making a certain outcome likely, or helpful to it, and it is usually followed by to. Think: it conducts you toward a result.
example: The quiet library was conducive to studying.

gre.s: Critics argued that the open-plan office, with its constant chatter and interruptions, was hardly ____ to the deep concentration that serious research demands.
gre.clue: with its constant chatter and interruptions

en: Relating to the physical body; material rather than spiritual
hook: CORPOREAL: CORPS, CORPSE, body.
story: Corporeal. Grandmother Rahima tells the village children about ghosts who walk through walls and leave no footprints. Her grandson Babu, a physics student, laughs: a ghost could never open a door, he says, because it has no body. Ghosts and spirits are imagined as non-physical. Humans, with hunger, bruises and tired feet, are corporeal: relating to the physical body, material rather than spiritual. Corpus is Latin for body, as in corpse and corps. The opposite is incorporeal.
example: Ghosts are often depicted as fading, insubstantial beings, lacking a corporeal form.

gre.s: The monks believed that ____ pleasures such as food and comfort were mere distractions; only by disciplining the body could they attend to the needs of the soul.
gre.clue: only by disciplining the body

en: Rigidly applying a theory without regard for practical considerations
hook: DOCTRINAIRE: follows the DOCTRINE no matter what.
story: Doctrinaire. A new manager at a garment factory near Dhaka had read one textbook on efficiency and believed every word. When workers explained that his new shift schedule ignored the monsoon flooding on their roads, he refused to change a single line, because the theory said so. Production collapsed. His approach was doctrinaire: rigidly applying a theory without regard for practical reality. The word comes from doctrine, a fixed set of beliefs. Opposite: pragmatic. Synonyms: dogmatic, inflexible.
example: The doctrinaire politician refused to compromise on any issue.

gre.s: Unlike her ____ predecessor, who insisted on following party ideology even when it produced obvious failures, the new minister was willing to adapt policies to local conditions.
gre.clue: insisted on following party ideology even when it produced obvious failures

en: Drawing from a wide variety of sources or styles
hook: ECLECTIC: ELECTS a bit from everywhere.
story: Eclectic. Joya's playlist confuses her friends. Rabindra Sangeet is followed by Korean pop, then a Bach cello suite, then a baul song from Kushtia, then American jazz. Her bookshelf is the same: poetry, physics, cookbooks and detective novels side by side. Her taste is eclectic: drawn from a wide variety of sources and styles. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to pick out, so an eclectic person selects the best from everywhere. Synonyms: diverse, wide-ranging.
example: The restaurant had an eclectic menu, offering dishes from all over the world.

gre.s: The architect's style resists easy categorization: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction, it is thoroughly ____.
gre.clue: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction

en: Mental calmness and composure, especially in difficulty
hook: EQUA-NIMITY: an EQUAL, balanced mind.
story: Equanimity. The power went out in the middle of Arif's online job interview. His laptop died, the generator failed, and he had to rejoin on his phone from the stairwell, fifteen minutes late. Instead of panicking, he apologised calmly, smiled, and answered every question clearly. The interviewers were impressed by his equanimity: mental calmness and composure, especially in difficulty. Equi means equal and animus means mind, so equanimity is an even mind. Synonyms: composure, poise, calm.
example: She handled the crisis with remarkable equanimity.

gre.s: Though her colleagues panicked when the funding was suddenly withdrawn, the director responded with remarkable ____, calmly drafting a new budget that same afternoon.
gre.clue: calmly drafting a new budget that same afternoon

en: Unreasonably high, especially of price
hook: EX-ORBIT-ANT: prices gone OUT OF ORBIT.
story: Exorbitant. The night before Eid, Imran went to buy a bus ticket home to Rangpur. The usual fare was eight hundred taka. The man at the counter demanded three thousand. Rickshaw fares had tripled, and even a cup of tea cost double. 'These prices are exorbitant,' Imran groaned: unreasonably high. Ex means out of, and orbit means track, so an exorbitant price has wandered right out of its normal orbit. Synonyms: excessive, extortionate, outrageous.
example: The exorbitant cost of the designer handbag was beyond her budget.

gre.s: Many families who once used the private clinic now avoid it, since its ____ fees put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers.
gre.clue: put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers

en: Changing frequently, especially in loyalty or affection
hook: FICKLE: FLICKERS like a candle.
story: Fickle. Last year the whole neighbourhood adored a young cricketer. Posters of him hung in every tea stall. Then he scored zero in two matches, and overnight the same fans tore down his posters and cheered a new hero. Public affection is fickle: changing frequently, especially in loyalty or affection. Dhaka's weather in April is fickle too, sunny one hour and stormy the next. Contrast with steadfast, which means firmly loyal. Synonyms: capricious, inconstant.
example: Fashion trends can be notoriously fickle.

gre.s: Politicians who rely on the ____ support of voters soon learn that a single unpopular decision can turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents.
gre.clue: turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents

en: Not literal; using figures of speech like metaphors
hook: FIGURATIVE: a FIGURE of speech.
story: Figurative. When Shuvo's mother said he had a mountain of homework, his little sister ran to the window looking for the mountain. She took the phrase literally. But their mother was speaking in a figurative way: not literal, using a figure of speech. Metaphors, similes and exaggerations are all figurative language. Telling an actor to break a leg is figurative; nobody wants an actual broken leg. The opposite of figurative is literal. Synonyms: metaphorical, symbolic.
example: The poet used figurative language to paint vivid images in the reader's mind.

gre.s: Readers who interpret the poet's 'burning city' as an actual fire miss the point; the phrase is ____, describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze.
gre.clue: describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze

en: Agitated, nervous, and confused
hook: FLUSTERED: FLUSHED and FLUTTERED.
story: Flustered. Lamia had rehearsed her presentation twenty times. But on the day, the projector would not connect, her notes slid onto the floor, and the professor said, 'We are short of time, please hurry.' Her cheeks went hot, she mixed up two slides, and she forgot her own opening line. She was flustered: agitated, nervous and confused. Fluster sounds like flutter, the way a frightened bird's wings flap about. Opposite: composed, unruffled. Synonyms: rattled, frazzled.
example: The surprise question flustered the speaker, momentarily interrupting his flow.

gre.s: Though normally unflappable in debate, the senator became visibly ____ when a reporter produced the documents, stammering and contradicting his own earlier statements.
gre.clue: stammering and contradicting his own earlier statements

en: Easily deceived or tricked
hook: GULLIBLE: like a sea GULL that swallows anything thrown at it.
story: Gullible. A text message arrived on Kamal's uncle's phone: 'Congratulations! You have won fifty lakh taka in a lottery. Send two thousand taka to claim your prize.' He had never bought a lottery ticket, yet he sent the money at once. Of course, there was no prize. He was gullible: easily deceived or tricked. Picture a hungry gull, a seabird that swallows anything thrown to it. Scammers hunt for gullible victims. Synonyms: credulous, naive.
example: The con artist preyed upon gullible tourists.

gre.s: Far from being ____, the investigator questioned every claim the witness made, insisting on documents for even the most trivial details.
gre.clue: questioned every claim the witness made

en: Peculiar to an individual; distinctive and unusual
hook: IDIO-SYNCRATIC: IDIO means one's own (as in idiom).
story: Idiosyncratic. Professor Haque always lectures barefoot, writes on the board only with his left hand, and opens every class by singing a line from Lalon. His students imitate him affectionately. His habits are idiosyncratic: peculiar to him alone, distinctive and unusual. Idios is Greek for one's own, the same root as idiom. An idiosyncrasy is one such personal quirk. An idiosyncratic writing style is instantly recognisable as one person's. Synonyms: quirky, eccentric, peculiar.
example: Her idiosyncratic sense of style made her stand out.

gre.s: The novelist's spelling and punctuation are so ____ that editors hesitate to correct them, fearing they would erase the very quirks that make her voice unmistakable.
gre.clue: the very quirks that make her voice unmistakable

en: Happening as a minor part or consequence of something more important
hook: INCIDENTAL: just a side INCIDENT.
story: Incidental. Ishita joined the photography club only to learn how to use her new camera. But on the club's trips she made five close friends and discovered a love of travel. Those friendships were incidental benefits: they came along as minor side effects of her main purpose. Incidental means happening as a minor part or consequence of something more important. Incidental expenses are small extra costs, like rickshaw fares on a business trip. Contrast with essential or central.
example: The costs of travel are incidental to the main purpose of the trip.

gre.s: The lawyer argued that the photograph was merely ____ to the case, a minor detail that had no bearing on the central question of who signed the contract.
gre.clue: a minor detail that had no bearing on the central question

en: Firmly fixed or established, hard to change
hook: INGRAINED: deep IN the GRAIN of the wood.
story: Ingrained. Rahim moved from his village to a modern Dhaka office where everyone drank coffee and spoke English in meetings. Yet ten years later he still woke at dawn without an alarm, still removed his shoes at every door, and still touched the feet of elders. These habits were ingrained: firmly fixed and hard to change. Picture a stain worked so deep into the grain of wood that no scrubbing can remove it. Synonyms: deep-rooted, entrenched.
example: The ingrained belief in superstitions was hard to shake off.

gre.s: Prejudices that are ____ in a culture rarely vanish with the passage of a single law; they persist for generations, handed down quietly from parents to children.
gre.clue: they persist for generations

en: Boldly rude and disrespectful
hook: INSOLENT: INSULTING.
story: Insolent. When the headmaster asked Sabbir why he was late again, Sabbir leaned back, chewed his gum loudly, and said, 'Why do you care? It is not your life.' The whole class gasped. Nobody spoke to the headmaster like that. Sabbir's reply was insolent: boldly rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone in authority. Contrast it with deferential, which means politely respectful. Insolent and impudent are close cousins. Synonyms: impertinent, cheeky, brazen.
example: The student's insolent remark earned him a detention.

gre.s: The new recruit's ____ remarks to the general, delivered with a smirk in front of the entire regiment, earned him a week of confinement to barracks.
gre.clue: delivered with a smirk in front of the entire regiment

en: To mock or ridicule through satire
hook: LAMPOON: like a cartoon that LAMPS (lights up) someone's flaws for laughs.
story: Lampoon. Every winter, Dhaka University students stage a comedy night. This year one sketch showed a minister promising smooth new roads while standing knee-deep in a flooded street, still smiling for the cameras. The audience howled. The students lampooned the minister: they mocked him through satire. Lampoon is also a noun, meaning a piece of writing or performance that ridicules someone. Cartoonists lampoon politicians every day. Synonyms: satirize, parody, ridicule.
example: The political cartoonist was famous for his sharp lampoons of public figures.

gre.s: Rather than attack the dictator directly, the playwright chose to ____ him, exaggerating his vanity until audiences could not stop laughing.
gre.clue: exaggerating his vanity until audiences could not stop laughing

en: Rich, elaborate, and generous; to give generously
hook: LAVISH: like a LAVA flow of luxury.
story: Lavish. Farhan's cousin's wedding lasted five days. There were three thousand guests, a stage covered in roses, fireworks over the river, and seven kinds of biryani. Everyone agreed it was lavish: rich, elaborate and generous. As a verb, to lavish means to give generously, as when the grandmother lavished gold on the bride. The word comes from an old French word for a downpour of rain: generosity pouring down. Opposite: frugal. Synonyms: sumptuous, extravagant.
example: The wedding reception was a lavish affair with a five-course meal.

gre.s: Critics accused the company of hypocrisy: even as it cut workers' wages, it held a ____ banquet for its executives, complete with imported wine and live music.
gre.clue: complete with imported wine and live music

en: Looking or sounding sad and dismal
hook: LUGUBRIOUS: LUG-ubrious, LUGGING sadness around.
story: Lugubrious. Tanvir's old neighbour plays sad songs on his harmonium every evening. His face is long, his voice is slow and heavy, and even his jokes sound like funeral speeches. When he says good morning, it sounds like bad news. He is lugubrious: looking or sounding sad and dismal, often in an exaggerated way. The word comes from the Latin lugere, to mourn. Notice the long, slow, heavy sound of the word itself. Synonyms: mournful, doleful, gloomy.
example: The lugubrious music set a somber tone for the funeral.

gre.s: The director's films are relentlessly ____: long, slow scenes of grieving widows set to funeral music leave audiences longing for even a moment of levity.
gre.clue: long, slow scenes of grieving widows set to funeral music

en: Disturbing and horrifying because involving death or injury
hook: MACABRE: think 'MAKE A BURIAL' scene.
story: Macabre. The village storyteller loved to frighten children. His favourite tale was of a graveyard where skeletons danced at midnight and a headless boatman rowed coffins across the river. The children shivered but begged for more. His stories were macabre: disturbing and horrifying because they dwelt on death. The word recalls the Dance of Death, a medieval image of skeletons leading the living to the grave. Synonyms: grisly, gruesome, ghoulish.
example: The horror movie was filled with macabre scenes.

gre.s: The museum's exhibit on the medieval plague was undeniably ____, displaying skulls, burial records, and paintings of corpses piled in the streets.
gre.clue: displaying skulls, burial records, and paintings of corpses piled in the streets

en: Sullen and gloomy
hook: MOROSE: MORE OF A ROSE losing its petals, wilting sadly.
story: Morose. After failing his driving test for the third time, Zayan came home, refused dinner, and sat on the balcony staring at the traffic. When his sister tried to cheer him up, he grunted and turned away. For two days he barely spoke. He was morose: sullen and gloomy. A morose person is not only sad but withdrawn and unwilling to talk. Contrast with lugubrious, which is sad in a showy, exaggerated way. Synonyms: sullen, glum, sulky.
example: The morose teenager refused to participate in any activities.

gre.s: Although he had once been the life of every party, years of illness left him ____ and withdrawn, rarely speaking even to his oldest friends.
gre.clue: rarely speaking even to his oldest friends

en: Too eager to tell people what to do; intrusively interfering
hook: OFFICIOUS: acts like an OFFICER nobody appointed.
story: Officious. At a government office in Motijheel, one junior clerk would not let anyone pass without checking their forms, even people looking for the toilet. He corrected spelling on documents that were not his job, told visitors where to stand, and lectured an old man about his handwriting. He was officious: too eager to tell people what to do, intrusively interfering. Careful: officious does not mean official. Synonyms: meddlesome, bossy, intrusive.
example: The officious store clerk kept trying to steer her towards more expensive items.

gre.s: The ____ hall monitor, who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on inspecting every student's bag and lecturing teachers about punctuality.
gre.clue: who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on

en: A complex consequence of an action or event
hook: RAMIFICATION: branches (rami) spreading out from a decision.
story: Ramification. The government raised the price of diesel by twenty taka. It seemed a small change. But soon bus fares rose, then vegetable prices climbed because trucks cost more to run, and farmers could no longer afford to run their irrigation pumps. Each of these was a ramification: a complex, often unexpected consequence. Ramus is Latin for branch, so one decision branches out into many results. Synonyms: consequence, repercussion, implication.
example: The company didn't fully understand the ramifications of its decision.

gre.s: The committee hastily approved the plan without weighing a single ____ of its decision; within a year, unforeseen effects had rippled through every department.
gre.clue: unforeseen effects had rippled through every department

en: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled
hook: SERENE: SERENITY.
story: Serene. At five in the morning, Priya sat on the shore of Kaptai Lake. Mist hung over the green hills, the water lay perfectly still, and the only sound was a distant boatman's oar. After months of Dhaka traffic, she felt her whole body relax. The scene was serene: calm, peaceful and untroubled. A serene person stays calm even in a crisis. Serenity is the noun. Contrast with turbulent. Synonyms: tranquil, placid.
example: The serene lake at dawn was a breathtaking sight.

gre.s: In contrast to the frantic, crowded market just outside its walls, the monastery garden remained ____, its stillness broken only by birdsong.
gre.clue: its stillness broken only by birdsong

en: To replace, especially by force or scheming
hook: SUP-PLANT: uproot one PLANT and put another in its place.
story: Supplant. For decades the pedal rickshaw ruled Dhaka's narrow lanes. Then battery-powered auto-rickshaws arrived, faster and cheaper, and slowly pushed the old rickshaws off route after route. In some neighbourhoods they have supplanted them entirely: replaced them and taken their place. Supplant often suggests replacing by force or scheming. The Latin root means to trip someone up by the heel and then take their spot. Synonyms: replace, oust, displace.
example: The new technology quickly supplanted the old methods.

gre.s: The ambitious deputy spent years flattering the board and quietly undermining his superior, plotting all the while to ____ her as head of the company.
gre.clue: quietly undermining his superior

en: Understood or implied without being stated
hook: TACIT: TACITURN, silent agreement.
story: Tacit. Mahin and his roommate share one small desk. Nobody ever discussed it, but Mahin uses it from seven to nine every evening, and his roommate takes over afterwards. They never quarrel about it. Their arrangement is tacit: understood without being stated. Tacit comes from the Latin for silent, the same root as taciturn, meaning a person of few words. Silence can signal tacit approval: by saying nothing, you agree. Synonyms: implicit, unspoken.
example: There was a tacit agreement between them to keep the matter secret.

gre.s: Although the treaty never explicitly mentioned the disputed island, both nations had reached a ____ understanding that neither would station troops there.
gre.clue: never explicitly mentioned

en: To go beyond the limits of
hook: TRANS-CEND: climb (scend) ACROSS (trans) the limits.
story: Transcend. Lalon, the mystic singer of Kushtia, lived in a society divided by religion and caste. Yet his songs are sung by Hindus and Muslims, farmers and professors, rich and poor alike. His music transcends those divisions: it goes beyond their limits. Trans means beyond, and the rest comes from a Latin verb meaning to climb, as in ascend. To transcend is to climb beyond. Great art can transcend language and time. Synonyms: surpass, exceed, rise above.
example: The artist's work transcended the limitations of her medium.

gre.s: The finest translations ____ the limits of a word-for-word rendering; rather than merely copying sentences, they recreate the spirit of the original.
gre.clue: rather than merely copying sentences

en: A formal written work dealing systematically with a subject
hook: TREATISE: a book that TREATS a subject thoroughly.
story: Treatise. Anika's grandfather spent twenty years writing a five-hundred-page book on the rice varieties of Bengal. It has chapters on soil, history, climate and cooking, each carefully argued, with tables and footnotes. Agricultural scholars still cite it today. It is a treatise: a formal written work dealing systematically with a subject. Do not confuse it with treaty, an agreement between nations. Kautilya's Arthashastra is a famous ancient treatise on statecraft. Synonyms: monograph, dissertation.
example: He wrote a lengthy treatise on the history of philosophy.

gre.s: Far from being a casual collection of anecdotes, the book is a rigorous ____, methodically working through every aspect of the philosopher's theory of justice.
gre.clue: methodically working through every aspect

en: To cause someone to become hostile or annoyed
bn: বিরূপ করে তোলা; শত্রুতা সৃষ্টি করা
hook: ANTAGONIZE: turn someone into your ANTAGONIST (enemy).
story: Antagonize. Nadia's new flatmate began by borrowing her shampoo without asking. Then she played loud music at midnight, mocked Nadia's cooking in front of guests, and parked her bicycle across Nadia's door. Within a month, the once friendly Nadia would not even say hello. Her flatmate had antagonized her: caused her to become hostile and annoyed. An antagonist is an opponent, like the villain of a film. Synonyms: provoke, alienate, offend.
example: The child loved to antagonize his younger sister.

gre.s: Eager not to ____ the powerful landlords whose support he needed, the reformer softened his proposals until they offended no one.
gre.clue: until they offended no one

en: Unable to produce crops, offspring, or results; empty
hook: BARREN: as empty as a BARREL with nothing inside.
story: Barren. After the river changed course, the fields of Shuvo's village turned to dry, cracked earth. Farmers planted rice, then wheat, then lentils, but nothing would grow. The land had become barren: unable to produce crops. Barren can also describe a woman or animal unable to have offspring, or anything empty of results, like a barren discussion that leads nowhere. Opposite: fertile, fruitful. Synonyms: infertile, sterile, desolate.
example: The desert landscape was stark and barren.

gre.s: Years of intensive farming without rest had left the once fertile valley ____, its exhausted soil yielding barely enough to feed the families who tilled it.
gre.clue: its exhausted soil yielding barely enough

en: Using pompous, inflated language with little meaning
hook: BOMBASTIC: words that sound like a BOMB but carry nothing.
story: Bombastic. At the village election rally, the candidate grabbed the microphone and roared, 'I shall be the sun that illuminates the eternal darkness of our glorious destiny!' He spoke for an hour in this style, and nobody could say what he had actually promised. His speech was bombastic: pompous and inflated, with little meaning. Bombast originally meant cotton stuffing used to pad clothes, so bombastic words are stuffed to look bigger. Synonyms: pompous, grandiloquent, overblown.
example: The speaker's bombastic style quickly bored the audience.

gre.s: Reviewers mocked the memoir's ____ prose, in which even a trip to the grocery store became an epic struggle described in grandiose, ornate language.
gre.clue: described in grandiose, ornate language

en: To persuade someone through flattery or gentle, persistent coaxing
bn: তোষামোদ করে রাজি করানো; ভুলিয়ে-ভালিয়ে রাজি করানো
hook: CAJOLE: CAGE them with sweet words, JOLLY them along.
story: Cajole. Little Tania wanted ice cream before dinner, and her father said no. So she climbed onto his lap, told him he was the best father in Bangladesh, rubbed his tired shoulders, and asked sweetly, again and again, for just one small cone. Twenty minutes later they were walking to the shop. She had cajoled him: persuaded him through flattery and gentle, persistent coaxing. Cajole and wheedle are near twins. Synonyms: coax, sweet-talk.
example: She managed to cajole her reluctant friend into going to the party.

gre.s: Unable to force the stubborn witness to testify, the detective tried instead to ____ him, offering compliments and small favors until he agreed to talk.
gre.clue: offering compliments and small favors

en: Cautious and wary; reluctant to give or risk
hook: CHARY: CAREFUL and wARY.
story: Chary. Tanvir once lent his notes to a classmate, who copied them, submitted them as his own, and got Tanvir accused of plagiarism. Since then, Tanvir is chary of lending anything. He asks questions, hesitates, and usually says no. He is chary: cautious and wary, reluctant to give or risk. Chary is related to care, so a chary person is careful. Being chary of praise means giving it rarely. Synonyms: wary, cautious, leery.
example: Investors were chary about putting money into the volatile market.

gre.s: Having lost heavily in the last market crash, investors were understandably ____ of new technology stocks, refusing to commit money without years of proven profits.
gre.clue: refusing to commit money without years of proven profits

en: A bad-tempered, grumpy person, especially an old one
hook: CURMUDGEON: a grumpy old CUR (dog) growling in the MUD.
story: Curmudgeon. Old Mr Karim in flat 3B complains about everything. The children are too noisy, the lift is too slow, the tea is too sweet, and modern music is a crime. When neighbours wish him a happy Eid, he grumbles that holidays are a waste of time. He is a curmudgeon: a bad-tempered, grumpy person, especially an old one. Picture a snarling cur, a stray dog, muttering at everyone who passes. Synonyms: grouch, crank, grump.
example: The old man had a reputation as a curmudgeon.

gre.s: Though he cultivated a reputation as a ____, grumbling at visitors and scowling in photographs, the old professor quietly paid the tuition of dozens of poor students.
gre.clue: grumbling at visitors and scowling in photographs

en: A mournful song or lament for the dead
