hook: DIRGE: sung at a funeral, with a slow, sad DRAG.
story: Dirge. When the old fisherman of the village died, his friends carried his body to the riverbank at dusk. As the boat moved slowly through the water, the women sang a slow, sorrowful song of farewell, and even the children fell silent. That song was a dirge: a mournful song or lament for the dead. The word comes from a Latin funeral chant beginning with dirige. Any slow, gloomy music may be called a dirge. Synonyms: lament, elegy.
example: The funeral procession played a slow, mournful dirge.

gre.s: The band's usually upbeat anthem sounded like a ____ that night: played slowly and softly in memory of their late drummer, it moved the entire stadium to tears.
gre.clue: in memory of their late drummer

en: Worthy of great respect
hook: ESTIMABLE: held in high ESTEEM.
story: Estimable. For forty years, Dr Tania Rahman ran a free clinic in a remote char village, treating thousands of patients and refusing every offer of a city job. When she retired, the whole district came to thank her. She was an estimable woman: worthy of great respect. Estimable shares a root with esteem, so think of someone held in high esteem. On the GRE it rarely means able to be estimated. Synonyms: admirable, respected, worthy.
example: The professor was an estimable scholar in her field.

gre.s: Despite their political differences, even the senator's rivals regarded him as thoroughly ____, a public servant whose integrity had never once been questioned.
gre.clue: whose integrity had never once been questioned

en: A mild word substituted for one considered harsh or blunt
hook: EU-PHEMISM: EU = good, PHEME = speech. Good-sounding speech.
story: Euphemism. When Rafi lost his job, the company's letter said he had been released to pursue other opportunities. When his grandfather died, relatives said he had passed away. And when the government raised taxes, it called them revenue enhancements. Each phrase is a euphemism: a mild word substituted for a harsh or blunt one. In Greek, eu means good and pheme means speech, so a euphemism is good-sounding speech. Its opposite is a dysphemism, a deliberately harsh term.
example: "Passed away" is a common euphemism for "died".

gre.s: Calling the mass layoffs a 'workforce optimization' was a transparent ____, a gentle phrase designed to disguise the harsh reality that thousands had lost their jobs.
gre.clue: a gentle phrase designed to disguise the harsh reality

en: To criticize very severely
hook: EX-CORIATE: to strip off the skin (corium), with harsh words.
story: Excoriate. A new bridge in a northern town cracked only six months after it opened. At the public hearing, an engineer stood up and tore the construction company apart: cheap steel, stolen funds, ignored warnings, and lies to the press. For an hour he spared nothing. He excoriated the company: he criticized it very severely. Literally, excoriate means to strip off the skin, from the Latin corium, meaning hide. Such criticism feels like being skinned. Synonyms: lambaste, castigate, berate.
example: The film critic excoriated the director's latest movie.

gre.s: Reviewers did not merely criticize the novel; they chose to ____ it, condemning its plot, its prose, and its author's integrity in the harshest possible terms.
gre.clue: in the harshest possible terms

en: Pressing; demanding immediate action
hook: EXIGENT: an EMERGENT, EXTREME need.
story: Exigent. At two in the morning, the river embankment near Sirajganj began to give way. Water was seeping through, and three villages lay behind it. There was no time for meetings or permits; volunteers grabbed sandbags in the dark. The situation was exigent: pressing, demanding immediate action. The noun is exigency, an urgent need. Exigent can also describe a demanding person, like an exigent boss who wants everything yesterday. Synonyms: urgent, pressing, critical.
example: The exigent situation required swift action.

gre.s: Because the circumstances were so ____, with the floodwaters rising by the hour, officials bypassed the usual approval process and evacuated the town at once.
gre.clue: with the floodwaters rising by the hour

en: Arrogantly superior and disdainful
hook: HAUGHTY: HIGH and mighty, nose in the air.
story: Haughty. At the school reunion, Imran's old classmate arrived in a new car, looked around the simple restaurant, and wrinkled his nose. He refused to shake hands with the waiter, talked only about his villa in Gulshan, and called his former friends you village people. He was haughty: arrogantly superior and disdainful. Haughty comes from an old word for high, so a haughty person holds his head high and looks down on others. Synonyms: arrogant, supercilious, condescending.
example: The haughty heiress treated her servants with disdain.

gre.s: The heiress was so ____ that she refused even to acknowledge the servants, addressing them only through her secretary as though they were beneath her notice.
gre.clue: as though they were beneath her notice

en: Having a strong, exciting, intoxicating effect
hook: HEADY: goes straight to your HEAD.
story: Heady. The night Bangladesh beat a cricket giant in a World Cup match, Dhaka exploded. Strangers hugged in the streets, horns honked until dawn, and Anika felt as if she were floating. Those were heady days: exciting, almost intoxicating. Heady means having a strong, exciting effect, like wine that goes straight to the head. A heady perfume is strong, and heady success can make people reckless. Synonyms: exhilarating, intoxicating, thrilling.
example: The heady scent of jasmine filled the air.

gre.s: For the young founders, the first months were ____: glowing press coverage and millions in investment arrived so quickly that they felt almost drunk with success.
gre.clue: felt almost drunk with success

en: Unable to be upset or excited; extremely calm
hook: IM-PERTURB-ABLE: can't be PERTURBED.
story: Imperturbable. The ferry rocked violently in a storm on the Padma. Passengers screamed, bags slid across the deck, and children cried. But the old captain stood at the wheel, sipping his tea and calmly giving orders, as if it were a quiet afternoon. He was imperturbable: unable to be upset or excited, extremely calm. To perturb is to disturb, so imperturbable means impossible to disturb. Synonyms: unflappable, composed, unruffled.
example: The yoga instructor maintained an imperturbable demeanor even in stressful situations.

gre.s: The chess champion remained ____ throughout the tournament; neither her opponent's taunts nor the roaring crowd produced so much as a flicker of emotion on her face.
gre.clue: neither her opponent's taunts nor the roaring crowd

en: Unable to be calmed or satisfied; relentless
hook: IM-PLACABLE: can't be PLACATED.
story: Implacable. Two families in a Barisal village have quarrelled over a strip of land for three generations. Elders tried to mediate, the courts ruled, and apologies were offered, but nothing worked. Each side rejects every compromise. Their hatred is implacable: unable to be calmed or satisfied, relentless. To placate is to calm someone down, so implacable means impossible to placate. An implacable enemy never gives up. Synonyms: relentless, unappeasable, unforgiving.
example: The detective was implacable in his pursuit of justice.

gre.s: No concession seemed enough for the ____ critic, who greeted each revision of the policy with fresh and even fiercer objections.
gre.clue: greeted each revision of the policy with fresh and even fiercer objections

en: To criticize harshly
hook: LAMBASTE: LAMB gets BASTED (beaten) with harsh words.
story: Lambaste. Arif's team submitted a careless project report, full of copied paragraphs and wrong numbers. In the next meeting, the department head lambasted them in front of everyone. She listed every error, called the work disgraceful, and demanded a full rewrite by Monday. To lambaste is to criticize harshly. The word joins two old verbs that both meant to beat, lam and baste. It is close to excoriate. Synonyms: berate, castigate, slam.
example: The coach lambasted the players for their poor performance.

gre.s: Rather than praising the minister's long-delayed reforms, opposition leaders chose to ____ them as too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises.
gre.clue: too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises

en: A person who behaves badly or breaks the law
hook: MIS-CREANT: a MIS-CREATED person who does wrong.
story: Miscreant. Every night for a month, someone slashed the tyres of motorcycles parked outside Rafi's building. The guards were puzzled and the residents furious, until a hidden camera caught the culprit: a teenager from the next street who did it for fun. The police called him a miscreant: a person who behaves badly or breaks the law. Bangladeshi newspapers often use the word for unidentified criminals. Mis means wrong. Synonyms: wrongdoer, villain, delinquent.
example: The police were searching for the miscreant who had vandalized the property.

gre.s: The townspeople regarded the young man as a hopeless ____ until he returned the stolen money and spent years volunteering to repay his debt to the community.
gre.clue: returned the stolen money

en: A small, relatively unimportant sin or fault
hook: PECCADILLO: a tiny sin, small as an armadillo.
story: Peccadillo. Babu's grandmother caught him sneaking an extra mishti from the kitchen before the guests arrived. She pretended to be angry, then laughed and gave him another. It was only a peccadillo: a small, relatively unimportant sin or fault. Peccadillo comes from the Spanish for little sin, from the same Latin root as impeccable, meaning without flaw. Voters may forgive a politician's peccadilloes but not his crimes. Synonyms: lapse, indiscretion.
example: They were willing to overlook his occasional peccadilloes.

gre.s: Supporters dismissed the scandal as a mere ____, but investigators soon showed that the senator's misconduct was neither minor nor isolated.
gre.clue: dismissed the scandal as a mere

en: A person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts
hook: PHILISTINE: thinks a museum is a waste of land.
story: Philistine. When the town council planned to demolish a two-hundred-year-old zamindar palace to build a parking lot, Ishita protested. One councillor shrugged: 'Old buildings, paintings, poetry, what use are they? They make no money.' Ishita called him a philistine: a person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts. The name comes from an ancient people portrayed in the Bible as enemies of the Israelites. Opposite: aesthete. Synonyms: boor, barbarian.
example: He dismissed the art exhibit as the work of philistines.

gre.s: Dismissing the museum as a waste of public money, the mayor revealed himself to be a ____, indifferent to the paintings and sculptures that had made the city famous.
gre.clue: indifferent to the paintings and sculptures

en: To move to a lower or less important position
hook: RELEGATE: sent back to the LEAGUE below.
story: Relegate. Lamia was the star of her university football team, until a new coach arrived who disliked her. He moved her to the bench, then to the reserve squad, and finally gave her the job of collecting balls. He had relegated her: moved her to a lower or less important position. In European football, a team that finishes last is relegated to a lower division. Re means back and legare means to send. Synonyms: demote, downgrade, consign.
example: The company relegated him to a less prestigious position.

gre.s: Although she was once celebrated as a pioneer, younger scholars now tend to ____ her work to footnotes, considering her methods hopelessly outdated.
gre.clue: considering her methods hopelessly outdated

en: Extremely distasteful; disgusting
hook: REPUGNANT: makes you REPEL and PUKE.
story: Repugnant. Kamal took a summer job at a trading company, then discovered that his manager was cheating poor farmers with rigged scales. When the manager offered him a bonus to keep quiet, Kamal felt sick. The very idea was repugnant to him: extremely distasteful, disgusting. Repugnant comes from the Latin for fighting back, as if your whole conscience fights against it. Do not confuse it with pungent, a strong smell. Synonyms: repellent, abhorrent, revolting.
example: The smell of rotting garbage was utterly repugnant.

gre.s: Although a few found his argument intellectually intriguing, most readers considered the author's defense of slavery morally ____, an idea too abhorrent to be entertained.
gre.clue: an idea too abhorrent to be entertained

en: Driven by tender or nostalgic feelings, sometimes excessively
hook: SENTIMENTAL: ruled by SENTIMENT (feeling).
story: Sentimental. Sara's father refuses to throw away his old Nokia phone. It does not work and the battery is swollen, but it holds the first message Sara ever sent him. He also keeps her childhood drawings in a tin box and cries at every wedding. He is sentimental: driven by tender or nostalgic feelings, sometimes excessively. A sentimental film pushes the audience toward tears with too much sweetness. Opposite: unsentimental, hard-headed. Synonyms: nostalgic, mawkish.
example: She kept all her old love letters for sentimental reasons.

gre.s: The critic faulted the film for being cloyingly ____, relying on tearful reunions and swelling violins rather than on genuine emotional insight.
gre.clue: tearful reunions and swelling violins

en: To waste money, time, or opportunities recklessly
hook: SQUANDER: SQUASH it and wander away.
story: Squander. Zayan received a scholarship of two lakh taka for his master's degree. Instead of paying his fees, he bought a new phone, threw parties for his friends, and took a trip to Cox's Bazar. By the end of the semester the money was gone and the fees were unpaid. He had squandered it: wasted it recklessly. People also squander time, talent and opportunities. Opposite: conserve. Synonyms: waste, fritter away, dissipate.
example: He squandered his inheritance on frivolous luxuries.

gre.s: Having inherited a vast fortune, the young heir managed to ____ nearly all of it within a decade, leaving his children with debts instead of an estate.
gre.clue: leaving his children with debts instead of an estate

en: To cheat someone out of money; a fraud
hook: SWINDLE: like a WINDOW that's actually a painting, a trick.
story: Swindle. A smooth-talking man visited Rumana's village promising to send young men to jobs in Dubai. Each family paid him three lakh taka for visas and tickets. On the day of departure he vanished, along with all the money. He had swindled them: cheated them out of their money. Swindle is also a noun, so the whole scheme was a swindle, and the man was a swindler, a con artist. Synonyms: cheat, defraud, con.
example: The con artist swindled unsuspecting victims out of their savings.

gre.s: The so-called investment firm existed only to ____ elderly retirees, promising guaranteed returns before disappearing with their life savings.
gre.clue: disappearing with their life savings

en: Able to be touched; clear and definite, real
hook: TANGIBLE: you can TOUCH it (tangere = to touch).
story: Tangible. For months, Mitu's charity promised a village that it would rebuild the school. The villagers were doubtful; they had heard promises before. Then one morning trucks arrived with bricks and desks, and within weeks there was a new roof and clean water. Finally there were tangible results: real, clear and definite, things you could actually touch. Tangere is Latin for touch, as in tangent. The opposite is intangible, like trust or goodwill. Synonyms: concrete, palpable.
example: They needed tangible evidence to support their claim.

gre.s: Despite years of lofty promises about reform, the government had produced few ____ improvements that ordinary citizens could actually see in their daily lives.
gre.clue: that ordinary citizens could actually see in their daily lives

en: Depravity; wickedness
hook: TURPITUDE: TURNING PUTRID morally.
story: Turpitude. A respected judge in a small town was found to have taken bribes to free murderers while sending innocent poor men to prison. The public was horrified, not only by the crime but by the deep wickedness behind it. Lawyers called it moral turpitude: depravity, wickedness. In law, moral turpitude means conduct that shocks the conscience. Turpis is Latin for shameful or base. Synonyms: depravity, vileness, iniquity.
example: The politician's acts of turpitude shocked the nation.

gre.s: Voters could forgive the mayor's clumsiness and even occasional dishonesty, but his profiting from child labor exposed a degree of ____ they found unforgivable.
gre.clue: his profiting from child labor

en: Complete and unreserved; pure
hook: UN-ALLOYED: pure gold, not mixed into an ALLOY.
story: Unalloyed. When Mahin opened the email saying he had won a full scholarship to study abroad, he screamed, danced around the room, and called his mother, who burst into happy tears. There was no worry and no doubt mixed in, only joy. It was unalloyed delight: complete, unreserved and pure. An alloy is a metal mixed with another, like brass. So unalloyed means not mixed with anything, like pure gold. Synonyms: pure, unmitigated, sheer.
example: The joy she felt at her graduation was unalloyed.

gre.s: Her joy at the verdict was hardly ____, for though her brother had been freed, the real culprit had escaped justice entirely.
gre.clue: though her brother had been freed, the real culprit had escaped justice

en: To offer lower prices than a competitor; to weaken or undermine
bn: কম দামে বিক্রি করা; দুর্বল করা
hook: UNDER-CUT: CUT the price UNDER theirs, or cut UNDER the foundation.
story: Undercut. A new grocery app in Dhaka began selling rice, lentils and oil for ten percent less than every shop in the neighbourhood. Within months, the corner shops had lost half their customers. The app had undercut them: offered lower prices than its competitors. Undercut also means to weaken or undermine, as when one lie undercuts a lawyer's whole case. Literally, it means to cut away from underneath. Synonyms: undersell, undermine, weaken.
example: The new store undercut its competitors' prices to attract customers.

gre.s: The witness's repeated contradictions served only to ____ the credibility of the defense, which had built its entire case on his reliability.
gre.clue: repeated contradictions

en: To use flattery or coaxing to get what one wants
hook: WHEEDLE: a WHEEZING, pleading voice, 'pleeease'.
story: Wheedle. Sabbir wanted his elder brother's motorcycle for the weekend, but he did not ask directly. Instead he praised his brother's cooking, ironed his shirts, and kept saying, 'You are so generous, Bhaiya.' By Friday he had the keys. He had wheedled them out of his brother: used flattery and coaxing to get what he wanted. Wheedle and cajole are near twins, though wheedle often hints at slyness. Synonyms: coax, sweet-talk, inveigle.
example: The child tried to wheedle an extra piece of candy from his mother.

gre.s: Too proud to demand a raise outright, the clerk tried to ____ one from his employer, praising her leadership at every opportunity and hinting at his financial troubles.
gre.clue: praising her leadership at every opportunity

en: Having a fear or hatred of foreigners
hook: XENO = foreign, PHOBIA = fear.
story: Xenophobic. When a group of foreign workers arrived to build a bridge near a small town, some residents welcomed them with food. Others put up signs saying foreigners go home, refused to sell them rice, and blamed them for every crime. That fear and hatred of outsiders is xenophobic. Xeno is Greek for stranger, and phobia means fear. Xenophobic politicians often blame immigrants for problems they did not cause. Opposite: cosmopolitan. Synonyms: nativist, chauvinistic.
example: The rise in xenophobic sentiment worried human rights activists.

gre.s: Critics warned that the party's ____ rhetoric, which blamed immigrants for every economic problem, would inflame hostility toward the nation's foreign-born residents.
gre.clue: blamed immigrants for every economic problem

en: A state of temporary suspension or inactivity
hook: ABEYANCE: 'A BAY' where ships wait, temporarily paused.
story: Abeyance. The government announced a new metro line through Shuvo's neighbourhood, and construction began. Then a court case was filed over land rights. Work stopped, the cranes stood idle, and the project was held in abeyance: a state of temporary suspension. It was not cancelled, only paused until the court decided. Things in abeyance can be revived later. Picture a ship waiting at anchor in a bay, going nowhere for now. Synonyms: suspension, dormancy, limbo.
example: The plans for the new library were put in abeyance due to budget cuts.

gre.s: Plans for the new stadium were held in ____ while the city awaited the outcome of the environmental review, though officials insisted the project had not been abandoned.
gre.clue: while the city awaited the outcome of the environmental review

en: Existing as an idea rather than a physical thing; not concrete
hook: ABSTRACT: pulled away (abs-tract) from the physical world.
story: Abstract. In philosophy class, Rafi's teacher asked, 'What is justice?' Rafi pointed out of the window at the court building. 'That is a building,' the teacher said. 'I asked about justice itself.' Justice, freedom and beauty are abstract: existing as ideas rather than physical things. You cannot touch them or put them in a bag. The opposite is concrete. Abstract art shows shapes and colours rather than recognizable objects. Synonyms: theoretical, conceptual, intangible.
example: Her paintings were abstract explorations of color and form.

gre.s: The professor's lectures were so ____ that students begged for concrete examples, unable to connect her elegant theories to anything in the real world.
gre.clue: students begged for concrete examples

en: An open insult; to insult intentionally
hook: AFFRONT: an insult right to your FRONT, to your face.
story: Affront. At a family wedding, Tanvir's elderly uncle was seated at the very back, behind the cooks, while younger relatives sat at the head table. He took it as a deliberate insult and left before dinner was served. He called it an affront: an open, intentional insult. As a verb, to affront someone is to insult them openly. The root means to the face, so an affront is an insult thrown right in your face. Synonyms: insult, slight, outrage.
example: The rude remark was considered a personal affront.

gre.s: The ambassador regarded the decision to seat him behind junior officials as a deliberate ____, a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology.
gre.clue: a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology

en: To make someone troubled or nervous; to campaign to arouse public concern
hook: AGITATE: like a washing machine's AGITATOR, stirring things up.
story: Agitate. For years, garment workers in Savar earned wages too low to live on. Then a group of young workers began to agitate for change. They organised rallies, wrote to newspapers, and spoke at the factory gates every morning until the minimum wage was raised. To agitate is to campaign to arouse public concern. It also means to make someone troubled or nervous. Literally, it means to stir, as a washing machine agitates clothes. Synonyms: campaign, stir, unsettle.
example: The political activist agitated the crowd with his fiery speech.

gre.s: The doctor warned visitors not to ____ the patient with distressing news, since even mild anxiety might strain her weakened heart.
gre.clue: since even mild anxiety might strain her weakened heart

en: Respected and impressive; majestic
hook: GRE trick: au-GUST, like Emperor AUGUSTUS, majestic.
story: August. When the eighty-year-old chief justice entered the hall in his black robes, white-haired and upright, every lawyer rose in silence. Even the noisiest journalists lowered their voices. His presence was august: respected and impressive, majestic. Note the stress, aw-GUST, unlike the month. Both come from Augustus, the Roman emperor whose title meant venerable. An august institution, like an ancient university, inspires awe. Synonyms: venerable, dignified, stately.
example: The august cathedral stood as a testament to centuries of devotion.

gre.s: The young scholar felt intimidated in the ____ company of Nobel laureates and former heads of state, and barely dared to speak during the entire dinner.
gre.clue: Nobel laureates and former heads of state

en: To polish until shiny; to enhance a reputation
hook: BURNISH: rub until it BURNS bright.
story: Burnish. Every Friday, Grandfather Rahim takes out the old brass lamp his father brought from Murshidabad and rubs it with a soft cloth until it gleams like gold. He burnishes it: polishes it until it shines. Burnish is also used figuratively. A politician who donates to hospitals just before an election is trying to burnish his image, to make his reputation look brighter. Think of rubbing until the metal almost burns with light. Synonyms: polish, shine, enhance.
example: She burnished the antique silver until it gleamed.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ her reputation after the scandal, the executive donated generously to local charities and gave interviews emphasizing her humble origins.
gre.clue: donated generously to local charities

en: Pretending to be shy; reluctant to give details
hook: COY: playing it COOL and shy.
story: Coy. When Nadia's friends asked whether she was engaged, she smiled, looked at the floor, and said, 'Maybe, maybe not,' while her cheeks turned pink. She clearly wanted them to keep guessing. She was being coy: pretending to be shy, or reluctant to give details. A company can also be coy about its profits, refusing to give exact numbers. Coy comes from the same Latin root as quiet. Synonyms: evasive, reticent, demure.
example: Her coy smile and playful glances hinted at her interest.

gre.s: The minister was uncharacteristically ____ about her plans, deflecting every question about the coming election with a smile and a vague remark about the weather.
gre.clue: deflecting every question

en: To express disapproval of; to belittle
hook: DEPRECATE: like DEPRECIATE, lowering something's value.
story: Deprecate. When Lamia won the national science fair, she told reporters, 'Oh, it was nothing, I was just lucky.' Her teachers noticed she always did this, belittling her own work. That habit is called being self-deprecating. To deprecate is to express disapproval of something, or to belittle it. Many editors deprecate the use of cliches. Do not confuse it with depreciate, which means to lose value, though the two are often mixed up. Synonyms: disparage, belittle, criticize.
example: I deprecate his reckless behavior and lack of concern for others.

gre.s: Although many modern linguists ____ strict grammar rules as elitist and arbitrary, most teachers still insist on them in student essays.
gre.clue: as elitist and arbitrary

en: The feeling that something is unworthy of respect; to scorn
hook: DIS-DAIN: you won't DEIGN to look at it.
story: Disdain. At a fancy restaurant in Banani, a wealthy man glanced at the menu, then at the waiter, and said, 'I do not eat this cheap food.' He pushed the plate away with two fingers as if it were dirty. His face showed disdain: the feeling that something is unworthy of respect. As a verb, to disdain is to scorn, so a proud person may disdain to answer a rude question. Dis means not, and the root means worthy. Synonyms: contempt, scorn.
example: The aristocrat looked upon the commoners with disdain.

gre.s: The aristocrat made no effort to hide his ____ for the newly rich merchants, refusing their invitations and mocking their manners at every opportunity.
gre.clue: mocking their manners at every opportunity

en: To scatter or spread over a wide area
hook: DIS-PERSE: like a SPRAY spreading out.
story: Disperse. Thousands of people gathered at Shahbag for an evening rally. When a sudden thunderstorm broke, they ran in every direction: under shop awnings, into rickshaws, down side streets. Within ten minutes the square was empty. The crowd had dispersed: scattered over a wide area. Wind disperses seeds, and police may disperse a crowd. Di means apart, and the root means to scatter. Opposite: gather, assemble. Synonyms: scatter, dissipate.
example: The crowd dispersed after the concert was over.

gre.s: Once the morning fog began to ____, the hikers could see the trail clearly again, though only an hour earlier the valley had been completely hidden.
gre.clue: the hikers could see the trail clearly again

en: To swell out from internal pressure
hook: DIS-TEND: EXTEND outward, swelling.
story: Distend. In photographs of famine, children often appear with thin arms but swollen bellies. Doctors explain that severe malnutrition lets fluid build up in the body, so the stomach becomes distended: swollen out from internal pressure. To distend is to swell from within. A balloon distends as you blow air into it. Dis means apart, and tend means stretch, so distend means stretched apart. Do not confuse it with distort. Synonyms: swell, bloat, inflate.
example: The balloon distended as more and more air was blown into it.

gre.s: After swallowing its prey whole, the python's body began to ____ visibly, its skin stretching to accommodate an animal nearly twice its own width.
gre.clue: its skin stretching to accommodate

en: Native to or regularly found in a particular place or group
hook: EN-DEMIC: IN the people (demos), always present there.
story: Endemic. Every monsoon, dengue fever returns to Dhaka. Doctors no longer treat it as a surprise; it is always present, rising and falling with the rains. Dengue is endemic in Bangladesh: regularly found in that place. The word also describes plants and animals native to one area, like the lemurs found only on Madagascar. Contrast it with epidemic, a sudden outbreak. En means in, and demos means people. Synonyms: native, prevalent, entrenched.
example: Malaria is endemic to certain tropical regions.

gre.s: Corruption was so ____ in the old regime that bribery was considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal.
gre.clue: considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal

en: Deep hostility; the state of being enemies
hook: ENMITY: ENEMY-ity.
story: Enmity. Two rival shopkeepers in Old Dhaka have not spoken for twenty years. They were once partners, until one accused the other of stealing. Now they cut prices just to hurt each other, warn customers against each other, and even their sons fight in the street. Between them lies deep enmity: hostility, the state of being enemies. Enmity and enemy share a root. Its opposite is amity, which means friendship. Synonyms: hostility, animosity, antagonism.
example: The enmity between the two nations had lasted for centuries.

gre.s: The ____ between the two clans, rooted in a dispute over land generations earlier, was so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings.
gre.clue: so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings

en: Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact
hook: GAUCHE: French for LEFT, as in left-handed and clumsy.
story: Gauche. At his first office party, Farhan asked his boss's wife how old she was, laughed loudly at the wrong moment, and wiped his hands on the tablecloth. Everyone smiled politely and looked away. His behaviour was gauche: socially awkward, lacking grace or tact. Gauche is French for left, from an old prejudice that the left hand is clumsy. Its opposite, adroit, comes from the French for right. Synonyms: awkward, tactless, maladroit.
example: His gauche attempts at flirting were embarrassing.

gre.s: Though brilliant in the laboratory, the young chemist was painfully ____ at receptions, blurting out tactless remarks and forgetting the names of her hosts.
gre.clue: blurting out tactless remarks

en: Showing uncontrolled emotion; extremely funny
hook: HYSTERICAL: emotions out of control, crying or laughing.
story: Hysterical. When the lights went out during a thunderstorm, Mitu's little cousin began screaming, crying and running around the room, and nobody could calm her for half an hour. She was hysterical: showing uncontrolled emotion. Strangely, the same word has a happy sense too. The next day, their uncle told a story so funny that the whole family laughed until they cried. Everyone agreed it was hysterical: extremely funny. Synonyms: frantic, overwrought, and for humour, hilarious.
example: The woman became hysterical as she searched for her lost child.

gre.s: News of the crash reached the families before any official statement, and the airport lounge became a scene of ____ grief, with relatives sobbing and screaming uncontrollably.
gre.clue: sobbing and screaming uncontrollably

en: Shamelessly rude and disrespectful
hook: IM-PUDENT: no shame (pudor = shame).
story: Impudent. When Mahin's younger brother was told to finish his homework, he stuck out his tongue at their father, said, 'Do it yourself,' and walked away whistling. Their father was too shocked to speak. The boy's reply was impudent: shamelessly rude and disrespectful. Impudent comes from the Latin for without shame, the opposite of pudor, meaning modesty. Impudent and insolent are near twins. Synonyms: cheeky, impertinent, brazen.
example: The impudent student was sent to the principal's office.

gre.s: The ____ student not only ignored the teacher's warning but mimicked her voice in front of the whole class, apparently without the slightest shame.
gre.clue: apparently without the slightest shame

en: Just begun and not fully formed
hook: INCHOATE: like a chick just INCHing out of its egg, not yet formed.
story: Inchoate. At two in the morning, Ishita had half an idea for a startup, something about connecting village farmers directly with city buyers. She scribbled a few words, drew some arrows, and fell asleep. The plan was inchoate: just begun and not fully formed. Say it in-KOH-it. It comes from the Latin for beginning, and despite the sound, it has nothing to do with chaos. An inchoate feeling is one you cannot yet put into words. Synonyms: embryonic, rudimentary, nascent.
example: The project was still in its inchoate stages, with only a rough outline in place.

gre.s: The committee's proposals remained ____, little more than a list of vague goals that had yet to be developed into any concrete plan.
gre.clue: had yet to be developed into any concrete plan

en: A strong liking or habitual tendency
hook: PENCHANT: leaning toward it like a PENDANT hangs down.
story: Penchant. Arif cannot pass a roadside tea stall without stopping. He drinks six cups a day, knows the best stall in every neighbourhood, and plans his walks around them. He has a penchant for tea: a strong liking or habitual tendency. Penchant comes from the French for leaning, so a penchant is something you lean toward. One may also have a penchant for exaggeration or for arriving late. Synonyms: fondness, inclination, proclivity.
example: He had a penchant for collecting antique clocks.

gre.s: Given the senator's well-known ____ for theatrical gestures, no one was surprised when he tore up the bill on live television.
gre.clue: no one was surprised

en: A state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
hook: QUANDARY: 'QUAND?' (when?) and 'where?' — totally stuck.
story: Quandary. Two job offers reached Nadia on the same day. One was in Dhaka, close to her ailing mother, with a modest salary. The other was in Singapore, with double the pay and a real chance to build a career. She paced the hostel corridor all night, unable to decide. She was in a quandary: a state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation. A quandary is close to a dilemma. Synonyms: dilemma, predicament, plight.
example: The unexpected situation left her in a quandary.

gre.s: The doctor faced a genuine ____: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate her duty of honesty.
gre.clue: revealing the diagnosis might devastate the fragile patient, yet concealing it would violate

en: Isolation to prevent the spread of disease; to isolate
hook: QUARANTINE: from Italian 'quaranta', forty days of isolation for ships.
story: Quarantine. In the spring of 2020, Zayan returned from abroad just as the pandemic was spreading. At the airport, officials sent him to a hotel room for fourteen days. He could not visit his family or even step into the corridor. That period of isolation was a quarantine: isolation to prevent the spread of disease. As a verb, to quarantine is to isolate. The word comes from the Italian for forty days, the time ships once waited outside Venice.
example: The ship was quarantined due to an outbreak of illness on board.

gre.s: Health officials decided to ____ the entire village after the outbreak, barring anyone from leaving until tests confirmed that the virus was no longer spreading.
gre.clue: barring anyone from leaving

en: To forcefully stop or suppress; to officially reject
hook: QUASH: SQUASH it flat.
story: Quash. A student newspaper at Sara's university uncovered a cheating scandal involving the son of a wealthy donor. Within hours, the administration ordered the article removed and threatened the editors. They were trying to quash the story: to forcefully stop or suppress it. In law, to quash means to officially reject, as when a higher court quashes a conviction. Think of squash, crushing something flat. Synonyms: suppress, crush, annul.
example: The rebellion was quashed by the government forces.

gre.s: The regime moved swiftly to ____ the rebellion, arresting its leaders and banning public gatherings before the unrest could spread to other cities.
gre.clue: before the unrest could spread to other cities

en: To argue about trivial matters; a minor objection
hook: QUIBBLE: a small QUIBBLE, like a QUIBBLING nibble.
story: Quibble. Shuvo and his roommate argued for twenty minutes about whether they had bought five eggs or six, and whether the electricity bill was two hundred and ten taka or two hundred and twelve. Meanwhile, their dinner burned on the stove. They were quibbling: arguing about trivial matters. A quibble is also a minor objection, as in, my only quibble with the book is its tiny font. Synonyms: nitpick, cavil, carp.
example: Let's not quibble over such small details.

gre.s: The reviewer admired the novel's ambition and its vivid characters; her only ____ concerned a handful of typographical errors that hardly diminished its power.
gre.clue: that hardly diminished its power

en: To cause severe and extensive damage
hook: RAVAGE: like a RAVENOUS SAVAGE destroying everything.
story: Ravage. In 2007, Cyclone Sidr struck the southwest coast of Bangladesh. Winds tore roofs from houses, the storm surge swept away fields and livestock, and whole villages were flattened. Cyclones like this ravage the coast: they cause severe and extensive damage. The ravages of time, war or disease are their destructive effects. Do not confuse ravage with ravish, which means to seize or enrapture. Synonyms: devastate, destroy, wreck.
example: The storm ravaged the coastal town.

gre.s: Unless farmers act quickly to control the locusts, the swarms will ____ the region's crops, leaving little to harvest and threatening famine.
gre.clue: leaving little to harvest

en: To publicly withdraw a statement or belief
hook: RE-CANT: un-CHANT what you said.
story: Recant. In 1633, the astronomer Galileo was brought before the Church and forced, under threat of punishment, to declare that the Earth does not move around the sun. He publicly recanted: he withdrew his statement and belief. Legend says he whispered afterwards, 'And yet it moves.' Re means back, and cant comes from the Latin for sing, so to recant is to sing your words back. Synonyms: retract, renounce, disavow.
example: He was forced to recant his earlier testimony.

gre.s: Despite intense pressure from church authorities, the scientist refused to ____ his theory, insisting that the evidence for it was overwhelming.
gre.clue: insisting that the evidence for it was overwhelming

en: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect
hook: RE-DOUBT-ABLE: you DOUBT you can beat them.
story: Redoubtable. In the chess club at Joya's school, one quiet girl had not lost a game in three years. Seniors avoided playing her, and visiting champions left shaking their heads. She was redoubtable: formidable, especially as an opponent, and worthy of respect. It comes from the Old French redouter, to dread, so a redoubtable person is someone others dread to face. Sports writers love it for a fierce rival team. Synonyms: formidable, fearsome, impressive.
example: The dragon was a redoubtable foe.

gre.s: Even seasoned lawyers dreaded facing her in court, for she was a ____ advocate whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses.
gre.clue: whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses

en: Shy and tending to avoid company
hook: GRE trick: RETIRING means shy — she RETIRES to her room when guests come.
story: Retiring. At every family gathering, Priya's cousin Sabbir sits quietly in a corner with a book. He smiles when spoken to but never starts a conversation, and he slips away before the group photographs. He is retiring: shy and tending to avoid company. This has nothing to do with stopping work at sixty, though both involve withdrawing. A retiring person withdraws from attention. Synonyms: reserved, diffident, shy.
example: She had a retiring personality and preferred to keep to herself.

gre.s: Though her paintings were bold and flamboyant, the artist herself was ____, avoiding interviews and rarely appearing even at her own exhibitions.
gre.clue: avoiding interviews and rarely appearing even at her own exhibitions

en: High-pitched and piercing; loud and forceful in criticism
hook: SHRILL: like a SHRIEKING whistle.
story: Shrill. In Babu's flat, the pressure cooker whistle pierced the air, and a moment later his little sister shrieked at the cat. Both sounds were shrill: high-pitched and piercing. Shrill also describes criticism that is loud and forceful, often too forceful. One newspaper attacked the minister in shrill editorials every single day, until readers stopped listening. Say the word aloud and you can hear its sharp, whistling sound. Synonyms: piercing, strident.
example: The shrill sound of the alarm made everyone jump.

gre.s: The opposition's attacks grew increasingly ____, so loud and relentless that even sympathetic voters began to dismiss them as hysteria rather than reasoned argument.
gre.clue: so loud and relentless

en: Clever but deliberately misleading argument
hook: SOPHISTRY: from the SOPHISTS, Greek teachers who could argue anything.
story: Sophistry. Caught looking at notes during an exam, Imran argued that he had not cheated, because the answers were already in his memory and the notes merely reminded him. For a moment it sounded clever, but it was nonsense. His argument was sophistry: clever but deliberately misleading reasoning. The Sophists were ancient Greek teachers accused of training students to win arguments rather than find the truth. Synonyms: casuistry, specious reasoning.
example: His argument was pure sophistry, devoid of any real logic.

gre.s: The lawyer's defense, though dazzlingly clever, was mere ____: each step seemed logical, yet the argument as a whole was designed to mislead the jury.
gre.clue: designed to mislead the jury

en: To provide evidence to support or prove
hook: SUBSTANTIATE: give it SUBSTANCE.
story: Substantiate. Rumana claimed that a factory upstream was poisoning the river. Officials laughed: 'Where is your proof?' So she collected water samples every week, had them tested in a university lab, and photographed the dead fish. Her report substantiated the claim: it provided evidence that supported it. The factory was fined. To substantiate is to give substance to a claim. Its opposite is refute. Synonyms: corroborate, verify, prove.
example: The detectives worked to substantiate their theory with concrete facts.

gre.s: The reporter's allegations, however sensational, were dismissed because she could not ____ them with any documents or credible witnesses.
gre.clue: with any documents or credible witnesses

en: Skilled at gaining advantage through cunning
hook: WILY: like WILE E. Coyote, always scheming.
story: Wily. In a famous Bengali folk tale, a crocodile sends her seven babies to the jackal to be educated. Each day the jackal eats one. Whenever the mother visits, he holds up the same surviving baby again and again, and she leaves happy. The jackal is wily: skilled at gaining advantage through cunning. Wily comes from wile, a clever trick. Contrast it with guileless, which means innocent and open. Synonyms: cunning, crafty, sly.
example: The wily fox managed to evade the hunters at every turn.

gre.s: The ____ negotiator let her opponents believe they had won every minor point, all the while maneuvering toward the one concession she actually wanted.
gre.clue: all the while maneuvering toward

en: To leave quickly and secretly, often to escape arrest or with stolen money
hook: ABS-COND: ABSent with the CONDominium money.
story: Abscond. For five years, the treasurer of a village savings group in Mymensingh collected deposits from two hundred families. One morning his house was empty and the safe stood open. A bus conductor remembered a man with a heavy bag buying a ticket to the border. He had absconded: left quickly and secretly, taking the money. The word comes from the Latin for to hide away. Prisoners abscond from jail; cashiers abscond with funds. Synonyms: flee, bolt, decamp.
example: The thief absconded with the jewels in the dead of night.

gre.s: Days before the auditors arrived, the firm's accountant chose to ____ with millions in client funds, slipping out of the country under a false name.
gre.clue: slipping out of the country under a false name

en: The highest or most successful point; the point in an orbit farthest from Earth
hook: APO-GEE: AWAY (apo) from Earth (geo), the farthest, highest point.
story: Apogee. Tanvir's grandfather was a village jatra actor. The apogee of his career came in 1985, when he performed before ten thousand people at a festival in Dhaka. After that, the crowds slowly shrank. An apogee is the highest or most successful point. In astronomy, it is the point in the orbit of the Moon or a satellite farthest from Earth: apo means away, and gee means earth. Its opposite is perigee. Synonyms: peak, zenith, pinnacle.
example: The company's expansionary phase reached its apogee in the early 2000s.

gre.s: Critics agree that the novelist's career reached its ____ with her third book; nothing she wrote afterward came close to its brilliance or its success.
gre.clue: nothing she wrote afterward came close

en: An attack on someone's reputation or character
hook: ASPERSION: SPRINKLING dirt on someone's name.
story: Aspersion. Before the student union election, anonymous posters appeared around campus claiming that Sara, the leading candidate, had bought her grades and stolen club funds. None of it was true, but some voters believed it. Her rivals were casting aspersions on her: attacking her reputation and character. The usual phrase is cast aspersions. Originally, aspersion meant sprinkling water, so picture someone spattering mud on your good name. Synonyms: slur, slander, smear.
example: The allegations were unsubstantiated aspersions on the politician's character.

gre.s: Unable to fault the research itself, her rivals resorted to an anonymous ____ on her character, hinting at plagiarism they could never prove.
gre.clue: hinting at plagiarism they could never prove

en: Humorously rude and indecent
hook: BAWDY: BAWLING out rude jokes.
story: Bawdy. At village weddings in the old days, women from the groom's side would sing teasing songs full of jokes about married life, making the bride blush and the aunties roar with laughter. The songs were bawdy: humorously rude and indecent. Bawdy humour is crude but cheerful, not cruel. Shakespeare's plays are full of bawdy puns that schoolbooks quietly skip. Its opposite is prudish. Synonyms: ribald, racy, risque.
example: The play was filled with bawdy humor that made some audience members uncomfortable.

gre.s: The comedian's ____ jokes, full of sexual innuendo, delighted the late-night crowd but would never have been permitted on family television.
gre.clue: full of sexual innuendo

en: Annoyance or distress caused by humiliation or failure
hook: CHAGRIN: you wanted to GRIN, but SHAME (cha) took over.
story: Chagrin. Farhan told all his friends that he would top the class in the final exam. When the results came out, he had failed one subject, and his quiet roommate had come first. Farhan's face burned with chagrin: annoyance and distress caused by humiliation or failure. It often appears as, much to his chagrin. Chagrin is not plain sadness; it is the sting of embarrassment. Despite the sound, there is no grin in it. Synonyms: mortification, vexation.
example: To her chagrin, she stumbled during her dance performance.

gre.s: Much to the general's ____, the battle he had boasted would last a single afternoon dragged on for months, exposing his strategy as hopelessly naive.
gre.clue: he had boasted would last a single afternoon

en: To cooperate secretly for a dishonest purpose
hook: COL-LUDE: playing (ludere) together secretly.
story: Collude. Three cement companies in one city met in secret and agreed to raise their prices together, so builders had no cheaper option. The government later fined them all. They had colluded: cooperated secretly for a dishonest purpose. The noun is collusion. Students who share answers during an online exam are colluding too. Col means together and ludere means to play, so to collude is to play together, but in a crooked game. Synonyms: conspire, connive, scheme.
example: Rival companies were accused of colluding to fix prices.

gre.s: Investigators suspected that the two rival bidders had secretly agreed to ____, inflating their offers so that the government would pay far more than the project was worth.
gre.clue: secretly agreed

en: To express sympathy or sorrow
hook: COM-MISERATE: share someone's MISERY.
story: Commiserate. After the exam results came out, Rumana and her friends sat on the hostel roof. Three of them had failed the same difficult course. They shared tea, complained about the impossible questions, and comforted one another until midnight. They were commiserating: expressing sympathy and sorrow for each other. Com means with, and miser means wretched, as in misery, so to commiserate is to share someone's misery. Synonyms: sympathize, console, condole.
example: He commiserated with her over the loss of her beloved pet.

gre.s: When the factory closed, former coworkers gathered every evening at the tea stall to ____ with one another over lost wages and uncertain futures.
gre.clue: over lost wages and uncertain futures

en: A large, destructive fire
hook: CONFLAGRATION: a FLAG-burning FLAME everywhere.
story: Conflagration. One night, a fire broke out in a chemical warehouse in Old Dhaka. Flames leapt from building to building through the narrow lanes, gas cylinders exploded, and firefighters battled for hours. By morning, whole blocks had turned to ash. It was a conflagration: a large, destructive fire. Con means together and flagrare means to burn, the root of flagrant. The word can also describe a war that spreads like fire. Synonyms: inferno, blaze, firestorm.
example: The conflagration destroyed acres of forest land.

gre.s: What began as a small kitchen fire soon became a ____ that consumed half the town, as dry winds drove the flames from roof to roof.
gre.clue: consumed half the town

en: An unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute
hook: CONTRE-TEMPS: French for 'against time' — bad timing.
story: Contretemps. At Joya's engagement ceremony, the groom's mother arrived wearing exactly the same sari as the bride's mother. There was an awkward silence, a few stiff smiles, and then a short argument about who should change. The family still laughs about that contretemps: an unexpected, embarrassing mishap or minor dispute. The word is French, meaning against the time, and is pronounced KON-truh-tahn. Synonyms: mishap, hitch, squabble.
example: A scheduling contretemps led to both speakers arriving at the same time.

gre.s: The diplomats' brief ____ over seating arrangements, though embarrassing at the time, was soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations that followed.
gre.clue: soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations

en: A firmly held belief; also, a formal declaration of guilt
hook: CONVICTION: you're CONVINCED.
story: Conviction. Tania's grandmother was the first woman in her village to send her daughters to college. Neighbours mocked her, relatives warned her, and money was always short. But she never wavered; she was certain that education would change her family. She acted from deep conviction: a firmly held belief. The word has a second meaning, a formal declaration that someone is guilty of a crime. Convict and convince share its root. Synonyms: belief, certainty, resolve.
example: She spoke with such conviction that she swayed the audience in her favor.

gre.s: Though the young activist spoke softly, she argued with such ____ that even her skeptical audience could not doubt she believed every word.
gre.clue: could not doubt she believed every word

en: To sing or hum softly and sentimentally
hook: CROON: like a CROONER singing softly into the moon.
story: Croon. Late at night on the river, an old boatman rows slowly and croons a bhatiali song, soft and low, his voice drifting across the dark water. In a house on the bank, Kamal's mother croons a lullaby until the baby falls asleep. To croon is to sing or hum softly and sentimentally. In the 1940s, smooth, gentle singers like Frank Sinatra were called crooners. Think of a voice that coos rather than shouts. Synonyms: hum, warble, murmur.
example: He crooned a sweet lullaby to his newborn daughter.

gre.s: Rather than belting out the song as most performers did, he chose to ____ it softly, turning the rousing anthem into an intimate lullaby.
gre.clue: Rather than belting out the song

en: To remove from power suddenly and forcefully
hook: DE-POSE: remove from the throne POSITION.
story: Depose. In 1757, Siraj ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab of Bengal, lost the Battle of Plassey because his own commander, Mir Jafar, secretly sided with the British. Siraj was deposed: removed from power suddenly and forcefully. Mir Jafar took his throne, and in Bengal his name still means traitor. In law, depose has another sense, to question a witness under oath. De means down, and pose means to put: to put down. Synonyms: overthrow, oust, topple.
example: The king was deposed in a military coup.

gre.s: Fearing that the increasingly erratic king would ruin the nation, his generals plotted to ____ him and install his young nephew on the throne.
gre.clue: install his young nephew on the throne

en: The easing of hostility between countries
hook: DETENTE: like DE-TENSE, reducing tension.
story: Detente. During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union aimed thousands of nuclear missiles at each other. In the 1970s, their leaders began signing arms agreements, trading grain, and even flying a joint space mission. That period of relaxed tension was called detente: the easing of hostility between countries. Detente is French for loosening, like releasing a tightly drawn bowstring. Its opposite is escalation. Synonyms: rapprochement, thaw.
example: After years of conflict, the two countries finally reached a detente.

gre.s: After decades of border skirmishes, the two neighbors entered a period of ____, reopening trade routes and exchanging ambassadors for the first time in a generation.
gre.clue: reopening trade routes and exchanging ambassadors

en: Dull and unfashionable in appearance
hook: DOWDY: DULL and DOWNbeat style.
story: Dowdy. At the office's annual party, everyone arrived in bright new outfits. Mitu's aunt appeared in a faded brown dress decades out of style, with a shapeless grey cardigan on top. A few colleagues whispered that she looked dowdy: dull and unfashionable in appearance. She did not care; she danced more than anyone. The word can describe places too, like a dowdy hotel with tired carpets. Its opposite is chic. Synonyms: frumpy, drab, unfashionable.
example: Her dowdy clothes made her seem much older than she was.

gre.s: Once dismissed as ____, with its faded wallpaper and outdated furniture, the old hotel was transformed by its new owners into the most stylish address in the city.
gre.clue: with its faded wallpaper and outdated furniture

en: A level or rank in an organization or society
hook: ECHELON: like the steps of a LADDER, rung by rung.
story: Echelon. In a large bank, tellers and clerks work at the bottom, managers in the middle, and a few directors at the very top make the big decisions. Each level is an echelon: a level or rank in an organization or society. People often speak of the upper echelons of power. The word comes from the French for a rung of a ladder. In the army, an echelon is also a formation of troops arranged like steps. Synonyms: rank, tier, level.
example: She quickly rose through the echelons of the corporation.

gre.s: Although she began as a junior typist, her talent eventually carried her to the highest ____ of the company, where she helped set policy for thousands of employees.
gre.clue: Although she began as a junior typist

en: A feeling of weariness and dissatisfaction from lack of interest
hook: ENNUI (on-WEE): French for boredom. 'Oh, wee, another day.'
story: Ennui. During the long summer break, Lamia had nothing to do. She scrolled her phone, napped, stared at the ceiling fan, and sighed. Even her favourite films felt dull. It was not sadness exactly, but a heavy, restless weariness. That feeling is ennui. Say it on-WEE. It is French, and related to the English word annoy. Ennui is deeper than ordinary boredom; it is a listless dissatisfaction with life itself. Synonyms: listlessness, tedium, languor.
example: A sense of ennui washed over him during the long, monotonous meeting.

gre.s: Wealthy beyond need and freed from any obligation to work, the aristocrats of the novel suffer from a pervasive ____, drifting from party to party without interest or purpose.
gre.clue: drifting from party to party without interest or purpose

en: To speak or write at great length
hook: EX-PATIATE: wander out (spatiari) in long speech.
story: Expatiate. Ask Professor Kabir a simple question about the weather, and he will expatiate on monsoon patterns, rainfall records since British times, climate change, and a rain poem by Jibanananda Das. Forty minutes later, you will still be standing there. To expatiate is to speak or write at great length. It comes from the Latin for wandering widely. Do not confuse it with expiate, to atone, or expatriate, to leave one's country. Synonyms: elaborate, expound, dilate.
example: The professor tended to expatiate on his favorite topics.

gre.s: Given just five minutes at the conference, the speaker could not ____ on her research as she had hoped, and offered only a brief summary of her findings.
gre.clue: offered only a brief summary of her findings

en: Filled with something undesirable; causing anxiety
hook: FRAUGHT: FREIGHT-loaded with danger.
story: Fraught. The night before the final match, the dressing room was fraught with tension. Two players had quarrelled, the captain was injured, and the coach's job depended on the result. Nobody slept. Fraught means filled with something undesirable, such as danger, tension or difficulty, and it is often followed by with. Used alone, it means causing anxiety, as in a fraught conversation. It shares a root with freight: heavily loaded. Synonyms: laden, tense, charged.
example: Their journey home was fraught with danger.

gre.s: The negotiations were ____ with danger from the start: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war that had only just ended.
gre.clue: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war

en: The support on which a lever pivots; a central or essential element
hook: FULCRUM: the PIVOT point of a seesaw.
story: Fulcrum. On a playground seesaw, the plank rests on a single support in the middle. That support is the fulcrum: the point on which a lever pivots. Archimedes boasted that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could move the Earth. Figuratively, a fulcrum is a central or essential element. In Rafi's family, his grandmother is the fulcrum; every big decision turns on her. Synonyms: pivot, linchpin, crux.
example: The politician's campaign promises became the fulcrum of his electoral strategy.

gre.s: As the only member trusted by both factions, the young senator became the ____ of the negotiations, the point around which every compromise turned.
gre.clue: the point around which every compromise turned

en: An extremely confused, complicated, or embarrassing situation
hook: IMBROGLIO: an EMBROIDERY of tangled threads.
story: Imbroglio. It began with a forwarded message in a family group chat. One cousin misread it as an insult, an aunt took sides, two uncles stopped speaking, a wedding invitation was withdrawn, and somehow an old land dispute was revived. Nobody remembered the original message. It was an imbroglio: an extremely confused, complicated or embarrassing situation. The word is Italian, related to embroil, to tangle someone up. Synonyms: entanglement, muddle, mess.
example: He became embroiled in an imbroglio over a financial dispute.

gre.s: What began as a minor accounting error grew into a diplomatic ____ involving three governments, two banks, and a tangle of contradictory lawsuits.
gre.clue: a tangle of contradictory lawsuits

en: Cheerful and lighthearted
hook: JOCUND: JOKING and JOLLY.
story: Jocund. Every year on Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year, Dhaka fills with jocund crowds. People in red and white laugh, sing, eat panta bhat with hilsa, and dance to the drums. Even strangers smile at one another. The mood is jocund: cheerful and lighthearted. It comes from the Latin for pleasant, influenced by the Latin word for joke. Wordsworth wrote of the jocund company of daffodils. Synonyms: merry, jovial, cheerful.
example: He was full of jocund laughter and playful banter.

gre.s: The mood at the reunion was ____, with old friends laughing and singing late into the night, utterly unlike the somber gathering the organizers had feared.
gre.clue: laughing and singing late into the night

en: To lose strength; to suffer from being in an unpleasant situation
bn: দুর্বল হয়ে পড়া; কষ্টে দিন কাটানো
hook: LANGUISH: become LANGUID, weak and fading.
story: Languish. A young activist was arrested and held without trial. Months turned into years. In a cramped cell he grew thin and pale, while his case file gathered dust in a government office. He languished in prison: he suffered in an unpleasant situation and slowly lost strength. Plants languish without water; projects languish without funding. Languish shares a root with languid, meaning weak and slow. Synonyms: wither, decline, waste away.
example: The prisoners languished in their cells for years.

gre.s: Without fresh investment, the once thriving port continued to ____, its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling into the harbor.
gre.clue: its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling

en: The lowest point
hook: NADIR: the opposite of zenith, the bottom of everything.
story: Nadir. The year Arif's father lost his business, the family sold their car, moved into a single rented room, and Arif nearly dropped out of school. That winter was the nadir of their lives: the lowest point. Slowly, things improved. In astronomy, the nadir is the point directly below an observer, opposite the zenith overhead. Both words come from Arabic. Remember: nadir is down, zenith is up. Synonyms: low point, rock bottom.
example: After the stock market crash, his wealth reached its nadir.

gre.s: The team's season reached its ____ in March, when a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place; only then did its slow recovery begin.
gre.clue: a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place

en: Quick and light in movement; quick-thinking
hook: NIMBLE: as quick as a NIMBLE squirrel.
story: Nimble. In the crowded Gulistan market, a young porter carries a basket of vegetables on his head, weaving between rickshaws, buses and shoppers without ever bumping anyone. His feet are nimble: quick and light in movement. Nimble also describes the mind, so a nimble debater answers tricky questions instantly. Remember the nursery rhyme: Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, Jack jump over the candlestick. Synonyms: agile, deft, spry.
example: The gymnast's movements were incredibly nimble.

gre.s: Though the old pianist's body had grown frail, his fingers remained astonishingly ____, racing through the most difficult passages without a single error.
gre.clue: racing through the most difficult passages

en: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen
hook: OMINOUS: an OMEN of bad things.
story: Ominous. Fishermen at Cox's Bazar noticed the sky turning a strange copper colour. The wind died, the birds disappeared, and the sea went flat and silent. The old men pulled their boats high up the beach. The signs were ominous: they suggested that something bad was about to happen. That night, the cyclone arrived. Ominous comes from omen, a sign of what the future holds. Synonyms: menacing, foreboding, sinister.
example: The ominous clouds overhead foreshadowed a storm.

gre.s: The doctors' sudden silence and averted eyes were ____, and the family braced themselves for bad news before a single word was spoken.
gre.clue: braced themselves for bad news

en: Bizarrely strange or unusual
hook: OUT-LANDISH: from an OUTside LAND, totally foreign and weird.
story: Outlandish. Sabbir arrived at his cousin's wedding wearing a purple suit covered in silver stars, green shoes, and a hat shaped like a fish. The aunties gasped, the children giggled, and the photographer could not stop laughing. His outfit was outlandish: bizarrely strange and unusual. An outlandish claim is one so strange it is hard to believe. Originally the word meant foreign, from out land, another country. Synonyms: bizarre, weird, preposterous.
example: Her outlandish fashion sense always turned heads.

gre.s: The theory that the pyramids were built by visitors from another planet is so ____ that serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it.
gre.clue: serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it

en: Favorable; indicating a good chance of success
hook: PROPITIOUS: PROPER time to act — the signs are favorable.
story: Propitious. Farmers in Rangpur waited anxiously for the planting season. Then the rains arrived on time, the soil was soft, fertiliser prices fell, and new seeds came from the research institute. Everything pointed to a good harvest. The conditions were propitious: favourable, indicating a good chance of success. Propitious comes from the Latin for gracious, as if the gods were smiling on you. Its close cousin is auspicious. Synonyms: favourable, opportune, promising.
example: The weather conditions were propitious for planting the new crop.

gre.s: Investors were wary of launching the venture during a recession, but the sudden drop in interest rates made the moment unexpectedly ____.
gre.clue: the sudden drop in interest rates

en: Having or encouraging an excessive interest in sexual or scandalous matters
hook: PRURIENT: like an ITCH (prurire = to itch) for scandal.
story: Prurient. When a famous actor was hospitalized, some tabloids printed almost nothing about his health. Instead, they ran pages of gossip about his secret romances, with blurry photos taken through windows. Readers bought every copy. The tabloids fed a prurient interest: an excessive interest in sexual or scandalous matters. Prurient comes from the Latin for itching, so think of an itch for scandal. Its opposite is prudish. Synonyms: lewd, salacious, voyeuristic.
example: The magazine was criticized for its prurient content.

gre.s: Critics charged that the documentary, despite its claims to serious journalism, merely catered to viewers' ____ curiosity, lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs.
gre.clue: lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs

en: Taking pleasure in causing pain or suffering to others
hook: SADISTIC: makes others SAD and enjoys it.
story: Sadistic. In an old prison film, a guard forces the prisoners to stand in the burning sun for hours, then laughs as they faint, and smiles while ordering more punishment. He enjoys their pain. He is sadistic: taking pleasure in causing pain or suffering to others. The word comes from the Marquis de Sade, an eighteenth-century French writer notorious for cruelty in his novels. Students sometimes joke that a brutal exam is sadistic. Synonyms: cruel, vicious, barbarous.
example: The sadistic murderer showed no remorse for his crimes.

gre.s: The guard was not merely strict but ____, devising humiliating punishments for minor offenses and visibly relishing the prisoners' suffering.
gre.clue: visibly relishing the prisoners' suffering

en: The highest point; the peak of success
hook: ZENITH: the sun straight overhead, the top of the sky.
story: Zenith. Mughal power reached its zenith in the seventeenth century, when the empire stretched across most of the subcontinent and Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal. After that, it slowly declined. The zenith is the highest point, the peak of success. In astronomy, it is the point in the sky directly above an observer. Remember: zenith is up, nadir is down. Both came into English from Arabic astronomy. Synonyms: peak, pinnacle, apex.
example: At the zenith of his career, the actor was beloved by fans worldwide.

gre.s: At the ____ of his fame, the singer could fill any stadium in the country; a decade later, he was performing in near-empty halls.
gre.clue: could fill any stadium in the country

en: Departing from what is normal or accepted
hook: AB-ERR-ANT: ERRing AWAY from the norm.
story: Aberrant. For three years, the hostel's old rickshaw puller arrived at the gate at exactly seven every morning. One Tuesday he did not come at all, and the next day he showed up at noon, singing loudly and refusing to take any fare. The guards were worried by such aberrant behavior: it departed sharply from his normal pattern. Aberrant means straying from what is normal or accepted. Ab means away and err means wander: wandering away from the path. Synonyms: deviant, anomalous.
example: Her aberrant behavior raised concerns among her colleagues.

gre.s: Because the patient's readings had been stable for years, the doctor was alarmed by one ____ result that departed sharply from every previous test.
gre.clue: departed sharply from every previous test

en: To tolerate; to accept or act in accordance with a rule
hook: ABIDE: can't ABIDE it = can't stand it. ABIDE BY = obey.
story: Abide. Mitu's new roommate played loud music until three every night. Mitu tried earplugs, then pillows, then polite notes. Finally she went to the hall supervisor and said, "I cannot abide this noise any longer." The supervisor reminded the roommate that every resident must abide by the quiet hours after eleven. To abide something is to tolerate it, usually said in the negative: she can't abide liars. To abide by a rule is to accept and obey it. Synonyms: tolerate, bear, obey.
example: Students must abide by the school's dress code.

gre.s: A meticulous editor, she could not ____ even minor errors of punctuation, and she returned any manuscript that contained them without reading further.
gre.clue: returned any manuscript that contained them

en: A bold show of courage meant to impress, often hiding fear
hook: BRAVADO: BRAVE-looking, but just a show.
story: Bravado. Before the debate final, Farhan swaggered around the hall, telling everyone he would crush the other team without even preparing. But his friends noticed that his hands shook as he held his cup of tea. His loud confidence was pure bravado: a bold show of courage meant to impress, hiding real fear underneath. Bravado is related to brave, but it is bravery put on for display. True bravery is often quiet; bravado is always loud. Synonyms: swagger, bluster.
example: His acts of bravado often landed him in trouble.

gre.s: Beneath the general's public ____ lay deep private doubts; in letters to his wife, he confessed that he fully expected the campaign to fail.
gre.clue: lay deep private doubts

en: To permit; also, to admit or concede that something is true
hook: GRE trick: ALLOW can mean ADMIT — 'he allowed that he was wrong.'
story: Allow. Rafi and his sister Nadia argued for an hour about whether Messi or Ronaldo was the greater player. Rafi refused to give an inch, until Nadia pulled up the statistics on her phone. Rafi sighed. "All right, I will allow that Messi has more assists," he said, "but Ronaldo is better in big matches." Here, to allow means to admit or concede that something is true. Its everyday meaning is to permit, as when parents allow a trip. Synonyms: concede, grant, acknowledge.
example: The teacher allowed the students to work in groups.

gre.s: Even her harshest critics would ____ that her research was meticulous, though they continued to dispute the conclusions she drew from it.
gre.clue: though they continued to dispute the conclusions

en: To surrender or give in
hook: CAPITULATE: surrender your CAPITAL city.
story: Capitulate. For two weeks, students at a Dhaka college camped outside the administration building, demanding that a sudden fee increase be cancelled. The principal swore he would never give in. But as newspapers covered the protest and parents joined the students, he finally capitulated and announced that the increase was withdrawn. To capitulate is to surrender or give in, usually after resisting. It comes from a Latin word for drawing up terms under headings, like the chapters of a surrender treaty. Synonyms: yield, surrender, submit.
example: After a long siege, the defenders were forced to capitulate.

gre.s: After months of insisting that it would never negotiate, the management finally chose to ____ to the union's demands when the strike began to cripple production.
gre.clue: when the strike began to cripple production

en: To think deeply about something
hook: COGITATE: 'Cogito, ergo sum' — I think, therefore I am.
story: Cogitate. Ishita stared at the chess board for twenty full minutes without touching a piece. Her opponent fidgeted, checked his phone, and sighed loudly. She was not frozen; she was cogitating, thinking deeply through every possible move and its consequences. Finally she moved her knight, and three turns later she won. To cogitate is to think deeply and carefully. It shares a root with the philosopher Descartes' famous line, cogito, ergo sum: I think, therefore I am. Synonyms: ponder, deliberate, mull.
example: The philosopher cogitated on the nature of existence.

gre.s: Rather than react impulsively to the offer, the cautious investor preferred to ____ for several days, weighing every possible risk before making a decision.
gre.clue: weighing every possible risk before making a decision

en: A person's behavior and manners; the way one carries oneself
hook: DEPORTMENT: how you COMPORT yourself.
story: Deportment. Before Anika's first job interview at a bank in Motijheel, her aunt gave her a lesson. "Sit straight, do not fidget, greet everyone politely, and never check your phone." The interviewers later told her they hired her partly for her deportment: the calm, courteous way she carried herself. Deportment means a person's behavior and manners, especially in public. Old finishing schools taught deportment by making girls walk with books balanced on their heads. Synonyms: bearing, demeanor, conduct.
example: Her impeccable deportment made her a favorite among the guests.

gre.s: Though the young diplomat's knowledge of policy was impressive, it was his impeccable ____ that won him admirers: he remained courteous and composed even under hostile questioning.
gre.clue: remained courteous and composed even under hostile questioning

en: To speak or perform without preparation; to improvise
hook: EX-TEMPOR-IZE: OUT of the moment (tempus = time).
story: Extemporize. Halfway through Sara's presentation at a university conference, her laptop died and the projector went dark. There were no slides, no notes, and two hundred people waiting. She took a breath, stepped forward, and extemporized, explaining her research from memory and drawing diagrams on the whiteboard as she went. The audience loved it. To extemporize is to speak or perform without preparation; to improvise. In Latin, ex tempore means out of the moment. Synonyms: improvise, ad lib.
example: The speaker had to extemporize when he forgot his notes.

gre.s: When the actor forgot his lines on opening night, he was forced to ____, inventing dialogue so convincingly that the audience never suspected anything had gone wrong.
gre.clue: inventing dialogue so convincingly

en: Inclined to cause disagreement and division into factions
hook: FACTIOUS: creating FACTIONS.
story: Factious. The university debating club once had forty happy members. Then two senior students began fighting over who would lead it. Each recruited loyal followers, spread rumours about the other, and blocked every proposal from the rival camp. By the end of the year, the club had split into two angry groups. Their factious behavior had divided everyone. Factious means inclined to cause disagreement and division into factions. Do not confuse it with fractious, meaning unruly, or factitious, meaning artificial. Synonyms: divisive, partisan.
example: The factious political climate made it difficult to pass legislation.

gre.s: The once unified party had grown so ____ that its members spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government.
gre.clue: spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government

en: Of land: left unplanted to restore fertility; inactive
hook: FALLOW: the field just lies there, FALLEN asleep.
story: Fallow. In a village near Rajshahi, Rahim's grandfather never planted the eastern field every third year. Neighbors thought he was wasting good land. But he explained that the soil needed rest; left unplanted for a season, it would regain its strength and give a richer harvest the following year. The field lay fallow: plowed but unplanted, resting. Fallow also describes any period of inactivity, like a writer's fallow years before a great novel. Synonyms: idle, dormant, inactive.
example: The fields lay fallow during the winter months.

gre.s: After a decade of furious productivity, the composer entered a ____ period in which he wrote almost nothing, though critics later saw it as a time of quiet renewal.
gre.clue: in which he wrote almost nothing

en: A deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent
hook: FEINT: a FAKE move. Sounds like FAINT but means FAKE.
story: Feint. In the final minute of the inter-hall football match, Shuvo dribbled toward the goal. He dropped his shoulder to the left as if to shoot. The goalkeeper dived left.
