Shuvo calmly rolled the ball into the right corner. That shoulder drop was a feint: a deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent. Boxers feint with one hand before striking with the other. Feint sounds like faint, and the goalkeeper nearly fainted when he realised he had been fooled. Synonyms: ruse, bluff, decoy.
example: The boxer used a feint to draw his opponent into an opening.

gre.s: The general's apparent retreat was merely a ____: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them and attacked their unguarded camp.
gre.clue: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them

en: Shockingly obvious and offensive
hook: FLAGRANT: as obvious as a FLAG waving in your face.
story: Flagrant. During a televised cricket match, a fielder scratched the ball with a bottle cap right in front of the camera. Millions of viewers saw it clearly in slow motion. There was no doubt and no excuse; it was a flagrant violation of the rules: shockingly obvious and offensive. Flagrant comes from the Latin for burning, like a fire blazing so brightly that nobody can miss it. Do not confuse it with fragrant, which simply smells nice. Synonyms: blatant, glaring, egregious.
example: The politician's corruption was a flagrant abuse of power.

gre.s: Far from being a subtle oversight, the company's dumping of chemicals into the river was a ____ violation of environmental law, carried out openly in daylight for years.
gre.clue: carried out openly in daylight for years

en: Unnecessary and unjustified; given free of charge
hook: GRATUITOUS: like a GRATUITY (tip), extra and not required.
story: Gratuitous. A new action film had a simple, touching love story, but the director added a ten minute scene of bloody violence that had nothing to do with the plot. Critics called the scene gratuitous: unnecessary and unjustified, added only to shock. Gratuitous shares a root with gratis, meaning free, so it can also mean given free of charge. On the GRE, though, it usually means uncalled for, as in a gratuitous insult. Synonyms: needless, unwarranted, unprovoked.
example: The movie contained scenes of gratuitous violence.

gre.s: The reviewer's remarks about the author's appearance were entirely ____: they had no bearing on the quality of the novel and served only to humiliate her.
gre.clue: had no bearing on the quality of the novel

en: To behave in an excessively humble way to win favor or forgiveness
hook: GROVEL: crawling in the GRAVEL begging.
story: Grovel. Tanvir missed his project deadline by a whole week. He went to his professor's office, apologised again and again, praised every lecture she had ever given, offered to carry her books for a semester, and nearly knelt on the floor. The professor looked uncomfortable. "Please stop groveling," she said, "and just submit the work." To grovel is to behave in an excessively humble way to win favor or forgiveness. Its old meaning was to lie face down on the ground. Synonyms: kowtow, fawn.
example: He refused to grovel before his superiors to get a promotion.

gre.s: Although the other courtiers were willing to ____ before the king to win his favor, the young poet refused to flatter him and addressed him as an equal.
gre.clue: refused to flatter him and addressed him as an equal

en: Not in keeping with good taste and propriety
hook: IN-DECOROUS: NOT showing DECORUM.
story: Indecorous. At a solemn funeral gathering in his village, Babu's phone suddenly rang with a loud dance song. Worse, he answered it and began laughing about a cricket score while the imam was still praying. The elders glared at him. His behavior was indecorous: not in keeping with good taste and the propriety the occasion demanded. Decorum means proper, dignified behavior, so indecorous is its opposite. It is milder than indecent; it means improper, not obscene. Synonyms: unseemly, improper, unbecoming.
example: His indecorous remarks shocked the other guests.

gre.s: Many guests found the best man's crude jokes at the memorial service ____, since such levity seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion.
gre.clue: seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion

en: A secret plot or scheme; to arouse curiosity
hook: INTRIGUE: the palace's secret plots that INTRIGUE you.
story: Intrigue. In the old Mughal courts, ministers whispered in dark corridors, bribed servants to read secret letters, and plotted to ruin their rivals. Historians call this palace intrigue: secret plotting and scheming. Lamia read about it in a historical novel and could not put the book down; the story intrigued her, arousing her curiosity until two in the morning. So as a noun, intrigue is a secret plot; as a verb, it means to fascinate. Synonyms: conspiracy, scheming; or, to fascinate.
example: The palace was rife with political intrigue.

gre.s: The royal court was rife with ____: ministers formed secret alliances, spread rumors about their rivals, and plotted against one another behind the king's back.
gre.clue: plotted against one another behind the king's back

en: Very small, far below real value; existing in name only
hook: NOMINAL: in NAME only (nomen).
story: Nominal. Zayan's uncle is the nominal head of the family business; his name is on the sign, but his sharp daughter makes every real decision. And when Zayan joined a coaching center, the registration fee was nominal, only fifty taka, far below the real cost. Nominal means existing in name only, or so small that it barely counts. It comes from the Latin nomen, meaning name, as in nominate. Synonyms: titular, token, trifling.
example: They charged a nominal fee for the service.

gre.s: Although she was the ____ chair of the committee, real authority rested with her deputy, who set the agenda and made every major decision.
gre.clue: real authority rested with her deputy

en: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or action
hook: OB-DURATE: DURABLE stubbornness, hardened.
story: Obdurate. For six months, villagers begged the factory owner to stop dumping waste into their river. Scientists showed him test results. Fishermen showed him dead fish. Even the local imam asked him to reconsider. He would not budge an inch. He was obdurate: stubbornly refusing to change his opinion or his actions. The word shares a root with durable, from the Latin for hard; an obdurate person has a hardened heart. Synonyms: intransigent, inflexible, unyielding.
example: The company's obdurate stance in negotiations led to a stalemate.

gre.s: Despite mounting evidence that his policy was failing, the minister remained ____, refusing even to consider the modest changes his own advisors proposed.
gre.clue: refusing even to consider the modest changes

en: Noisy and difficult to control
hook: OBSTREPEROUS: makes an OBSTACLE with noise.
story: Obstreperous. The night train from Dhaka to Chittagong was quiet until six young men boarded. They shouted, banged on the windows, played music at full volume, and argued with the ticket checker who asked them to sit down. When he threatened to call the police, they only shouted louder. The other passengers sighed at the obstreperous group: noisy and difficult to control. The word comes from Latin for making a racket, and it even sounds loud and clumsy. Synonyms: unruly, boisterous, rowdy.
example: The obstreperous crowd made it difficult for the speaker to be heard.

gre.s: The substitute teacher could not control the ____ students, who shouted over one another, ignored her instructions, and refused to stay in their seats.
gre.clue: shouted over one another, ignored her instructions

en: Extremely unpleasant; hateful
hook: ODIOUS: full of ODOR and hatred.
story: Odious. Arif's new manager took credit for his team's work, shouted at junior staff in front of clients, and cut the cleaner's wages for arriving five minutes late. Within a month, nobody in the office could stand him. Everything about his conduct was odious: extremely unpleasant and hateful. Odious comes from odium, the Latin word for hatred. Think of an odor so foul that you cannot stay in the same room. Synonyms: repugnant, detestable, abhorrent.
example: The crime was so odious that it shocked the entire nation.

gre.s: Though the essayist praised the dictator's economic reforms, she found his persecution of journalists so ____ that she refused to attend any event held in his honor.
gre.clue: refused to attend any event held in his honor

en: Brave and determined in difficult circumstances
hook: PLUCKY: has PLUCK (courage).
story: Plucky. During the floods in Sylhet, twelve year old Joya noticed that her neighbor's goats were trapped on a sinking platform. The adults were busy moving rice sacks. Joya tied a rope to a mango tree, waded through the waist deep water, and led all four goats to safety. The whole village called her plucky: brave and determined in a difficult situation. Pluck is an old word for courage, used especially for someone small or outmatched. Synonyms: spirited, gutsy, intrepid.
example: The plucky firefighter rushed into the burning building to save a child.

gre.s: Though heavily outmatched by the professional teams, the ____ amateur squad fought for every point and refused to concede even when defeat was certain.
gre.clue: refused to concede even when defeat was certain

en: Showing unusually early development, especially mental
hook: PRE-COCIOUS: PRE-COOKED early, ripe too soon.
story: Precocious. Mahin was four years old when he began reading his father's newspaper aloud at breakfast. By seven, he was solving his sister's high school math problems and asking his teacher about black holes. Relatives called him precocious: showing unusually early development, especially mental. The word comes from the Latin for ripened early, like fruit that ripens before its season. A precocious child seems older than his years. Synonyms: advanced, forward, gifted.
example: The precocious child was reading college-level textbooks by the age of ten.

gre.s: Remarkably ____, the boy was reading novels at three and solving algebra problems at six, years before most of his peers could do either.
gre.clue: years before most of his peers could do either

en: Money paid for work or a service
hook: RE-MUNER-ATION: MONEY (munus) given back for work.
story: Remuneration. Priya translated a two hundred page novel for a Dhaka publishing house. When she asked about payment, the editor offered her a free copy of the book and a thank you in the preface. Priya politely explained that her landlord did not accept thanks as rent. She wanted proper remuneration: money paid for work or a service. The root munus is Latin for gift or service. Careful with spelling: it is remuneration, not renumeration. Synonyms: payment, compensation, pay.
example: The employees demanded fair remuneration for their overtime work.

gre.s: Many of the volunteers worked for years without ____, motivated not by money but by their deep commitment to the cause.
gre.clue: motivated not by money

en: Messy and careless in appearance or work
hook: SLOVENLY: SLOPPY and LOVE-less care.
story: Slovenly. Sabbir's hostel room was famous. Dirty socks hung from the ceiling fan, rice plates sat under the bed for days, and his shirts were always wrinkled and half tucked in. His lab reports looked the same, with tea stains, crossed out numbers and missing units. His teacher finally wrote at the top: "Brilliant ideas, slovenly work." Slovenly means messy and careless, in appearance or in work. Think of a sloppy sloth that never cleans. Synonyms: untidy, sloppy, unkempt.
example: His slovenly appearance made a poor impression on the interviewer.

gre.s: The editor rejected the manuscript not for its ideas but for its ____ presentation: pages were out of order, quotations were unattributed, and typos littered every paragraph.
gre.clue: typos littered every paragraph

en: A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud alone
hook: SOLI-LOQUY: SOLO speech (loqui = speak).
story: Soliloquy. In the drama club's production of Hamlet, Imran stood alone on the dark stage under a single spotlight. No other actor was present. He spoke the prince's thoughts aloud: "To be, or not to be." The audience heard everything going on in Hamlet's troubled mind. That speech is a soliloquy: a speech in which a character, alone, speaks his thoughts aloud. Solus means alone and loqui means to speak in Latin: speaking alone. Compare monologue, which may be addressed to others.

en: To reduce the value or quality of something

en: Causing harm or damage

en: Using dishonest or tricky methods to achieve goals

en: Temporarily inactive or sleeping

en: Excessively harsh and severe, especially of laws
hook: DRACONIAN: from DRACO, an ancient Greek lawmaker who gave the death penalty for small crimes.

en: Former; previous

To reflect is to think deeply, or to show and reveal, the way a mirror reflects a face. Synonyms: ponder, mirror, indicate.
example: She took some time to reflect on her choices before making a decision.

gre.s: The novel's bleak tone may ____ the author's own despair during the war years, a period she described in her letters as the darkest of her life.

en: Able to find quick, clever ways to overcome difficulties
hook: RESOURCEFUL: full of RESOURCES in your mind.
story: Resourceful. A storm knocked out the power in Sabbir's village an hour before his online exam. He did not panic. He borrowed a motorbike battery, wired it to his router, charged his phone from a neighbour's solar panel, and logged in with two minutes to spare. He was resourceful: able to find quick, clever ways around difficulties. A resourceful person is full of resources, especially inner ones like wit and imagination. Synonyms: ingenious, inventive, enterprising.
example: The resourceful scout found a way to build a shelter with limited supplies.

gre.s: Stranded without tools when their car broke down in the desert, the ____ travelers repaired the fan belt with a pair of nylon stockings and reached the next town by nightfall.
gre.clue: repaired the fan belt with a pair of nylon stockings

en: To reduce costs or spending
hook: RE-TRENCH: dig back into a TRENCH, cutting back.
story: Retrench. When export orders fell sharply, the owner of a garment factory in Narayanganj called his managers together. "We must retrench." They closed one production line, cancelled the new building, cut overtime, and stopped all foreign travel. To retrench is to reduce costs or spending, usually because money is tight. It comes from an old French word meaning to cut off. Retrenchment often means laying off workers as well. Synonyms: economize, cut back, downsize.
example: The company had to retrench during the recession.

gre.s: Faced with a steep decline in enrollment, the college was forced to ____, suspending construction of its new library and freezing all hiring.
gre.clue: suspending construction of its new library and freezing all hiring

en: Excessively indulging one's own desires
hook: SELF-INDULGENT: INDULGING the SELF too much.
story: Self-indulgent. A famous director released a new film that ran four hours, with long scenes of himself walking on a beach reading his own poems aloud. Audiences walked out. Critics called it self-indulgent: excessively satisfying the maker's own desires and tastes, with little thought for anyone else. The word can also describe someone who eats a whole box of mishti alone. To indulge is to give in to a desire. Synonyms: hedonistic, intemperate, self-absorbed.
example: Her self-indulgent lifestyle led to financial problems.

gre.s: The editor urged the novelist to cut her lengthy digressions about her own childhood, which, however satisfying to write, struck readers as ____ and irrelevant to the plot.
gre.clue: however satisfying to write

en: To form a theory without firm evidence; to invest riskily
hook: SPECULATE: look (specere) ahead and guess.
story: Speculate. When a famous cricketer missed three practice sessions in a row, the newspapers began to speculate. Was he injured? Was he quarrelling with the coach? Was he about to retire? Nobody actually knew anything. To speculate is to form theories without firm evidence. The word has a second sense: to invest riskily, hoping for a quick profit, as when people speculate on land prices. It comes from the Latin for to look, as in spectacle. Synonyms: conjecture, theorize, surmise.
example: Scientists speculated about the origins of the mysterious signal.

gre.s: In the absence of reliable records, historians can only ____ about the poet's early years; even the city of her birth remains a matter of dispute.

en: Serious, respectable, and unadventurous
hook: STAID: STAYED the same forever, never adventurous.

He distrusts jokes, loud colours, and new ideas. He is staid: serious, respectable, and unadventurous. Staid is an old spelling of stayed, as if fixed in place. A staid newspaper has a dignified, conservative style. Opposite: flamboyant. Synonyms: sedate, sober, conservative.
example: The staid professor rarely showed any emotion in his lectures.

gre.s: Once known for its ____ coverage of parliamentary procedure, the newspaper has lately reinvented itself with splashy headlines and celebrity gossip.
gre.clue: has lately reinvented itself with splashy headlines and celebrity gossip

en: To forcibly stop; to prevent from being expressed
hook: SUP-PRESS: PRESS it down.
story: Suppress. In the middle of a solemn condolence meeting, Rumana's phone suddenly played a ringtone of a quacking cartoon duck. Everyone turned. Her friend beside her had to suppress a laugh, biting her lip until her eyes watered. To suppress is to forcibly stop something or keep it from being expressed: suppress a yawn, suppress a rebellion, suppress evidence. Sup comes from sub, under, so to suppress is to press something down. Synonyms: quell, stifle, squelch.
example: The military tried to suppress the rebellion.

gre.s: Though the regime tried to ____ news of the protests, reports spread quickly through encrypted messaging apps beyond the reach of state censors.
gre.clue: beyond the reach of state censors

en: Remaining as a small trace of something that once was larger or more important
hook: VESTIGIAL: a VESTIGE, a remnant.
story: Vestigial. In biology class, Mahin learned that humans still have a tailbone, the tiny remains of a tail our distant ancestors once had. It no longer works as a tail at all. Such an organ is vestigial: remaining only as a small trace of something that was once larger or more important. A vestige is a trace, literally a footprint. In some countries the monarchy is vestigial, a ceremonial trace of old power. Synonyms: rudimentary, residual, leftover.
example: Some animals have vestigial organs that no longer serve a purpose.

gre.s: Although the office of governor-general still exists, its powers are now largely ____: the post survives as a ceremonial remnant of an era when it truly governed.
gre.clue: survives as a ceremonial remnant

en: Agreement or harmony; a formal treaty; to give or grant
hook: ACCORD: hearts (cor) in agreement.
story: Accord. Two families near Comilla had quarrelled for years over a narrow strip of land between their fields. Finally, the elders brought them together under the banyan tree. After hours of talk, both sides agreed to share the strip as a footpath. They had reached an accord: an agreement, a state of harmony. An accord can also be a formal treaty, like a peace accord. As a verb, to accord means to give or grant, as in according someone respect. Synonyms: agreement, pact.
example: The two countries finally reached an accord after months of negotiation.

gre.s: After decades of hostility, the two neighboring states finally reached a historic ____ on sharing the river's waters, though skeptics doubted it would survive the next drought.
gre.clue: though skeptics doubted it would survive the next drought

en: To stick firmly; to follow a rule or belief
hook: ADHERE: like ADHESIVE tape.
story: Adhere. Before every exam, Priya's hostel puts up a notice: phones off and lights out by eleven. Most of the girls ignore it. Priya adheres to it strictly, every single night, and her roommates tease her for it. To adhere is to follow a rule or belief faithfully. Its first meaning is physical: to stick firmly, the way a stamp adheres to an envelope. Adhesive tape sticks to paper; an adherent sticks to a cause. Synonyms: stick, abide, comply.
example: The wet poster adhered to the wall.

gre.s: Although the committee claimed to ____ to the principle of transparency, it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors and published no minutes.
gre.clue: it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors

en: Created for a particular purpose only, not planned in advance
hook: AD HOC: Latin for 'for this' — for this one purpose only.
story: Ad hoc. When floodwater suddenly poured into the ground floor of a hospital in Sylhet, there was no plan for it. Doctors, cleaners, and patients' relatives formed an ad hoc team on the spot, passing beds and medicine boxes upstairs in a human chain. Ad hoc means created for one particular purpose only, not planned in advance. The Latin literally means for this. An ad hoc committee dissolves when its task is done. Contrast systematic. Synonyms: improvised, impromptu, makeshift.
example: An ad hoc committee was formed to address the sudden increase in complaints from customers.

gre.s: Rather than developing a coherent policy, the ministry responded to each crisis in a purely ____ fashion, devising quick fixes that were abandoned once the emergency passed.
gre.clue: Rather than developing a coherent policy

en: Including everything
hook: ALL-ENCOMPASSING: a COMPASS that circles everything.
story: All-encompassing. When Rafi's grandfather began writing a history of their village, he did not stop at the important families. He recorded every pond, every mosque and temple, every flood since 1950, even the names of cows and the recipes for festival sweets. His notebook was all-encompassing: including absolutely everything. To encompass is to surround or include, as if drawing a circle with a compass around it all. An all-encompassing grief fills every corner of life. Synonyms: comprehensive, exhaustive, universal.
example: The encyclopedia offered an all-encompassing look at world history.

gre.s: Far from the narrow survey its modest title suggested, the study was nearly ____, covering every aspect of the region's economy from river fishing to software.
gre.clue: covering every aspect of the region's economy

en: A short, wise statement of a general truth
hook: APHORISM: a short AFFIRMATION of truth.
story: Aphorism. Mitu's grandmother rarely gave long lectures. Instead, she offered short, wise sentences that stuck forever. "An empty pitcher makes the most noise." "The branch heavy with fruit bends low." Years later, Mitu still quotes them at the office. These were aphorisms: short, wise statements of a general truth. The word comes from the Greek for marking a boundary, the same root as horizon; an aphorism draws a sharp line around a truth. Synonyms: maxim, adage, proverb.
example: Ben Franklin was famous for his aphorisms like, "Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise."

gre.s: The essay closes with a single pithy ____, "Certainty ages a face faster than doubt," which has been quoted far more often than any of the arguments that precede it.
gre.clue: a single pithy

en: A standard against which things are measured
hook: BENCHMARK: a mark on the workbench to measure against.
story: Benchmark. When Tanvir joined a running club in Ramna Park, the coach timed him over five kilometres: thirty-four minutes. That number became his benchmark, the standard against which every later run was measured. Three months later, he finished in twenty-seven. A benchmark is a standard or point of reference for comparison. Originally, surveyors cut a mark into stone to rest their levelling bench on. Companies benchmark their products against rivals. Synonyms: standard, yardstick, touchstone.
example: The company's sales figures were used as a benchmark for the rest of the industry.

gre.s: For decades, the textbook's rigorous treatment of the subject served as the ____ against which all later introductions were judged, and few of them measured up.
gre.clue: against which all later introductions were judged

en: Damaged or spoiled; suffering from decay
hook: BLIGHT: a plant disease that withers crops.
story: Blighted. One monsoon, a fungus crept across the rice fields of Babu's uncle in Dinajpur. Within two weeks, the green stalks had turned brown and withered. The crop was blighted: damaged and spoiled, struck by disease or decay. A neighbourhood can be blighted too, with empty buildings, broken windows, and heaps of rubbish. A blight is anything that spoils or ruins, as the potato blight ruined Ireland's harvests in the 1840s. Synonyms: ruined, spoiled, devastated.
example: The once-beautiful neighborhood was blighted by crime and poverty.

gre.s: Once a thriving industrial district, the riverside neighborhood is now ____, its factories abandoned and its streets lined with crumbling, boarded-up houses.
gre.clue: its factories abandoned and its streets lined with crumbling, boarded-up houses

en: Peacefully satisfied
hook: CON-TENT (stress on TENT): happy in your little tent.
story: Content. Rahim, a boatman on the Meghna, owns one wooden boat, a tin-roofed house, and three goats. Each evening he sits by the river with a cup of tea and watches the sunset. When a visitor from the city asked whether he wanted more, he laughed. "What more? I have enough." He is content: peacefully satisfied with what he has. Stress the second syllable, con-TENT. Do not confuse it with CON-tent, what something contains. Synonyms: satisfied, serene.
example: The baby looked content as it slept soundly in its crib.

gre.s: Unlike her restless siblings, who constantly chased new ventures, she was ____ with the quiet life of a village schoolteacher and never sought promotion.

en: Reduced in quality, value, or moral character
hook: DE-BASED: brought to a BASE (low) level.
story: Debased. Long ago, rulers sometimes mixed cheap copper into their silver coins so they could mint more of them. The coins looked the same, but each one was worth less. The currency had been debased: lowered in quality and value. A person can be debased too, morally degraded, and a word can be debased through overuse; think of how awesome now describes a sandwich. De means down: brought down to a baser level. Synonyms: degraded, corrupted, cheapened.
example: The once-noble ideals of the revolution were debased by the dictator's greed.

gre.s: Critics lamented that the once-dignified art of political debate had become ____, reduced to an exchange of personal insults and slogans crafted for television.

en: Causing one to feel unsettled or uneasy

story: Disconcerting. During her visa interview, Ishita answered every question carefully. The officer said nothing. He simply stared at her file and kept writing for two full minutes without looking up. The silence was disconcerting: it made her feel unsettled and uneasy. A painting whose eyes seem to follow you around the room is disconcerting too. Concert suggests harmony, and dis breaks it: something disconcerting throws you out of tune. Synonyms: unsettling, unnerving, disquieting.
example: The news reports about the rising crime rates were disconcerting.

gre.s: Audiences found the film's abrupt shifts in tone ____: scenes of broad slapstick gave way, without warning, to moments of genuine brutality.
gre.clue: gave way, without warning, to moments of genuine brutality

en: Still in existence
hook: EXTANT: still standing, not EXTINCT.
story: Extant. Thousands of terracotta plaques once covered the walls of the Kantajew temple in Dinajpur. An earthquake in 1897 toppled its towers, and over the years some plaques were stolen. Thankfully, most are still extant: still in existence, surviving today. Historians love this word. Of the more than one hundred plays the Greek writer Sophocles wrote, only seven are extant. Do not confuse it with extinct, its opposite, meaning gone forever. Synonyms: surviving, existing, remaining.
example: There are only a few extant copies of the original manuscript.

gre.s: Although the playwright is known to have written more than forty comedies, only three are ____ today; the rest perished when the theater's archives burned.

en: Natural ease or skill in doing something

His teachers are amazed by his facility with melody: a natural ease and skill in doing something. The word is related to facile and facilitate, all from the Latin for easy. Facility also means a building, like a sports facility, but the GRE prefers the ease sense. Synonyms: aptitude, fluency, knack.
example: The artist had a remarkable facility for painting lifelike portraits.

gre.s: Despite her obvious ____ with languages, which allowed her to pick up conversational Italian in a matter of weeks, she struggled for years with basic arithmetic.

en: Active or occurring in irregular bursts; not steady

A fitful wind gusts and then dies; fitful progress lurches forward, then stalls. Synonyms: intermittent, sporadic, erratic.
example: The storm brought fitful gusts of wind and rain throughout the night.

gre.s: Progress on the bridge has been ____ at best, with long stretches of inactivity interrupted by brief bursts of construction whenever funds arrived.

en: To persuade; to bring about or cause

gre.s: No amount of flattery could ____ the reclusive author to grant an interview; she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years.

en: An inappropriate expression or action; unhappiness
hook: IN-FELICITY: NOT FELICITOUS, not well chosen.

It was an infelicity: an inappropriate expression, a remark badly suited to the moment. Infelicity is literally the lack of felicity, which means both happiness and aptness of expression. example: An infelicity of phrase led to a misunderstanding between the two diplomats.

gre.s: The translation is generally elegant, yet one glaring ____ mars the final chapter: a solemn funeral oration rendered in breezy, comic slang.
gre.clue: a solemn funeral oration rendered in breezy, comic slang

en: Able to be understood
hook: INTELLIGIBLE: your INTELLIGENCE can grasp it.
story: Intelligible. Sabbir's grandfather in Chittagong speaks a dialect so thick that his Dhaka-born grandchildren catch barely half his words. hook: MAKESHIFT: MAKE do in a SHIFT.
story: Makeshift. When the cyclone shelter overflowed, families on the coast of Patuakhali built makeshift tents from old saris, bamboo poles, and plastic sheets. A school bench became a bed; an upturned bucket became a table. Everything was makeshift: serving as a temporary substitute until something better was available. The word comes from the old phrase to make shift, meaning to manage somehow with what you have. Synonyms: improvised, temporary, stopgap.
example: After the storm, the survivors had to build makeshift shelters from fallen branches.

gre.s: Because the hospital had been destroyed by the earthquake, doctors treated patients in a ____ clinic set up in a school gymnasium until a permanent facility could be built.
gre.clue: until a permanent facility could be built

en: Former
hook: ONETIME: ONE TIME in the past.
story: Onetime. At a cricket coaching camp in Khulna, the boys noticed an old man quietly correcting their batting stances. Someone whispered that he was a onetime national team opener, famous back in the nineteen eighties. Onetime means former: what someone used to be. A onetime rival can become a friend; a onetime jute mill can become a shopping centre. Do not confuse it with one-time, meaning happening only once. Synonyms: former, erstwhile, previous.

en: Taking advantage of opportunities without regard to principles
hook: OPPORTUNISTIC: grabs every OPPORTUNITY, ethical or not.
story: Opportunistic. When a rumour of a salt shortage swept through Dhaka, a few traders hid their stock, then sold it at five times the usual price to panicking customers. In medicine, opportunistic infections strike when the immune system is weak. Synonyms: exploitative, unprincipled, expedient.
example: The opportunistic politician changed his stance to align with popular opinion.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the politician's sudden embrace of environmental causes as ____, noting that he had opposed every green initiative until polls showed voters cared about them.

en: Seeming reasonable or probable
hook: PLAUSIBLE: deserves APPLAUSE for sounding right.
story: Plausible. Shuvo arrived at class forty minutes late. His first excuse, that a tiger had blocked the road in Mohammadpur, made everyone laugh. Note that plausible means believable, not necessarily true; a skilled liar tells a plausible story. Opposite: implausible, far-fetched. Synonyms: credible, believable, likely.
example: The detective presented a plausible theory for how the crime had occurred.

en: Behavior intended to impress or mislead

en: Having great power or effect
hook: POTENT: full of POTENTIAL power.
story: Potent. Lamia's grandmother brewed a tea of ginger, black pepper, tulsi leaves, and honey whenever anyone caught a cold. One cup and your eyes watered; two, and the cough seemed to vanish. Opposite: impotent, weak. Synonyms: powerful, forceful, strong.
example: The medicine proved to be a potent remedy for the illness.

gre.s: Though the drug is administered in tiny doses, it is remarkably ____: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse.
gre.clue: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse

en: No longer needed; unnecessary repetition
hook: REDUNDANT: RE-DONE, repeated without need.

Personal, I think, in the end, final, total: all redundant, unnecessary repetition. Redundant also means no longer needed; in Britain, workers made redundant lose their jobs. example: The report was filled with redundant phrases and could have been much shorter.

en: Too important or sacred to be interfered with

story: Sacrosanct. In Kamal's family, Friday lunch is sacrosanct. Nobody schedules meetings, nobody travels, and even his busy surgeon aunt switches off her phone. The word is often used with irony, as when a minister's favourite project is treated as sacrosanct. Synonyms: inviolable, untouchable, sacred.

gre.s: For decades the rule was considered ____, but the new director treated it as merely one tradition among many, open to revision like any other.

en: Showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters
hook: SHREWD: sharp as a SHREW's teeth.
story: Shrewd. Anika's mother runs a small sari shop in Mirpur. When a big chain store opened nearby, she did not panic. She is shrewd: showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters like business. Shrewd once meant wicked; today it means clever and canny. Synonyms: astute, canny, sharp.
example: The shrewd investor made a fortune in the stock market.

gre.s: A ____ investor, she sold her shares months before the crash, having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed as insignificant.

en: Plain; without decoration
hook: UN-ADORNED: not ADORNED.
story: Unadorned. Most buildings along one Gulshan avenue sparkle with glass and gold paint. But one small mosque stands apart: plain white walls, a simple wooden door, no decoration at all. Writing can be unadorned too, simple and direct, like a good news report. Synonyms: plain, austere, unembellished.
example: The writer's style was unadorned and direct, focusing on clarity over flourish.

gre.clue: In contrast to the ornate, metaphor-laden style of his contemporaries

en: Serving as a farewell
hook: VALEDICTORY: say VALE (farewell).
story: Valedictory. On the last day of the academic year, the oldest professor in the department gave one final lecture before retiring. example: The valedictory speech at the graduation ceremony was both touching and inspiring.

gre.s: The retiring minister's ____ speech, delivered on her final day in parliament, graciously thanked even her fiercest opponents for decades of spirited debate.

en: Justified; having good reason
hook: WARRANTED: a WARRANT gives justification.
story: Warranted. When Nadia's landlord raised the rent by fifty percent, she complained to the building committee. A warrant is an official justification, as in a search warrant. The opposite, unwarranted, means without justification, as in unwarranted criticism. Synonyms: justified, legitimate, merited.
example: The police officer felt that a search of the suspect's house was warranted based on the evidence.

gre.clue: Given the company's long record of concealing defects

en: Having a feeling of vague or regretful longing
hook: WISTFUL: WISHFUL with a little sadness.
story: Wistful. Years after moving to Toronto, Imran found an old photograph of his school friends in Barishal, all grinning with muddy knees after a football match in the rain. example: The old photograph filled her with a wistful longing for her childhood.

gre.s: Looking through photographs of the village where she grew up, the elderly novelist grew ____, longing for a world she knew had vanished forever.
gre.clue: longing for a world she knew had vanished forever

en: To regard something as caused by; a quality or feature
hook: ATTRIBUTE: give TRIBUTE (credit) to the cause.
story: Attribute. One summer, Mahin's mango tree suddenly produced twice as much fruit as usual. His father attributed it to the new fertiliser; his mother attributed it to her daily prayers; the neighbour attributed it to pure luck. To attribute is to regard something as caused by a particular source. As a noun, stressed on the first syllable, an attribute is a quality or feature: patience is a fine attribute in a teacher. Synonyms: ascribe, credit, assign.
example: She attributes her success to hard work and a positive attitude.

gre.s: Although the coach was quick to ____ the team's victory to his new training regimen, most observers credited the opposing goalkeeper's uncharacteristic blunders.
gre.clue: most observers credited the opposing goalkeeper's uncharacteristic blunders

en: Causing great disaster or misfortune
hook: CALAMITOUS: a CALAMITY.
story: Calamitous. In November 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck the coast of what is now Bangladesh. In a single night, a wall of seawater swept away entire villages, and hundreds of thousands of people died. Historians call it one of the most calamitous storms ever recorded: causing great disaster and terrible misfortune. A calamity is a disaster; calamitous describes anything that brings one. A calamitous decision can ruin lives or fortunes. Synonyms: disastrous, catastrophic, devastating.
example: The calamitous earthquake left the city in ruins.

gre.s: What began as a minor accounting error proved ____ for the firm: within a year it had lost its largest clients, its reputation, and finally its license to operate.
gre.clue: within a year it had lost its largest clients, its reputation, and finally its license to operate

en: To examine and remove objectionable parts from media
hook: CENSOR: CUTS out what's forbidden. Not censure (criticize).
story: Censor. Under a military government, a newspaper editor had to send his pages to a government office every night. Officers read each article and cut any line that criticised the rulers. Some mornings, the paper appeared with blank white columns. The officers were censoring the news: examining it and removing parts they considered objectionable. A censor is also the person who does this. Do not confuse censor with censure, which means to criticise harshly. Synonyms: suppress, redact, expurgate.
example: The government tried to censor news reports about the scandal.

gre.s: Rather than ____ the novel's explicit passages, as the publisher had demanded, the author withdrew the manuscript entirely, insisting that every word remain intact.
gre.clue: insisting that every word remain intact

en: To publicly support or fight for a cause
hook: GRE trick: to CHAMPION a cause means to fight FOR it.
story: Champion. When the local council planned to fill in an old pond in Mymensingh to build a market, a retired schoolteacher named Rumana refused to stay quiet. She wrote letters to newspapers, organised students, and spoke at every public meeting. Thanks to her, the pond survived. She had championed its cause: publicly supported and fought for it. As a verb, to champion means to defend a cause, not to win a trophy. Synonyms: advocate, espouse, defend.
example: She has been a tireless champion of women's rights.

gre.s: Though she was initially skeptical of renewable energy, the senator went on to ____ it more vigorously than any of her colleagues, sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power.
gre.clue: sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power

en: To make a problem worse
hook: GRE trick: COMPOUND interest grows; a COMPOUNDED problem grows worse.
story: Compound. Zayan dented his father's car in a minor bump. Instead of confessing, he hid the damage and later blamed a rickshaw. When the truth came out a week later, his father was far angrier about the lie than about the dent. Zayan had compounded his mistake: made a bad situation worse. In GRE English, to compound a problem means to add to it, just as compound interest piles interest on top of interest. Synonyms: aggravate, exacerbate, worsen.
example: The heavy rain compounded the traffic problems.

gre.s: The governor's initial delay in ordering an evacuation was a serious error, but her subsequent refusal to admit it served only to ____ the damage to her reputation.
gre.clue: her subsequent refusal to admit it

en: To discourage someone from doing something, usually by fear
hook: DETER: like a TERROR that keeps you away.
story: Deter. A string of burglaries hit the flats on Tanvir's street in Uttara. The building owners installed bright lights, cameras, and a large sign: "This building is watched day and night." The burglaries stopped. The cameras had deterred the thieves: discouraged them, usually through fear of the consequences. A deterrent is something that deters, like a heavy fine for littering. The Latin root means to frighten away, the same root as terror. Synonyms: discourage, dissuade, daunt.
example: The high prices deterred many potential buyers.

gre.s: Lawmakers hoped that steeper fines would ____ drivers from using their phones at the wheel, but accident rates remained unchanged a year later.
gre.clue: hoped that steeper fines would

en: Skillful, especially with the hands
hook: DEXTEROUS: DEXTER is Latin for right hand, the skilled hand.
story: Dexterous. At a roadside stall in Old Dhaka, an old man repairs mobile phones with tools no bigger than toothpicks. His fingers move so quickly that customers lean in to watch: a tiny screw here, a wire soldered there, and the screen glows again. He is dexterous: skillful, especially with the hands. Dexter is Latin for right hand, so dexterity was once right-handed skill. The word can describe a quick mind as well. Synonyms: deft, nimble, adroit.
example: He was a dexterous craftsman, able to create intricate wood carvings.

gre.s: Though his eyesight was failing, the elderly watchmaker remained remarkably ____, able to reassemble a tiny movement of a hundred parts without a single wasted motion.
gre.clue: without a single wasted motion

en: A formal or authoritative statement; a short saying
hook: DICTUM: what is DICTATED, spoken (dictus).
story: Dictum. Every new reporter at a Dhaka newspaper hears the same dictum from the chief editor on the first day: "If your mother says she loves you, check it out." He repeats it at every meeting until it becomes a reflex. A dictum is a formal or authoritative statement, often a short saying that guides practice. It comes from the Latin dicere, to say, as in dictate and dictionary. Courts also issue dicta, their formal remarks. Synonyms: maxim, pronouncement, edict.
example: The judge’s dictum carried the weight of law.

gre.s: The founder's ____ that the customer is always right was treated by her managers as an unquestionable law, though she herself frequently ignored it.
gre.clue: treated by her managers as an unquestionable law

en: Conscientiously fulfilling one's duties
hook: DUTIFUL: full of DUTY.
story: Dutiful. Every morning before work, Rahim walks to his parents' house, buys their medicine, checks their blood pressure, and pays their bills. He has done this for twelve years without a single complaint. Neighbours call him a dutiful son: one who conscientiously fulfils his duties and obligations. Dutiful can also hint at doing something because one must rather than from passion, as in the dutiful applause after a dull speech. Synonyms: conscientious, devoted, obedient.
example: She was a dutiful daughter, always caring for her aging parents.

gre.s: A ____ civil servant, she never missed a deadline in thirty years, though colleagues noted that she seemed to take little pleasure in her work.
gre.clue: never missed a deadline in thirty years

en: Able to understand and share the feelings of others
hook: EMPATHETIC: feeling IN (em) someone else's pain (pathos).
story: Empathetic. When Sara failed her driving test, most friends said, "Never mind, try again." But Ishita sat beside her and said, "I remember how humiliated I felt when I failed mine. It is awful." For the first time that day, Sara felt understood. Ishita was empathetic: able to understand and share the feelings of others. Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy is feeling with them, as if in their place. Synonyms: understanding, compassionate, sensitive.
example: An empathetic therapist can help their clients work through difficult emotions.

gre.s: The best nurses are not only technically skilled but also ____, able to sense a frightened patient's anxiety and respond to it before a word is spoken.
gre.clue: able to sense a frightened patient's anxiety

en: To happen afterward as a result
hook: ENSUE: follows like a SEQUEL.
story: Ensue. At a village wedding, the generator suddenly died in the middle of the feast. Total darkness. Chaos ensued: children shrieked, someone knocked over a pot of borhani, and three uncles shouted instructions at once. To ensue is to happen afterward, as a result. It comes from the Latin for to follow, the same root as sequel and sequence. In the ensuing confusion, someone found a torch, and the meal went on. Synonyms: follow, result, arise.
example: Chaos ensued after the announcement of the controversial policy.

gre.s: When the dam's floodgates were opened without any warning, panic was bound to ____, and thousands of downstream residents fled their homes in the middle of the night.
gre.clue: thousands of downstream residents fled their homes

en: To understand after much thought
hook: FATHOM: measuring deep water — and deep ideas.
story: Fathom. Nadia's grandmother could not fathom why anyone would pay five hundred taka for a cup of coffee in Gulshan. She turned the receipt over twice, as if the explanation might be printed on the back. To fathom is to understand something after much thought, and it is often used with not: I cannot fathom it. A fathom is also a sailor's measure of depth, about six feet, so to fathom a mystery is to sound its depths. Synonyms: comprehend, grasp.
example: I could not fathom the complexities of quantum physics.

gre.s: Even after decades of study, physicists struggle to ____ the strange behavior of particles at the quantum level, which seems to defy every intuition about cause and effect.
gre.clue: which seems to defy every intuition about cause and effect

en: Open, honest, and direct
hook: FRANK: Frank always tells it straight.
story: Frank. When Shuvo asked his mentor to read his first short story, he hoped for praise. Instead she said, "The opening is dull, the dialogue is stiff, and the ending is borrowed. But the third page is brilliant; build from there." It stung, but it helped. She was frank: open, honest, and direct. Frank once meant free, from the Franks, a free people; frank speech is free of disguise. Synonyms: candid, blunt, forthright.
example: She gave her frank opinion on the artwork.

gre.s: Rather than offering the vague reassurances his patients expected, the doctor was always ____, telling them plainly what their prognosis was even when the news was grim.
gre.clue: telling them plainly what their prognosis was

en: Relevant to the subject
hook: GERMANE: GERMAN relatives belong to the family — relevant.
story: Germane. In a seminar on climate policy, a student raised his hand to talk about the price of cricket tickets. The professor smiled politely. "Interesting, but not germane. Let us stay with sea levels." Germane means relevant to the subject at hand. Lawyers object when testimony is not germane to the case. Think of the germ of the matter: something germane sits close to the core. Opposite: irrelevant, extraneous. Synonyms: relevant, pertinent, apposite.
example: Her comments were not germane to the topic at hand.

gre.s: The judge excluded the witness's account of the defendant's childhood, ruling that it was not ____ to the question of whether he had signed the contract.
gre.clue: The judge excluded the witness's account

en: To complain in a bad-tempered, muttering way
hook: GRUMBLE: like a grumbling, rumbling stomach.
story: Grumble. Every morning in the queue for the hostel's single working shower, Rafi grumbles: about the cold water, the broken lock, the student who always takes twenty minutes. He never complains to the provost's office; he just mutters under his breath. To grumble is to complain in a bad-tempered, muttering way. The word even sounds like a rumbling empty stomach. Grumbling is complaint without action. Synonyms: grouse, gripe, mutter.
example: He grumbled about the long wait at the restaurant.

gre.s: Although the workers continued to ____ about the new schedule among themselves, none of them was willing to raise a formal complaint with management.
gre.clue: none of them was willing to raise a formal complaint with management

en: Unwilling to accept new ideas; narrow and conventional
hook: HIDEBOUND: bound tight in an old HIDE (skin).
story: Hidebound. When a young teacher at Joya's school suggested group projects instead of rote memorisation, the old headmaster refused. "We have taught this way for fifty years. Why change now?" He rejected computers and new textbooks too. He was hidebound: narrow-minded and unwilling to accept new ideas. Originally, hidebound described underfed cattle whose skin clung tightly to their bones, too stiff to grow. Opposite: progressive. Synonyms: conservative, rigid, inflexible.
example: The company was criticized for its hidebound attitude towards technology.

gre.s: The institute's ____ administrators rejected every proposal for curricular reform, insisting that methods good enough for their grandparents were good enough for today's students.
gre.clue: insisting that methods good enough for their grandparents were good enough

en: A person who claims beliefs or virtues they don't follow
hook: HYPOCRITE: a Greek actor (hypokrites), playing a role.
story: Hypocrite. Every Friday, a local leader gave fiery speeches against corruption, demanding honesty from every official. Then a newspaper revealed that he had quietly taken bribes for years to approve building permits. People were furious, not only about the bribes but about the speeches. He was a hypocrite: someone who claims beliefs or virtues that he does not actually follow. In ancient Greek, a hypokrites was a stage actor, someone playing a part. Synonyms: pretender, phony, dissembler.
example: He accused the politician being a hypocrite.

gre.s: The minister who lectured citizens about saving electricity was exposed as a ____ when reporters discovered that his own residence ran air conditioners day and night.
gre.clue: his own residence ran air conditioners day and night

en: Unwise; likely to cause trouble or offense
hook: IM-POLITIC: NOT POLITIC, not diplomatic.
story: Impolitic. At a job interview, Kamal was asked why he had left his previous company. He answered honestly: "My boss was a fool, and the owners were thieves." It might have been true, but it was impolitic: unwise, and likely to cause trouble or offence. Impolitic means not politic, not prudent. It differs from impolite, which is merely rude; an impolitic remark is a strategic blunder. Synonyms: imprudent, injudicious, ill-advised.
example: It would be impolitic to criticize our new business partners at this early stage.

gre.s: Though privately he agreed with the protesters, the ambassador judged it ____ to say so publicly, since doing so would surely offend the host government.
gre.clue: since doing so would surely offend the host government

en: Proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects
hook: INSIDIOUS: sneaks INSIDE you quietly.
story: Insidious. High blood pressure is often called the silent killer. Arif's father felt perfectly healthy for years while the pressure was quietly damaging his heart and kidneys. By the time any symptoms appeared, the harm was serious. The disease was insidious: proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects. The Latin root means to lie in wait, as in an ambush. Rumours, too, can spread insidiously. Synonyms: stealthy, subtle, treacherous.
example: The spread of the disease was insidious, often showing no symptoms at first.

gre.s: The danger of the pollutant lies in its ____ nature: it accumulates in the body slowly and without symptoms, causing irreversible harm long before it can be detected.
gre.clue: slowly and without symptoms

en: A person who acts as a link between two parties
hook: INTER-MEDIARY: in the MIDDLE between.
story: Intermediary. When two cousins stopped speaking after a fight over their grandfather's land, the family asked their uncle Mahbub to help. For months he carried messages between them, softened their words, and suggested compromises, until finally they agreed. He acted as an intermediary: a person who acts as a link between two parties. Inter means between, and medius means middle: someone in the middle. Brokers are intermediaries in business. Synonyms: mediator, go-between, broker.
example: The union leader acted as an intermediary in the contract negotiations.

gre.s: Because the two governments had no formal diplomatic relations, they were forced to negotiate through a neutral ____, who relayed each side's proposals to the other.
gre.clue: who relayed each side's proposals to the other

en: Accepting what happens without active response or resistance
hook: PASSIVE: lets everything PASS by without acting.
story: Passive. In group discussions, Tania sits quietly while louder classmates take over. When someone presents her idea as his own, she says nothing. When her group skips its share of the work, she does it all herself, without protest. Tania is passive: accepting what happens without active response or resistance. The word comes from the Latin pati, to suffer or endure, as in patient. Its opposite is active or assertive. Synonyms: submissive, acquiescent, inert.
example: He had a passive attitude towards his studies, never taking initiative.

gre.s: Far from being ____ spectators of the reforms, the village women organized committees, petitioned officials, and ultimately shaped how the new laws were enforced.
gre.clue: the village women organized committees, petitioned officials

en: Good-humored teasing
hook: RAILLERY: friends RALLY around you with jokes.
story: Raillery. Whenever Farhan's friends gather at the tea stall after class, the teasing begins. They mock his giant headphones, his love of old Hindi film songs, and the way he always orders three samosas. Farhan laughs loudest of all and gives it right back. This is raillery: good-humoured teasing among friends. It shares a French root with rail, as in to rail against, but raillery is light and friendly, not bitter. Contrast ridicule, which wounds. Synonyms: banter, ribbing.
example: There was much laughter and raillery at the dinner party.

gre.s: The two old rivals enjoyed a long tradition of affectionate ____, trading gentle jokes about each other's age and failing memory whenever they met.
gre.clue: trading gentle jokes

en: To talk or write at length in a confused, aimless way; to walk aimlessly
hook: RAMBLE: like a RAMBLING road with no destination.
story: Ramble. Asked a simple question about his thesis during his viva, Sabbir began with the history of rice farming, drifted to his grandfather's village, mentioned a cricket match, and returned twenty minutes later without ever answering. His examiners exchanged looks. He was rambling: talking at length in a confused, aimless way. To ramble also means to walk aimlessly, as on a lazy ramble through the countryside. Synonyms: digress, meander, wander.
example: The speaker tended to ramble, making it difficult to follow his presentation.

gre.s: Asked a direct question about the budget, the candidate began to ____, drifting from anecdote to anecdote for ten minutes without ever offering a concrete figure.
gre.clue: drifting from anecdote to anecdote

en: To feel bitterness about unfair treatment
hook: RE-SENT: the insult is SENT back again and again in your mind.
story: Resent. For years, Imran's younger brother got the new clothes, the bigger room, and all the praise, while Imran did the chores. He never said a word, but he resented it deeply: he felt bitter about the unfair treatment. To resent is to feel bitterness or indignation at being treated unfairly. Resentment can simmer quietly for decades. Re means again, and sent comes from the Latin for feel: feeling a hurt again and again. Synonyms: begrudge, grudge.
example: She resented having to do all the housework while her brother did nothing.

gre.s: Veteran staff members tended to ____ the newcomers' rapid promotions, which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit.
gre.clue: which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit

en: Remaining after most has gone
hook: RESIDUAL: the RESIDUE left behind.
story: Residual. After the floodwaters finally drained from Mitu's village, a thin layer of mud remained on every floor, and a faint smell lingered for weeks. That leftover mud was residual: remaining after most of something has gone. A residue is what remains. Even after an apology, there can be residual anger, a little bitterness that has not quite left. Residual income keeps arriving after the work is done. Synonyms: remaining, lingering, leftover.
example: There was some residual bitterness after the argument.

gre.s: Although the fever subsided within a week, the patient suffered from ____ fatigue that persisted for months after the infection itself had cleared.
gre.clue: after the infection itself had cleared

en: Firm determination; to decide firmly or settle
hook: RESOLVE: a RESOLUTION you stick to.
story: Resolve. After Tanvir failed the bar council exam twice, his friends told him to give up. Instead, he moved into a tiny room near the library, studied ten hours a day, and turned down every wedding invitation for a year. His resolve never weakened: his firm determination. He passed with distinction. As a verb, to resolve means to decide firmly, or to settle a problem, as in resolving a dispute. Synonyms: determination, tenacity, grit.
example: She made a New Year's resolve to exercise more regularly.

gre.s: Repeated setbacks only strengthened the climbers' ____: after each failed attempt on the summit, they returned the following season eager to try again.
gre.clue: eager to try again

en: A substitute, especially a person acting in another's place
hook: SURROGATE: a SUBSTITUTE who stands in.
story: Surrogate. When Lamia's parents moved abroad for work, her aunt in Rajshahi raised her. She packed her lunch, attended parent meetings, and sat up with her through every fever. For ten years, her aunt was a surrogate mother: a substitute, someone acting in another's place. In medicine, a surrogate mother carries a baby for others. The word comes from the Latin for to elect in place of another. Synonyms: substitute, proxy, stand-in.
example: The vice president acted as a surrogate for the president while he was ill.

gre.s: Unable to attend the ceremony himself, the ailing laureate sent his daughter as a ____ to accept the award and read the speech he had written.
gre.clue: Unable to attend the ceremony himself

en: To speak or write about in an abusively disparaging manner
hook: VILIFY: make someone a VILLAIN.
story: Vilify. After a young journalist exposed a tax scandal, a group of powerful businessmen launched a campaign against her. Posters called her a traitor; anonymous accounts spread lies about her family. They vilified her: spoke and wrote about her in a viciously insulting way, trying to turn the public against her. Vilify contains vile: to make someone seem vile. It is far stronger than criticise. Opposite: praise, extol. Synonyms: malign, defame, revile.
example: The rival politicians vilified each other in the press.

gre.s: Rival newspapers chose to ____ the reformer, branding her a traitor and inventing scandals, even though her proposals were modest and widely popular.
gre.clue: branding her a traitor and inventing scandals

en: Lacking; not good enough
hook: GRE trick: FOUND WANTING means found lacking, not desiring.
story: Wanting. Rafi's first research paper had good data, but his professor returned it with a single comment: "The analysis is wanting." Rafi was puzzled at first. Then he understood: wanting here means lacking, not good enough. When something is weighed and found wanting, it falls short of a standard. In older English, want meant lack, as in the proverb: for want of a nail, the shoe was lost. Synonyms: deficient, lacking, inadequate.
example: The report was found wanting in factual evidence.

gre.s: The proposal was praised for its ambition, but on close examination its financial projections were found ____, resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept.
gre.clue: resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept

en: Intentional; stubbornly determined to do as one wants
hook: WILL-FUL: full of your own WILL.
story: Willful. Rumana's three-year-old nephew refused to wear shoes to the wedding. Shoes were offered, then sandals, then a bribe of chocolate. He sat on the floor and screamed, determined to go barefoot no matter what. He was willful: stubbornly determined to do as he wants. Willful also means intentional, as in willful damage, done on purpose rather than by accident. In British English it is spelled wilful. Synonyms: headstrong, obstinate, deliberate.
example: Her willful defiance of the rules led to her suspension.

gre.s: The court ruled that the company's failure to report the leak was not an innocent oversight but a ____ deception, carried out with full knowledge of the risks.
gre.clue: not an innocent oversight

en: Complaining in a whining or irritable way
hook: QUERULOUS: always QUERYING and complaining.
story: Querulous. Chowdhury Saheb in flat 4B complains about everything. The lift is too slow, the guard too sleepy, the neighbours' children too loud, and the mangoes at the market too sour. Even on a perfect spring morning, he finds something to whine about in a thin, irritable voice. He is querulous: complaining in a whining, peevish way. The word comes from the Latin queri, to complain, the same root as quarrel. Synonyms: peevish, petulant, cantankerous.
example: The querulous customer, peevish about the long wait time, demanded to speak to the manager.

gre.s: Age had made the once-genial professor ____: he now found fault with every seminar, every meal, and every student, and his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints.
gre.clue: his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints

en: Not genuine; fake; a person who pretends
hook: PHONY: like a fake PHONE call from a 'bank'.
story: Phony. A man in a crisp white coat set up a stall at the Gabtoli bus terminal, selling a bottle of oil he promised would cure diabetes, baldness, and heartbreak. He called himself a doctor and displayed framed certificates. A curious student searched his name online: no such doctor existed. The certificates were phony: fake, not genuine. As a noun, a phony is a person who pretends. In The Catcher in the Rye, Holden calls almost everyone a phony. Synonyms: fake, sham, fraudulent.
example: The art dealer was arrested for selling fraudulent paintings he claimed were originals, discovering his collection was filled with spurious and counterfeit works.

gre.s: Investigators discovered that the charity was ____: the orphanage featured in its glossy brochures did not exist, and the donations had gone straight into the founder's bank account.
gre.clue: the orphanage featured in its glossy brochures did not exist
